    Define as a generalised expectancy (Rotter, 1966). Internal: outcomes depend on one's own behaviour. External: outcomes depend on luck, fate or powerful others. Mention the I–E scale (29 items, forced choice), that it is a continuum, and an example of each. End with Rotter's caution that neither end is always healthy.

    Write a short note on the Rep Test. 5 marks

    Kelly's Role Construct Repertory Test. Client lists role figures; examiner presents triads; client says how two are alike and differ from the third, which yields a bipolar construct. Repeated triads build a grid showing the client's main constructs. It is used to understand how the client sees the world before therapy.

    Psychopathology · Unit I

    Introduction to Psychopathology

    What is psychopathology?

    Psychopathology (Greek psyche mind + pathos suffering + logos study) is the scientific study of mental disorders: their features, causes, course and treatment. The same field is also called abnormal psychology.

    Four ways of seeing "normal" (Offer & Sabshin, 1966)

    Normality as health

    Normal = no signs of disease. Medical view.

    Normality as utopia

    Normal = the ideal, harmonious functioning (Freud, Maslow's self-actualisation).

    Normality as average

    Normal = most people. Statistical view, based on the bell curve.

    Normality as transactional process

    Normal = healthy change and adaptation over time and context.

    Normal and abnormal are not two boxes. They lie on a continuum: everyone has some worries, sadness or odd habits.

    Criteria of abnormality: the 5 Ds

    CriterionMeaningLimitation
    Statistical infrequencyRare behaviour is abnormalGenius is rare too; common problems like depression are still disorders
    Deviation from social normsBreaks cultural rulesNorms differ by culture and change with time (homosexuality was removed from DSM in 1973)
    Personal distressThe person suffersSome disorders (mania, psychopathy) cause no distress; some distress is normal
    Maladaptiveness / dysfunctionInterferes with daily life and goalsHard to judge; some harmful habits are legal and common
    DangerThreat to self or othersMost people with mental illness are not violent
    Remember5 Ds: Deviance, Distress, Dysfunction, Danger, Duration. Rosenhan & Seligman (1989) added others: irrationality, unpredictability, vividness, observer discomfort and violation of moral standards.
    Key study · Rosenhan, 1973

    "On being sane in insane places"

    Eight sane people (pseudo-patients) told 12 hospitals they heard voices saying "empty", "hollow", "thud". All were admitted, 7 of 8 were diagnosed with schizophrenia, and then they acted normally. Staff never detected them (although many real patients did), and normal behaviour such as note-taking was read as "writing behaviour". It showed the power of labels and the unreliability of diagnosis. Critics (Spitzer) argued the method was flawed.

    Signs and symptoms

    Symptom

    What the patient reports (subjective): "I feel hopeless", "I hear voices".

    Sign

    What the clinician observes (objective): slow speech, tearfulness, restlessness.

    Syndrome

    A group of signs and symptoms that occur together.

    Disorder

    A syndrome with a pattern, course, and impairment; diagnosed by criteria.

    Main areas of disturbance

    AreaAbnormal signs and symptomsMeaning
    PerceptionIllusion; hallucinationMisreading a real stimulus (rope seen as a snake); perceiving something with no stimulus (hearing voices)
    Thought: contentDelusion; obsession; phobiaFalse, fixed belief despite proof ("I am being poisoned"); intrusive unwanted thought; irrational fear
    Thought: form (speech)Loosening of association; word salad; flight of ideas; thought blocking; neologismIllogical shifts; jumbled words; racing ideas; sudden stop; invented words
    Mood and affectDepressed mood; elation; irritability; flat or blunted affect; labile affect; incongruent affectMood = sustained feeling; affect = outward expression at the moment
    Psychomotor activityAgitation; retardation; stupor; catatonia; stereotypyToo fast, too slow, motionless, odd postures, repeated movements
    CognitionDisorientation; memory loss; poor attentionNot knowing time, place, person
    Insight and judgementLack of insightNot aware one is ill; poor decisions
    RememberMental Status Examination = ASEPTIC: Appearance and behaviour, Speech, Emotion (mood, affect), Perception, Thought, Insight and judgement, Cognition.

    Illusion vs hallucination: an illusion has a real stimulus that is misperceived; a hallucination has none. Common in everyone at times; abnormal when persistent and not understood as unreal.

    Why classify disorders?

    • Common language for clinicians
    • Guides diagnosis and treatment choice
    • Allows research and health statistics
    • Helps predict course and outcome

    Criticisms: labels can stigmatise; categories hide a continuum; reliability and validity problems; Western bias; "medicalising" normal distress.

    History

    1896Kraepelin

    First scientific classification: dementia praecox vs manic-depressive illness.

    1948ICD-6

    WHO's ICD first includes a section on mental disorders.

    1952DSM-I

    American Psychiatric Association's first manual; 106 disorders.

    1968DSM-II

    Based on psychodynamic ideas; vague descriptions.

    1980DSM-III

    Landmark: explicit diagnostic criteria; multiaxial system; atheoretical.

    1992ICD-10

    Chapter F (F00–F99) on mental and behavioural disorders; still widely used in India.

    1994 / 2000DSM-IV / IV-TR

    Five axes; about 300 disorders.

    2013DSM-5

    Dropped the axes; added dimensional ratings; new chapters.

    2022ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR

    ICD-11 came into effect on 1 January 2022; DSM-5-TR is a text revision.

    Comparison of ICD and DSM

    PointICDDSM
    Full nameInternational Classification of DiseasesDiagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders
    PublisherWorld Health Organization (WHO)American Psychiatric Association (APA)
    ScopeAll diseases; mental disorders are one chapterMental disorders only
    UseWorldwide; official in IndiaMainly USA; research and teaching everywhere
    LatestICD-11 (2022); ICD-10 still usedDSM-5-TR (2022)
    StyleClinical descriptions and guidelines; shorterDetailed checklists with exact cut-offs
    CodesF00–F99 (ICD-10)ICD-10-CM codes
    CostFree accessPaid manual
    Cultural focusGlobal; fewer culture-specific labelsIncludes a cultural formulation interview

    DSM-5 groups disorders in chapters such as neurodevelopmental, schizophrenia spectrum, bipolar, depressive, anxiety, OCD-related, trauma- and stressor-related, dissociative, somatic symptom and neurocognitive disorders.

    Case history

    A case history is a detailed, organised account of a person's problem and life, collected from the client and informants (family, teachers, records). It gives a base for diagnosis and a treatment plan.

    1Identifying data

    Name, age, sex, education, occupation, marital status, religion, informant and reliability.

    2Chief complaints

    Main problems in the patient's and family's own words, with duration.

    3History of present illness

    Onset, course, triggers, what has helped or worsened it, effect on functioning.

    4Past history

    Earlier psychiatric, medical, surgical illness; head injury; substance use.

    5Family history

    Mental illness, suicide, substance use; family structure and relationships (genogram).

    6Personal history

    Birth and development, childhood, education, work, marriage, sexual history, habits.

    7Premorbid personality

    Temperament and habits before the illness: social relations, interests, mood, coping.

    8Mental status examination

    Current state (ASEPTIC) and behavioural observations.

    9Tests, formulation, diagnosis

    Psychological tests, working diagnosis, causes (predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating) and plan.

    Good practice: build rapport, use open questions, be non-judgemental, protect confidentiality, record facts separately from impressions, and verify with a second informant.

    Unit I self-test

    Define psychopathology.

    The scientific study of mental disorders: features, causes, course and treatment.

    The 5 Ds of abnormality?

    Deviance, distress, dysfunction, danger, duration.

    What did Rosenhan (1973) show?

    Sane pseudo-patients were admitted and diagnosed with schizophrenia; staff did not detect them. It showed the power of labels and weak diagnostic reliability.

    Sign vs symptom?

    Symptom is reported by the patient; sign is observed by the clinician.

    Illusion vs hallucination?

    Illusion misreads a real stimulus; hallucination has no stimulus.

    Which edition of DSM introduced explicit criteria?

    DSM-III (1980).

    Who publishes ICD and DSM?

    ICD: World Health Organization. DSM: American Psychiatric Association.

    What does ASEPTIC stand for?

    Appearance, Speech, Emotion, Perception, Thought, Insight/judgement, Cognition.

    2. Five Ds (draw) with limitations (table).
    3. Rosenhan study; continuum idea.

    2. History timeline.
    3. Comparison table; criticisms.

    Psychopathology · Unit II

    Approaches to Psychopathology

    Biological (medical) approach

    Mental disorders are illnesses of the brain and body, caused by genes, brain chemistry, brain structure or infection.

    Genetics

    Studied by family, twin and adoption studies. Higher concordance in identical (MZ) than fraternal (DZ) twins suggests genes matter. Genes give vulnerability, not certainty.

    Neurotransmitters

    Imbalances in brain chemicals (table below).

    Brain structure and function

    Enlarged ventricles in schizophrenia; amygdala overactivity in anxiety; frontal lobe changes; neuroimaging (MRI, PET).

    Endocrine system

    Over-active stress axis (HPA) and raised cortisol in depression.

    Infection and prenatal factors

    Maternal flu in pregnancy, birth complications, brain infections.

    NeurotransmitterLinked disordersDrug evidence
    DopamineSchizophrenia (too much); Parkinson's (too little)Antipsychotics block dopamine receptors
    SerotoninDepression, OCD, anxietySSRIs raise serotonin
    NorepinephrineDepression, anxiety, panicSNRIs, tricyclics
    GABAAnxiety (too little calming)Benzodiazepines boost GABA
    GlutamateSchizophreniaPCP and ketamine mimic symptoms
    AcetylcholineAlzheimer's diseaseCholinesterase inhibitors

    Treatments and evaluation

    Treatments

    Psychotropic drugs (antipsychotic, antidepressant, antianxiety, mood stabiliser), electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), brain stimulation (TMS), rarely psychosurgery.

    Evaluation
    • + Strong evidence for genes and drugs
    • + Reduced stigma ("it is an illness")
    • − Correlation is not cause: are brain changes cause or effect?
    • − Ignores life experience; drug side effects

    Psychodynamic approach

    Disorders arise from unconscious conflicts between the id, ego and superego, rooted in early childhood (Freud).

    Anxiety and defence

    The ego is threatened by id impulses or superego guilt. Anxiety is controlled with defence mechanisms (repression, displacement, regression, reaction formation).

    Fixation

    Trauma or over-gratification at a psychosexual stage leaves a weak point (oral → depression; anal → obsessive traits).

    Symptoms are symbolic

    Symptoms express hidden conflict. Anna O's paralysis and cough were linked to buried memories (Breuer and Freud).

    Neurosis vs psychosis

    Neurosis: ego manages conflict but with anxiety and symptoms. Psychosis: ego breaks down, contact with reality is lost.

    Depression: Mourning and Melancholia (1917)

    Loss of a loved one stirs anger; the anger is turned inward as self-blame.

    Later developments

    Object relations (Klein), attachment and early loss (Bowlby), Erikson's identity crises.

    Treatment: psychoanalysis: free association, dream interpretation, transference, interpretation of resistance. Evaluation: + highlights the role of early experience and unconscious defences; − hard to test scientifically, and based on a small clinical sample.

    Behavioural approach

    Abnormal behaviour is learned in the same way as normal behaviour. Focus is on observable behaviour, not hidden causes.

    Classical conditioning

    Fear learned by pairing. Little Albert (Watson & Rayner, 1920) learned to fear a rat paired with a loud noise.

    Operant conditioning

    Behaviour shaped by consequences. A child who gets attention for tantrums repeats them. Lewinsohn: depression follows loss of positive reinforcement.

    Social learning

    Learning by observation. Mineka (1984): lab monkeys developed snake fear by watching a parent fear snakes.

    Treatment: systematic desensitisation (Wolpe), exposure, flooding, aversion therapy, token economy, modelling. Evaluation: + testable, effective for phobias and habits; − ignores thinking and biology; not all phobics recall a conditioning event.

    Cognitive approach

    Disorders come from faulty thinking: negative beliefs, biased interpretations and irrational assumptions.

    Aaron Beck (1921–2021)Founder of cognitive therapy for depression. Theory of the cognitive triad and cognitive distortions.Photo: public domain (1942 yearbook), Wikimedia Commons
    Cognitive distortions (Beck)
    • Arbitrary inference: conclusion without evidence
    • Selective abstraction: focus on one negative detail
    • Overgeneralisation: "I failed once, so I always fail"
    • Magnification / minimisation
    • Personalisation: blaming oneself for outside events
    • Dichotomous (all-or-none) thinking
    Ellis: ABC model (REBT)

    Activating event → Belief (irrational: "I must be perfect") → Consequence (distress). It is the belief, not the event, that causes distress.

    Learned helplessness and attributions

    Seligman: uncontrollable events lead to passivity. Depressed people blame internal, stable, global causes for failure (Abramson).

    Treatment: cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT), REBT: challenge and replace distorted thoughts. Evaluation: + strong evidence, practical; − does not explain why the thoughts arise; may blame the patient.

    Socio-cultural approach

    Disorders are shaped by society, family and culture: poverty, social roles, relationships and labels.

    Social causation

    Poverty, low class, unemployment and discrimination raise risk. Hollingshead & Redlich (1958): serious disorders were most common in the lowest social class.

    Family

    High expressed emotion (criticism, hostility, over-involvement) predicts relapse in schizophrenia. Family systems theory: the "patient" shows the family's problem.

    Life events and support

    Loss, divorce, migration. Social support buffers stress.

    Labelling theory

    Scheff: being labelled "mentally ill" produces a self-fulfilling role. Rosenhan's study supports this.

    Culture

    What is abnormal depends on culture. Some disorders are culture-bound (below).

    Stigma

    Discrimination keeps people from seeking help, causing the large treatment gap in India.

    Culture-bound syndromeWhereDescription
    Dhat syndromeIndia, South AsiaAnxiety and weakness blamed on semen loss in urine or night emissions
    KoroSouth-East Asia, ChinaFear that the genitals are shrinking and will disappear, with risk of death
    AmokMalaysiaSudden violent outburst after brooding, then amnesia
    Taijin kyofushoJapanFear of offending or embarrassing others by one's body or behaviour
    Ataque de nerviosLatin AmericaShouting, trembling, crying after a stressful event

    Treatment: family therapy, community mental health, social skills training, social support, reducing stigma. Evaluation: + widens focus to context; − hard to separate social from biological causes.

    Comparing the five approaches

    ApproachCause of disorderKey namesTreatment
    BiologicalGenes, brain chemistry, structureKraepelin, KallmannDrugs, ECT
    PsychodynamicUnconscious conflict, early childhoodFreud, Klein, BowlbyPsychoanalysis
    BehaviouralFaulty learningWatson, Skinner, Wolpe, MowrerExposure, conditioning
    CognitiveDistorted thinkingBeck, Ellis, SeligmanCBT, REBT
    Socio-culturalSociety, family, cultureScheff, Rosenhan, HollingsheadFamily and community work

    The integrated view: diathesis–stress and biopsychosocial

    Diathesis–stress model (Meehl; Zubin & Spring): disorder appears when a vulnerability (diathesis: genes, early adversity) meets enough stress. The biopsychosocial model (Engel, 1977) adds that biological, psychological and social factors all interact.

    Unit II self-test

    Which neurotransmitter is too active in schizophrenia?

    Dopamine.

    What are the three studies used to test genetics?

    Family, twin and adoption studies.

    What did Freud say about depression?

    After a loss, anger is turned inward as self-blame (Mourning and Melancholia).

    Mowrer's two-factor theory?

    Fear is learned by classical conditioning and kept alive by avoidance, which is negatively reinforced.

    Beck's cognitive triad?

    Negative views of self, world and future.

    Ellis's ABC?

    Activating event, Belief, Consequence.

    What is expressed emotion?

    Criticism, hostility and over-involvement by family, predicting relapse in schizophrenia.

    One culture-bound syndrome of India?

    Dhat syndrome.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the biological and psychodynamic approaches to psychopathology. 10 marks
    1. Biological: genes, neurotransmitters (table), brain, treatment, evaluation.
    2. Psychodynamic: conflict, defences, fixation, treatment, evaluation.
    Discuss the behavioural and cognitive approaches. 10 marks
    1. Conditioning, social learning; Mowrer (draw).
    2. Beck's triad (draw), distortions; Ellis; learned helplessness.
    3. Treatments and evaluation.
    Explain the socio-cultural approach and the diathesis-stress model. 10 marks
    1. Social causation, family, labelling, culture-bound syndromes.
    2. Diathesis-stress graph; biopsychosocial model.
    Psychopathology · Unit III

    Anxiety, OCD, Trauma, Dissociative and Somatoform Disorders

    Anxiety and its disorders

    Fear

    Response to a real, present threat. Short-lived and useful.

    Anxiety

    Worry about a future or unclear threat. Becomes a disorder when excessive, long-lasting and impairing.

    These disorders were once all called "neuroses" (Freud). ICD-10 groups them as neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders (F40–F48).

    Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)

    Clinical features (DSM-5)
    • Excessive worry about many things (health, money, family, work), more days than not for at least 6 months
    • Hard to control the worry
    • At least 3 of 6: restlessness, easily tired, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep problems
    • "Free-floating" anxiety; autonomic signs in ICD-10
    Aetiology
    • Biological: low GABA, serotonin and noradrenaline; overactive amygdala; moderate heritability
    • Cognitive: intolerance of uncertainty; worry as a way to avoid vivid fear (Borkovec); threat bias
    • Psychodynamic: unresolved unconscious conflict
    • Learning and environment: anxious parents, chronic stress

    Treatment: CBT, relaxation, SSRIs/SNRIs, buspirone; benzodiazepines only short term. Twice as common in women.

    Panic disorder

    Clinical features
    • Recurrent unexpected panic attacks: sudden surge of terror peaking within minutes
    • 4 or more of 13 symptoms: palpitations, sweating, trembling, breathlessness, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills, numbness, derealisation, fear of losing control, fear of dying
    • At least 1 month of worry about further attacks or changed behaviour
    • Often with agoraphobia
    Aetiology
    • Cognitive (Clark, 1986): catastrophic misinterpretation of normal body sensations
    • Biological: over-sensitive brain alarm (locus coeruleus, amygdala); CO2 sensitivity (Klein's false suffocation alarm)
    • Conditioning: body sensations become cues for panic (interoceptive)
    • Anxiety sensitivity; genes

    Treatment: CBT with interoceptive exposure (deliberately causing the sensations), breathing training, SSRIs.

    Phobias

    A phobia is an intense, irrational fear of an object or situation, out of proportion to the danger, causing avoidance and lasting at least 6 months.

    TypeFear ofExamples
    Specific phobiaA particular object or situationAnimals (zoophobia), heights (acrophobia), blood–injury, enclosed spaces (claustrophobia), flying, storms
    Social anxiety disorder (social phobia)Being judged or embarrassed in social situationsPublic speaking, eating in public, meeting strangers
    AgoraphobiaSituations where escape or help may be hardCrowds, public transport, queues, open spaces (fear of 2 or more)

    Aetiology

    Classical conditioning

    Little Albert (Watson & Rayner, 1920).

    Observational learning

    Mineka's monkeys; children copy parents' fears.

    Preparedness (Seligman, 1971)

    We are biologically ready to fear snakes, spiders, heights, which were once dangerous.

    Rachman's 3 pathways

    Direct experience, vicarious learning, information and instruction.

    Psychodynamic

    Little Hans (Freud, 1909): fear of horses was a displaced fear of his father.

    Temperament

    Behavioural inhibition in infancy (Kagan) predicts social anxiety; genes.

    Treatment: systematic desensitisation (Wolpe: relaxation + fear hierarchy), flooding, graded exposure, modelling, CBT; SSRIs for social anxiety.

    Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)

    Obsessions

    Recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges or images that cause anxiety; the person tries to ignore or neutralise them.

    "My hands are contaminated"; "I may have hurt someone"; forbidden sexual or religious thoughts.

    Compulsions

    Repetitive behaviours or mental acts done to reduce anxiety or prevent a feared event, according to rigid rules. Excessive and not realistically connected to the fear.

    Washing, checking locks, counting, ordering, praying, repeating words.

    • Takes more than 1 hour a day or causes impairment; the person usually has some insight ("this is silly") but cannot stop
    • Common themes: contamination, checking, symmetry, taboo thoughts. In DSM-5 OCD has its own chapter (with hoarding, body dysmorphic disorder, trichotillomania)
    Aetiology
    • Biological: low serotonin; overactive loop between orbitofrontal cortex, caudate nucleus and thalamus; genes (twin heritability roughly 40–50%)
    • Behavioural: Mowrer's two-factor; compulsions are negatively reinforced
    • Cognitive: thought-action fusion ("thinking it is as bad as doing it"), inflated responsibility (Salkovskis), thought suppression backfires
    • Psychodynamic: anal stage fixation; undoing, isolation, reaction formation
    Treatment
    • Exposure and response prevention (ERP): face the trigger, do not perform the ritual (Meyer, 1966). First-line therapy
    • SSRIs (fluoxetine) or clomipramine
    • Deep brain stimulation in severe resistant cases

    Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)

    A disorder after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence: directly, by witnessing, by learning it happened to a close person, or by repeated exposure (first responders).

    1 · Intrusion

    Unwanted memories, nightmares, flashbacks, intense distress at reminders.

    2 · Avoidance

    Avoiding thoughts, places, people linked to the trauma.

    3 · Negative mood and thoughts

    Guilt, shame, numbness, detachment, memory gaps, loss of interest.

    4 · Arousal and reactivity

    Hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, irritability, poor sleep and concentration.

    • Symptoms last more than 1 month. Acute stress disorder lasts 3 days to 1 month
    • ICD-11 adds complex PTSD (after prolonged trauma such as abuse): PTSD symptoms plus problems with emotions, self-image and relationships
    • Examples in India: Bhopal gas tragedy (1984), Gujarat earthquake (2001), the 2004 tsunami, riots and violence
    Aetiology
    • Risk factors: severity of trauma, interpersonal trauma (assault), prior trauma, female sex, low social support, earlier anxiety
    • Conditioning: trauma cues become fear triggers; avoidance maintains them
    • Cognitive (Ehlers & Clark; Foa): trauma memory is poorly integrated; beliefs that the world is dangerous
    • Biological: overactive amygdala, smaller hippocampus, weaker prefrontal control, altered cortisol
    Treatment
    • Trauma-focused CBT: prolonged exposure (Foa), cognitive processing therapy
    • EMDR (Shapiro, 1987)
    • SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine)
    • Psychological first aid soon after; compulsory debriefing is not advised

    Dissociative disorders

    Dissociation is a disruption in the normal integration of consciousness, memory, identity or perception. It is usually a way of escaping from overwhelming stress.

    Dissociative amnesia

    Inability to recall important personal information, usually of a traumatic or stressful event, too much for normal forgetting. Can be localised, selective or generalised. With dissociative fugue: sudden travel away from home with loss of identity.

    Dissociative identity disorder (DID)

    Two or more distinct personality states ("alters") that take control, with gaps in memory for everyday events. Strongly linked to severe childhood abuse.

    Depersonalisation / derealisation disorder

    Persistent feeling of being detached from oneself ("watching from outside") or the world as unreal. Reality testing is intact.

    Aetiology
    • Trauma and abuse, especially in childhood: dissociation as escape
    • Janet: failure to integrate memories; Freud: repression
    • Suggestibility, fantasy proneness; sociocognitive view: alters may be shaped by therapy and media
    • State-dependent learning of memories
    Treatment and notes
    • Long-term psychotherapy aiming to integrate identities; hypnosis; treating comorbid depression and anxiety
    • Famous cases: The Three Faces of Eve (Thigpen & Cleckley, 1957) and Sybil (1973), both later questioned
    • ICD-10 (F44) includes trance and possession disorders, important in Indian settings

    Somatoform disorders

    Physical symptoms that suggest a medical condition but have no adequate medical explanation, and are linked to psychological factors. The symptoms are not faked.

    Disorder (ICD-10)Main featureDSM-5 equivalent
    Somatisation disorderMany recurrent, changing physical complaints (pain, stomach, sexual, neurological) over at least 2 yearsSomatic symptom disorder
    Hypochondriacal disorderPersistent belief of having a serious disease, despite reassuranceIllness anxiety disorder
    Persistent somatoform pain disorderSevere pain not fully explained medicallySomatic symptom disorder with pain
    Conversion disorder (ICD-10 F44, dissociative)Loss or change of voluntary motor or sensory function: paralysis, blindness, loss of voice, psychogenic seizuresConversion (functional neurological symptom) disorder
    Body dysmorphic disorderPreoccupation with an imagined flaw in appearanceOCD and related disorders
    Conversion: key points
    • Symptoms do not fit anatomy (e.g. "glove" numbness)
    • La belle indifférence: calm unconcern (not reliable)
    • Primary gain: anxiety reduced; secondary gain: attention, escaping duties
    • History: hysteria; Charcot, Janet, and Anna O (Breuer and Freud)
    Aetiology
    • Psychodynamic: repressed conflict "converted" into a body symptom
    • Learning: the sick role is rewarded
    • Cognitive: amplifying and misreading body sensations (Barsky); alexithymia
    • Socio-cultural: in cultures where emotional distress is stigmatised, people present "body aches", "burning", "weakness"
    • Childhood illness or abuse; genes
    PointSomatoform / conversionMalingeringFactitious disorder
    Symptoms producedNot consciouslyConsciouslyConsciously
    MotiveUnconscious conflictExternal gain (money, avoid duty)To assume the sick role

    Treatment: a trusting relationship with one doctor, reassurance, avoiding unnecessary tests, CBT, graded activity, physiotherapy for functional neurological symptoms, SSRIs for depression or anxiety.

    Unit III self-test

    Minimum duration for GAD (DSM-5)?

    6 months of excessive worry.

    How many symptoms define a panic attack?

    4 or more of 13.

    Clark's cognitive explanation of panic?

    Catastrophic misinterpretation of normal body sensations.

    Preparedness (Seligman)?

    Biological readiness to learn fears of ancient dangers such as snakes and heights.

    First-line therapy for OCD?

    Exposure and response prevention (ERP), with or without an SSRI.

    How long must PTSD symptoms last?

    More than 1 month (acute stress disorder: 3 days to 1 month).

    What is dissociative fugue?

    Sudden travel away from home with amnesia for identity, as part of dissociative amnesia.

    Primary vs secondary gain?

    Primary gain: anxiety is reduced by the symptom. Secondary gain: external benefits such as attention.

    Long-answer outlines

    Describe the clinical features and aetiology of GAD and panic disorder. 10 marks
    1. Fear vs anxiety.
    2. GAD: features, causes, treatment.
    3. Panic: features, panic cycle (draw), causes, treatment.
    Explain phobias and OCD. 10 marks
    1. Phobia types (table), causes, systematic desensitisation.
    2. OCD: obsessions and compulsions, cycle (draw), causes, ERP.
    Discuss PTSD, dissociative and somatoform disorders. 10 marks
    1. PTSD: four symptom clusters, causes, treatment.
    2. Dissociative: amnesia, DID, depersonalisation.
    3. Somatoform and conversion; comparison with malingering.
    Psychopathology · Unit IV

    Schizophrenia, Mood and Delusional Disorders

    Emil Kraepelin (1856–1926)German psychiatrist. In 1896 he named the illness dementia praecox (early dementia) and separated it from manic-depressive illness.Photo: public domain, Wikimedia Commons
    Eugen Bleuler (1857–1939)Swiss psychiatrist. In 1911 he renamed it schizophrenia ("split mind"), meaning a split between thought, emotion and behaviour. It is not multiple personality.Photo: public domain, Wikimedia Commons

    Schizophrenia

    A severe psychotic disorder with disturbed thought, perception, emotion and behaviour, and loss of contact with reality. About 1% of people develop it, usually between the late teens and early 30s (earlier in men).

    DSM-5 criteria
    • At least 2 of 5 symptoms for a significant part of one month: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, disorganised/catatonic behaviour, negative symptoms
    • At least one must be delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech
    • Continuous signs for at least 6 months (including prodromal and residual phases)
    • Decline in work, relationships or self-care
    Course and types
    • Phases: prodromal (withdrawal, odd behaviour) → active (psychosis) → residual
    • ICD-10 subtypes: paranoid (most common), hebephrenic (disorganised), catatonic, undifferentiated, residual, simple
    • DSM-5 dropped subtypes and rates severity on a dimension
    • First-rank symptoms (Schneider): hearing voices comment on you, thought insertion or withdrawal, passivity, delusional perception
    RememberBleuler's "4 A's": Associations loosened, Affect flattened, Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal into inner world).

    Causes of schizophrenia

    Genetic risk (Gottesman, 1991)

    Dopamine hypothesis

    Over-activity of dopamine (D2) in the mesolimbic pathway causes positive symptoms. Evidence: antipsychotics block D2; amphetamines can cause psychosis. Glutamate (NMDA) is also involved: ketamine and PCP mimic symptoms.

    Brain differences

    Enlarged ventricles, reduced frontal and temporal grey matter, low prefrontal activity ("hypofrontality").

    Neurodevelopmental view

    Prenatal infection or malnutrition, birth complications, winter or urban birth, adolescent cannabis use, then a brain "second hit" at puberty.

    Psychological and social
    • Expressed emotion in family predicts relapse (Brown, Leff)
    • Double bind (Bateson, 1956) and the "schizophrenogenic mother": discredited
    • Stressful life events, migration, social isolation

    Diathesis–stress model (Meehl; Zubin & Spring) is the accepted explanation: inherited vulnerability + stress → illness.

    Treatment

    Antipsychotic drugs
    • First generation (typical): chlorpromazine (1952), haloperidol. Side effects: stiffness, tremor, tardive dyskinesia
    • Second generation (atypical): risperidone, olanzapine, clozapine (for resistant cases); weight gain, diabetes risk
    Psychosocial treatment
    • Family psychoeducation (lowers expressed emotion)
    • CBT for psychosis; social skills training
    • Cognitive remediation, supported employment, community care

    Medicine and therapy work best together. Relapse is common without continued medication.

    Mood (affective) disorders

    Disorders in which mood disturbance is the main feature: depressive disorders and bipolar disorders.

    Major depressive disorder (MDD)

    At least 2 weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest, plus others to make 5 of 9:

    1 · Depressed mood most of the day

    2 · Loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia)

    3 · Weight or appetite change

    4 · Sleep disturbance (insomnia or oversleeping)

    5 · Psychomotor agitation or slowing

    6 · Fatigue or loss of energy

    7 · Worthlessness or excessive guilt

    8 · Poor concentration or indecision

    9 · Thoughts of death or suicide

    RememberSIG E CAPS: Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicide, plus depressed mood.
    • Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia): milder, lasting at least 2 years
    • Specifiers: melancholic, psychotic, seasonal pattern, postpartum
    • MDD is about twice as common in women; leading cause of disability worldwide

    Bipolar disorders

    Bipolar I

    At least one manic episode: abnormally high or irritable mood and energy for at least 1 week (or any length if hospitalised). Depression is common but not required.

    Bipolar II

    At least one hypomanic episode (4 days or more, milder, no major impairment) and one major depressive episode.

    Cyclothymic disorder

    Two years of many mild hypomanic and depressive symptoms that do not meet full criteria.

    RememberMania = DIGFAST: Distractibility, Indiscretion (risky acts), Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep need decreases, Talkativeness (pressured speech).

    Bipolar disorder affects men and women about equally and begins in late teens to the 20s. Risk of suicide is high in both depression and bipolar disorder.

    Causes of depression and bipolar disorder

    Biological
    • Genes: heritability of MDD about 35–40%; bipolar much higher, around 60–80%
    • Monoamine hypothesis: low serotonin and norepinephrine (and dopamine)
    • Stress hormone overactivity (HPA axis, high cortisol)
    • Brain: smaller hippocampus, low prefrontal and high amygdala activity
    Cognitive
    • Beck's triad and distortions
    • Learned helplessness (Seligman) and hopelessness theory (Abramson): internal, stable, global attributions for failure
    • Rumination (Nolen-Hoeksema) helps explain higher rates in women
    Behavioural and psychodynamic
    • Lewinsohn: fewer rewarding activities, then low mood, then even fewer activities
    • Freud: anger turned inward after loss; Bowlby: early loss and insecure attachment
    Social
    • Stressful life events (loss, divorce, unemployment)
    • Brown & Harris (1978): for women, vulnerability factors were no confiding partner, three or more children at home, unemployment, early loss of mother
    • Low social support; poverty

    Treatment

    TreatmentDetails
    AntidepressantsSSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline), SNRIs, tricyclics, MAOIs. Take 2–4 weeks to work.
    Mood stabilisers (bipolar)Lithium (Cade, 1949), valproate, lamotrigine; antipsychotics in mania
    CBTChallenge negative thoughts and rebuild activity. About as effective as drugs for mild to moderate depression and helps prevent relapse
    Interpersonal therapy (IPT)Works on grief, role changes and relationships (Klerman)
    Behavioural activationSchedule pleasant and meaningful activities
    ECT and brain stimulationECT (Cerletti and Bini, 1938) for severe, psychotic or suicidal depression under anaesthesia; rTMS
    PsychoeducationKey in bipolar: regular sleep, medication adherence, early warning signs

    Suicide: always ask directly about suicidal thoughts, assess risk, remove means, build a safety plan and involve family. Asking does not plant the idea.

    Delusional disorder

    A disorder in which a person has one or more fixed, false beliefs (delusions) for at least 1 month, but does not meet criteria for schizophrenia. Apart from the delusion, behaviour and functioning are relatively normal, and hallucinations are not prominent. ICD-10: persistent delusional disorders (F22). Onset is usually in middle or late life.

    SubtypeCentral delusionExample
    PersecutoryBeing harmed, spied on, poisoned or plotted againstA neighbour is trying to ruin him
    Jealous (Othello syndrome)Partner is unfaithful, without evidenceChecks partner's phone for "proof"
    Erotomanic (de Clérambault)Someone, often of higher status, is in love with the personA celebrity "secretly" loves her
    GrandioseSpecial talent, power or identityBelieves he is a prophet or has discovered a cure
    SomaticA defect or disease in the bodyBelieves insects live under the skin
    Mixed / unspecifiedSeveral themes
    • Non-bizarre delusions (could happen in real life) are typical; bizarre delusions suggest schizophrenia
    • Folie à deux (induced or shared delusional disorder): a delusion is taken over by a close partner. It is listed in ICD-10 (F24) but no longer separate in DSM-5
    Aetiology
    • Genes: runs with paranoid personality and schizophrenia in relatives
    • Brain disease, sensory loss (deafness, poor vision), substance use
    • Social isolation, migration, low status; stress
    • Cognitive: jumping to conclusions, blaming others for bad events
    • Psychodynamic: projection of one's own unacceptable feelings onto others (Freud on Schreber)
    Treatment
    • Build trust first; do not argue or confirm the belief
    • Antipsychotics (modest effect); CBT to question evidence gently
    • Hospital if risk to others (e.g. in jealous or persecutory types)
    • Treat any medical or substance cause

    Schizophrenia vs mood disorders vs delusional disorder

    PointSchizophreniaMood disordersDelusional disorder
    Main problemThought, perception, reality contactMood (low or high)One fixed false belief
    HallucinationsCommonOnly in severe (psychotic) formsNot prominent
    DelusionsOften bizarreMood-congruent, if anyNon-bizarre
    FunctioningMarked declineImpaired during episodes; recovery betweenRelatively preserved
    Typical onsetLate teens to 30sAny age; peak in 20s–40sMiddle or late life
    Key drugAntipsychoticAntidepressant; lithiumAntipsychotic (limited effect)

    Unit IV self-test

    Who named schizophrenia?

    Eugen Bleuler (1911); Kraepelin called it dementia praecox.

    Positive vs negative symptoms?

    Positive are added (delusions, hallucinations); negative are lost (avolition, flat affect).

    Minimum duration for schizophrenia (DSM-5)?

    6 months of continuous signs, including at least 1 month of active symptoms.

    Concordance in identical twins (Gottesman)?

    About 48%.

    The dopamine hypothesis in one line?

    Excess dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathway causes positive symptoms.

    Bipolar I vs bipolar II?

    Bipolar I has full mania; bipolar II has hypomania plus major depression.

    Which drug treats bipolar disorder?

    Lithium (and other mood stabilisers).

    Duration for delusional disorder?

    At least 1 month of delusions without meeting schizophrenia criteria.

    Long-answer outlines

    Describe the clinical features and aetiology of schizophrenia. 10 marks
    1. History; symptom clusters (draw).
    2. DSM-5 criteria; ICD-10 subtypes; course.
    3. Genetics (chart), dopamine, brain, neurodevelopment, psychosocial.
    4. Diathesis-stress; treatment.
    Explain mood disorders: features, causes and treatment. 10 marks
    1. MDD criteria; dysthymia; bipolar I, II, cyclothymia (draw mood graph).
    2. Biological, cognitive, behavioural, social causes.
    3. Treatments; suicide risk.
    Write notes on delusional disorder. 5 marks
    1. Definition and criteria; subtypes.
    2. Causes and treatment; difference from schizophrenia.
    Psychopathology · Unit V

    Delirium, Dementia and Amnestic Syndromes

    Organic (neurocognitive) disorders

    Disorders caused by a physical brain disease or injury, or by a medical illness or substance that affects the brain. They show up mainly as problems in attention, memory and thinking. DSM-5 groups them as neurocognitive disorders; ICD-10 calls them organic mental disorders (F00–F09).

    Delirium

    An acute, short-lived confusional state: a sudden disturbance of attention and awareness that develops over hours or days and fluctuates through the day. It is a medical emergency and is usually reversible.

    Clinical features
    • Inattention: cannot focus, easily distracted
    • Reduced awareness of surroundings; clouding of consciousness
    • Disorientation (time, place), poor memory
    • Perceptual disturbance: illusions and hallucinations, often visual
    • Disturbed sleep–wake cycle (worse at night: "sundowning")
    • Emotional lability, fear, agitation or drowsiness
    Types
    • Hyperactive: restless, agitated, hallucinating
    • Hypoactive: sleepy, quiet; often missed
    • Mixed: swings between the two

    Delirium tremens: severe alcohol withdrawal, with tremor, hallucinations and fever.

    Aetiology (any acute medical stress to the brain)

    Infection

    Urinary or chest infection, sepsis, meningitis

    Metabolic

    Low or high sugar, kidney or liver failure, dehydration, low sodium

    Drugs and substances

    Intoxication, withdrawal (alcohol, benzodiazepines), side effects

    Brain and body

    Head injury, stroke, surgery, hypoxia, fever

    Risk factors: old age, existing dementia, many medicines, hospital stay, sensory loss. Treatment: find and treat the cause; calm, well-lit room; family presence; reorientation; sleep hygiene; low-dose antipsychotic only if needed. Often clears in days to weeks.

    Alois Alzheimer (1864–1915)German psychiatrist. In 1906 he described the brain of Auguste Deter, a woman with memory loss, who died at 55, finding plaques and tangles. The disease is named after him.Photo: public domain, Wikimedia Commons

    Dementia (major neurocognitive disorder)

    A gradual, usually progressive decline in memory and other thinking abilities, severe enough to interfere with daily life, in a person who was previously well. Consciousness is clear until late in the illness.

    Amnesia

    Memory loss: recent first, remote later.

    Aphasia

    Loss of language: word-finding difficulty.

    Apraxia

    Cannot carry out skilled movements (dressing).

    Agnosia

    Cannot recognise objects or faces.

    Plus problems with executive function (planning), personality change, mood symptoms, wandering and loss of independence. These are the "4 A's".

    Early (mild)1–3 yrs

    Forgets recent events and names; trouble with money and planning; still independent mostly.

    Middle (moderate)2–10 yrs

    Lost in familiar places; needs help with daily tasks; speech problems; behaviour change.

    Late (severe)

    Little speech; cannot walk or eat unaided; full-time care.

    Types

    TypeShareCause and features
    Alzheimer's disease≈ 60–70%Beta-amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles; loss of acetylcholine neurons; shrinkage starting in the hippocampus. Gradual, steady decline; memory first
    Vascular dementia≈ 15–20%Strokes or small-vessel disease; stepwise decline; linked to hypertension, diabetes, smoking
    Lewy body dementia≈ 5–10%Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein); fluctuating alertness, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism
    Frontotemporal (Pick's) dementia≈ 5%Frontal and temporal lobe damage; early personality and behaviour change, language loss; younger onset
    OthersParkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, HIV, Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, head injury, alcohol
    Aetiology of Alzheimer's
    • Age is the biggest risk factor
    • Genes: APOE ε4 raises risk; rare early-onset genes (PSEN1, PSEN2, APP)
    • Down syndrome, head injury, low education, hypertension, diabetes, depression, inactivity, loneliness
    Assessment and care
    • Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE): 30 points; around 23 or below suggests impairment. MoCA; Hindi Mental State Examination (HMSE) for Indian settings
    • Brain scan and blood tests to exclude treatable causes
    • Drugs: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine), memantine; they slow, not cure
    • Reality orientation, reminiscence, routine, safety, caregiver support and training

    Pseudodementia: depression in the elderly can mimic dementia and is treatable. Some dementias (from thyroid disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, normal-pressure hydrocephalus) are reversible if found early.

    Amnestic syndromes

    A disorder with severe memory impairment but, unlike dementia, other thinking abilities (attention, language, intelligence) are relatively intact, and there is no delirium. It results from damage to memory structures: the hippocampus, medial temporal lobe, thalamus and mammillary bodies.

    Korsakoff's syndrome

    Caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, usually in chronic alcoholism with poor diet. It often follows Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, unsteady gait, abnormal eye movements). Features: severe anterograde amnesia, some retrograde loss, confabulation (filling gaps with invented stories), disorientation, apathy, little insight. Damage to mammillary bodies and thalamus. Treatment: high-dose thiamine, stop alcohol; often only partial recovery.

    Other causes
    • Head injury (post-traumatic amnesia)
    • Herpes simplex encephalitis
    • Stroke, hypoxia, tumour, surgery
    • Transient global amnesia: sudden memory loss for hours, then recovers
    • Drugs and electroconvulsive therapy (temporary)
    Famous case · patient H.M. (Henry Molaison)

    Memory needs the hippocampus

    In 1953 surgeon Scoville removed H.M.'s medial temporal lobes to treat severe epilepsy. Afterwards he could not form new declarative memories (anterograde amnesia), yet his short-term memory, intelligence and procedural learning (mirror drawing, which improved with practice, studied by Brenda Milner) were intact. It showed that different memory systems depend on different brain areas.

    Famous case · Clive Wearing

    Memory span of seconds

    A musician who developed herpes encephalitis in 1985. He retained musical skill but lived in a continuous "just woke up" state, with memory lasting seconds.

    Management: treat the cause, memory aids (diaries, phones, routines), errorless learning, use preserved procedural memory, family support.

    Delirium vs dementia vs amnestic syndrome

    PointDeliriumDementiaAmnestic syndrome
    OnsetSudden (hours or days)Gradual (months or years)Sudden or gradual
    CourseFluctuates, worse at nightSteady, progressiveStable or slowly improving
    Main problemAttention and awarenessMemory plus other cognitionMemory only
    ConsciousnessCloudedClear until lateClear
    DurationDays to weeksYearsLong-term
    Reversible?Usually yesUsually noPartly
    Typical causeInfection, drugs, metabolicAlzheimer's, strokesAlcohol (thiamine), injury, encephalitis

    Unit V self-test

    Main feature of delirium?

    Acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness, usually reversible.

    What are the "4 A's" of dementia?

    Amnesia, aphasia, apraxia, agnosia.

    Two brain changes in Alzheimer's?

    Beta-amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles.

    Which gene raises risk of late-onset Alzheimer's?

    APOE ε4.

    Pattern of decline in vascular dementia?

    Stepwise, after strokes.

    Korsakoff's syndrome is caused by deficiency of?

    Thiamine (vitamin B1), usually from chronic alcoholism.

    What is confabulation?

    Filling memory gaps with invented, but sincerely believed, stories.

    Anterograde vs retrograde amnesia?

    Anterograde: cannot form new memories. Retrograde: cannot recall past events.

    Long-answer outlines

    Describe delirium and dementia: features and aetiology. 10 marks
    1. Organic disorders; delirium: features, types, causes, treatment.
    2. Dementia: 4 A's, stages, types (table), Alzheimer's causes.
    3. Comparison table and graph.
    Write notes on amnestic syndromes. 5 marks
    1. Definition; anterograde vs retrograde (draw).
    2. Korsakoff's syndrome; H.M.; management.
    Disabilities & Rehabilitation · Unit I

    Introduction to Disabilities

    Impairment, disability and handicap

    The WHO (1980) ICIDH separated three ideas that people often mix up:

    Impairment

    Loss or abnormality of a body structure or function (psychological, physiological or anatomical).

    Disability

    Restriction or lack of ability to perform an activity in the normal way because of impairment.

    Handicap

    The disadvantage in society that limits a role considered normal for that person (age, sex, culture).

    Models of disability

    Medical model

    Disability is a problem inside the person to be cured or treated by professionals.

    Social model

    Disability is created by barriers in society (steps, attitudes, laws). Change society, not the person.

    The WHO ICF (2001) replaced ICIDH. It uses neutral terms (body functions, activities, participation) and looks at the person's environment. The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD, 2006) follows the social/rights model. India ratified it in 2007. Preferred words today: "person with disability", and in India "Divyang" is used officially.

    Aetiology: causes of disabilities

    PeriodCauses
    Prenatal (before birth)Genetic: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), fragile X, phenylketonuria. Maternal: rubella, syphilis, HIV, alcohol (fetal alcohol syndrome), drugs, radiation, malnutrition, age, diabetes
    Perinatal (around birth)Birth asphyxia (lack of oxygen), premature or very low birth weight, birth injury, neonatal jaundice and infections
    Postnatal (after birth)Meningitis and encephalitis, head injury, severe malnutrition, lead or other poisoning, lack of stimulation, accidents, iodine deficiency
    RememberAetiology = Pre, Peri, Post-natal. Prevention: immunisation, antenatal care, safe delivery, nutrition, early screening.

    Intellectual disability (ID)

    Earlier called mental retardation. Significant limits in intellectual functioning AND in adaptive behaviour, beginning in the developmental period (before 18 years). About 1% of people.

    1 · Low intellectual functioning

    IQ roughly 70 or below (about 2 standard deviations below the mean of 100).

    2 · Deficits in adaptive behaviour

    Conceptual (language, reading, money), social (rules, relationships) and practical (daily living) skills.

    3 · Onset before 18

    Distinguishes it from dementia or brain injury in adults.

    LevelMental age (adult)What they can usually do
    Mild9–12 yearsLearn basic school skills; live independently with some support; hold simple jobs
    Moderate6–9 yearsLearn self-care and basic communication; need supervision; sheltered work
    Severe3–6 yearsVery limited speech; need close support; simple self-help skills with training
    Profoundbelow 3 yearsNeed constant care; very limited communication and mobility
    Common conditions
    • Down syndrome: extra chromosome 21; about 1 in 700 births; flat face, slanted eyes, heart problems
    • Fragile X: most common inherited cause
    • PKU: enzyme defect; avoidable by diet if found at birth
    • Fetal alcohol syndrome
    Associated problems

    Speech and language delay, epilepsy, hearing and vision problems, emotional and behaviour difficulties, and vulnerability to abuse.

    Specific learning disability (SLD)

    Difficulty in reading, writing or arithmetic that is unexpected given the child's average or above-average intelligence, normal senses and schooling. It is not caused by low IQ, poor teaching, or vision or hearing problems. About 5–15% of school children.

    Dyslexia

    Reading: slow, inaccurate, confuses b/d, p/q, reverses letters, poor spelling and phonological awareness.

    Dysgraphia

    Writing: poor handwriting, trouble putting thoughts on paper, spelling errors.

    Dyscalculia

    Maths: difficulty with number sense, counting, calculation and word problems.

    Causes
    • Genetic (runs in families)
    • Differences in brain areas for language and reading (left temporoparietal)
    • Prenatal or birth complications, low birth weight
    • Not due to laziness or poor intelligence
    Help
    • Early identification; individualised education plan
    • Multisensory teaching (see, hear, say, trace)
    • Extra time, reader or scribe, assistive tools
    • Emotional support to protect self-esteem

    Often occurs with ADHD (inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity). Famous people with dyslexia include Einstein (reported), Leonardo da Vinci (suspected) and Abhishek Bachchan. The film Taare Zameen Par (2007) raised awareness in India.

    Leo Kanner (1943) and Hans Asperger (1944)Kanner described "early infantile autism" in 11 children. Asperger described a milder form with good language, now part of the spectrum.Photo: Johns Hopkins University, public domain, Wikimedia Commons

    Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)

    A neurodevelopmental condition that begins in early childhood. DSM-5 merged autistic disorder, Asperger's and PDD-NOS into one "spectrum". About 1–2% of children.

    • Signs present in the early developmental period, usually noticed by age 2–3; they cause impairment in daily life
    • Severity levels (DSM-5): Level 1 (needs support), Level 2 (substantial support), Level 3 (very substantial support)
    • Co-occurring: intellectual disability (about 30–40%), epilepsy, ADHD, anxiety, sleep and feeding problems
    • Boys are 3–4 times more often diagnosed than girls; "masking" may hide autism in girls
    Aetiology
    • Strongly genetic (heritability about 80%); hundreds of genes
    • Prenatal factors: advanced parental age, maternal infection, some drugs (valproate)
    • Differences in brain connectivity and development
    • Not caused by "cold" parenting (the refrigerator-mother idea is discredited) or by vaccines
    Theories and intervention
    • Theory of mind deficit (Baron-Cohen); weak central coherence; executive dysfunction
    • Early intervention: ABA, speech and occupational therapy, social skills training, parent training, special education (TEACCH, PECS)
    • Medicines only for associated symptoms

    Unit I self-test

    Impairment vs disability vs handicap?

    Impairment: loss at body level. Disability: activity limitation. Handicap: social disadvantage.

    Medical vs social model?

    Medical: the problem is in the person. Social: barriers in society create disability.

    Three criteria of ID?

    Low intellectual functioning (IQ ≈ 70 or less), deficits in adaptive behaviour, onset before 18.

    IQ range of mild ID (ICD-10)?

    50–69.

    Genetic cause of Down syndrome?

    Trisomy 21 (extra chromosome 21).

    Dyslexia, dysgraphia, dyscalculia?

    Difficulties in reading, writing and arithmetic.

    Two core domains of ASD?

    Social communication/interaction deficits; restricted, repetitive behaviours and interests.

    Who first described autism?

    Leo Kanner (1943).

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the concept and aetiology of disability. 10 marks
    1. Impairment, disability, handicap (draw chain); models; ICF.
    2. Pre-, peri- and post-natal causes (table).
    Describe intellectual disability. 10 marks
    1. Criteria; levels by IQ (draw bar).
    2. Causes, common conditions, associated problems.
    Write notes on learning disability and autism. 10 marks
    1. SLD types, causes, help.
    2. ASD two domains (draw), levels, causes, intervention.
    Disabilities & Rehabilitation · Unit II

    Assessment of Disabilities

    Why assess?

    Assessment is the process of collecting and interpreting information to understand a person's strengths, needs and level of functioning. It is the base of every plan for education and rehabilitation.

    Screening

    Quick check to find who may need a full assessment.

    Diagnosis and classification

    Identify the condition and its severity.

    Planning and placement

    Choose goals, services and school or job placement.

    Monitoring

    Measure progress and review the programme.

    Certification

    Decide the percentage of disability for legal benefits.

    Basic principles

    • Multi-source and multi-method: use tests, observation, interviews and records from parents and teachers
    • Use valid, reliable and culturally suitable tools with Indian norms
    • Assess in natural settings, not only the clinic; observe over time
    • Team approach: psychologist, doctor, special educator, therapists, parents
    • Focus on strengths as well as problems and link results to intervention
    • Ethics: informed consent, confidentiality, no labelling, share results sensitively
    • Repeat assessment because children change

    Types of assessment

    PointNorm-basedCriterion-basedFunction-based
    Compares the person with…A reference group of same-age peers (norms)A fixed standard of skill masteryWhat the person actually does in daily life
    ResultIQ, percentile, age equivalentSkills achieved / not achievedDescription of abilities, supports needed
    Answers"How does he rank?""What can he do and teach next?""How does he manage at home, school, work?"
    ExampleWISC (IQ)Checklists of skills (e.g. BASIC-MR Part A)Vineland Social Maturity Scale; functional assessment in home

    Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC)

    David Wechsler (1896–1981)Developed the Wechsler scales. He defined intelligence as "the global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment".Photo: NYU School of Medicine, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
    • An individually administered test for children aged 6–16 years. Versions: WISC (1949), -R, -III, -IV, WISC-V (2014)
    • Scores are deviation IQs with mean 100 and standard deviation 15
    • Gives a Full Scale IQ and index scores; in WISC-V five indexes: Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory, Processing Speed
    • Older version: Verbal and Performance IQ (verbal: information, similarities, vocabulary, comprehension, digit span; performance: picture completion, block design, object assembly, coding)
    • Use in disability: classify ID (IQ about 70 or below), identify strengths and weaknesses, find learning disability (gap between IQ and achievement)
    • In India the Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children (MISIC) is an adaptation of the WISC, and Indian versions of the WISC are used

    Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS)

    What it is

    Developed by Edgar Doll (1935). Measures social competence (ability to look after oneself and take responsibility) from birth to adulthood. An informant, usually the mother, is interviewed about what the person actually does. Indian adaptation by A. J. Malin (1971).

    Structure and scores
    • 89 items in 8 categories: self-help general, self-help eating, self-help dressing, self-direction, occupation, communication, locomotion, socialisation
    • Gives Social Age (SA) and Social Quotient (SQ)
    SQ = (Social Age ÷ Chronological Age) × 100

    Example: a 10-year-old with a social age of 6 has SQ = 6 ÷ 10 × 100 = 60. It is used together with IQ to judge adaptive behaviour, the second criterion of ID.

    Indian Scale for Assessment of Autism (ISAA)

    • Developed by the National Institute for the Mentally Handicapped (now NIEPID), Secunderabad, with the National Trust (2009). Used to assess autism and its severity for disability certification
    • Completed by a trained clinician after interview with the parent or caregiver and observation. For ages roughly 3 years and above
    • 40 items, each rated 1 to 5 (never to always), in 6 domains: social relationship and reciprocity; emotional responsiveness; speech, language and communication; behaviour patterns; sensory aspects; cognitive component
    • Total score: below 70 = no autism; 70–106 mild; 107–153 moderate; 154 and above severe. The score is converted to a percentage of disability for the certificate

    BASIC-MR

    SV
    Reeta Peshawaria and S. Venkatesan (1992)Behavioural Assessment Scales for Indian Children with Mental Retardation, published by NIEPID, Secunderabad.
    • A criterion-referenced behavioural checklist for children (about 3–12 years) with ID, completed from parent or teacher information
    • Part A: adaptive (skill) behaviours, e.g. motor, daily living, language, number, domestic and occupational skills. Shows what the child can do and what to teach next
    • Part B: behaviour problems, e.g. violence, destruction, anti-social acts, odd behaviour, hyperactivity, self-injury. Shows what to reduce
    • Gives a profile for programme planning and for measuring progress
    TestMeasuresTypeUse
    WISCIntelligence (IQ)Norm-based, direct testingClassify ID; find learning disability
    VSMSSocial competence (SQ)Function-based, informantAdaptive behaviour
    ISAAAutism and its severityRating scale, informantDiagnosis and certification
    BASIC-MRSkills and behaviour problemsCriterion-based checklistProgramme planning

    Determining severity

    Severity is judged from test results, clinical examination and functioning by a team, not from one score.

    • ID: IQ band and adaptive behaviour (VSMS/BASIC-MR); mild, moderate, severe, profound
    • Autism: ISAA score bands (mild, moderate, severe)
    • Learning disability: gap between ability and achievement; level of support needed
    • Consider age, other disabilities (multiple disability), and the environment

    Disability certification in India

    Benchmark

    Under the RPWD Act 2016, a "person with benchmark disability" has at least 40% of a specified disability. Many benefits depend on this.

    Certificate

    Issued by a medical authority (board of doctors, with a psychologist for ID and autism) using government guidelines, stating type and percentage.

    UDID

    The Unique Disability ID card gives one national identity for benefits, through the online UDID portal.

    Psychologists must report results fairly, avoid over- or under-stating severity, and remember that benefits depend on the certificate.

    Unit II self-test

    Norm-based vs criterion-based assessment?

    Norm-based compares a person with peers; criterion-based compares with a fixed skill standard.

    Age range and mean IQ of WISC?

    6–16 years; mean 100, SD 15.

    Who developed the Vineland Social Maturity Scale?

    Edgar Doll (1935); Indian adaptation by Malin.

    How is SQ calculated?

    (Social age ÷ chronological age) × 100.

    How many items and domains in ISAA?

    40 items, 6 domains.

    ISAA score for moderate autism?

    107–153.

    What do Parts A and B of BASIC-MR measure?

    A: adaptive skills. B: behaviour problems.

    What is the benchmark disability level?

    At least 40% (RPWD Act 2016).

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the principles and types of assessment of disabilities. 10 marks
    1. Purposes; principles.
    2. Norm-, criterion- and function-based (table).
    Describe WISC, VSMS, ISAA and BASIC-MR. 10 marks
    1. Each test: author, age, structure, scores, use.
    2. Comparison table.
    How is severity of disability determined and certified? 5 marks
    1. Multi-source judgement; bands by condition.
    2. Benchmark 40%, certificate, UDID.
    Disabilities & Rehabilitation · Unit III

    Behaviour Modification

    What is behaviour modification?

    Behaviour modification is the systematic use of learning principles (especially operant and classical conditioning, and observational learning) to increase useful behaviours and decrease problem behaviours.

    Behaviour is learned

    Both skills and problems are shaped by their consequences.

    Focus on observable behaviour

    Define the target in measurable terms ("hits others 6 times a day"), not labels ("aggressive").

    Environment can be changed

    Change antecedents and consequences to change behaviour.

    Data-based

    Measure the behaviour before, during and after (baseline).

    B. F. Skinner, Thorndike, Pavlov, Bandura, WolpeThe basis is operant conditioning (Skinner), the law of effect (Thorndike), classical conditioning (Pavlov) and modelling (Bandura).Photo: Silly rabbit, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

    Techniques for skill acquisition

    TechniqueWhat it isExample
    Positive reinforcementGive something pleasant right after the behaviourPraise and a sticker after putting on a shirt
    Task analysisBreak a skill into small teachable stepsHand washing in 8 steps
    PromptingHelp to get the right response (physical, gestural, verbal, visual)Guiding the hand to hold a spoon
    FadingGradually withdraw prompts so the person acts independentlyFrom hand-over-hand, to touch, to pointing, to nothing
    ShapingReinforce successive approximations toward the goalReward any sound, then "ba", then "ball"
    ChainingLink steps in order: forward (first step first), backward (last step first), or total taskTeaching tooth brushing
    ModellingShow the behaviour to be copiedTherapist demonstrates greeting
    Token economyEarn tokens for good behaviour, exchange for rewardsStars on a chart exchanged for play time
    Discrete trial training (DTT)Structured teaching: instruction → response → consequence, repeated"Touch red" → correct → praise
    RememberT-P-F-S-C-M: "Teachers Prompt, Fade, Shape, Chain and Model."

    Managing problem behaviours

    Step 1: understand why it happens (functions of behaviour)

    Sensory

    Feels good in itself (rocking, hand-flapping).

    Escape

    To avoid a demand or task.

    Attention

    To get notice from others, even scolding.

    Tangible

    To get an item or activity.

    RememberFunctions = SEAT: Sensory, Escape, Attention, Tangible. Use functional behavioural assessment (FBA) with ABC charts to find it.

    Step 2: choose a technique

    TechniqueMeaningExample
    ExtinctionStop reinforcing the behaviourIgnore attention-seeking screaming (expect an initial extinction burst)
    DRO (differential reinforcement of other behaviour)Reward any time the problem behaviour is absentReward every 5 minutes without hitting
    DRI / DRAReward an incompatible or alternative behaviourTeach asking for a break instead of screaming
    Time-outBrief removal from reinforcementTwo minutes away from the play area after hitting
    Response costLose a token or privilege for the behaviourLose a star for shouting
    OvercorrectionCorrect the damage and practise the right wayClean the spilled water and wipe the whole table
    Antecedent changeChange the triggerUse a visual schedule; give choices
    PunishmentAversive consequence (last resort)Needs strict ethical safeguards

    Ethics: use the least intrusive effective method; teach a replacement skill; get informed consent; never use harsh physical punishment; monitor data; involve parents. Positive approaches come first.

    Applied behaviour analysis (ABA)

    ABA is the science of applying learning principles to improve socially important behaviour, and measuring whether the intervention really caused the change. It is the leading approach for autism and ID.

    Applied

    Targets socially important behaviour.

    Behavioural

    Measurable behaviour.

    Analytic

    Shows a functional relation between the intervention and the change (e.g. ABAB design).

    Technological

    Procedures described so clearly that others can repeat them.

    Conceptually systematic

    Based on principles of behaviour.

    Effective

    Produces large enough change to matter.

    Generality

    Change lasts and spreads to other settings and people.

    The seven dimensions come from Baer, Wolf and Risley (1968).

    Process
    1. Define and record the target behaviour (baseline)
    2. Functional assessment (ABC)
    3. Set goals; choose intervention
    4. Teach (DTT, naturalistic teaching, chaining)
    5. Collect data; make decisions
    6. Promote generalisation and maintenance; train parents
    History and evidence
    • Lovaas (1987): intensive early ABA (about 40 hours a week) reported that 47% of a small group reached normal functioning. Later studies support early intervention but show smaller gains
    • Criticised for early aversive methods (now abandoned) and for focusing on compliance. Modern ABA emphasises play, choice and the child's dignity

    Unit III self-test

    Define behaviour modification.

    Systematic application of learning principles to increase desirable and decrease undesirable behaviour.

    What does ABC stand for?

    Antecedent, Behaviour, Consequence.

    Prompting vs fading?

    Prompting gives help to get the response; fading gradually removes the help.

    What is shaping?

    Reinforcing successive approximations toward the target behaviour.

    Four functions of behaviour?

    Sensory, escape, attention, tangible.

    What is an extinction burst?

    A temporary increase in the behaviour when reinforcement is first withheld.

    DRO means?

    Differential reinforcement of other behaviour: reward absence of the problem behaviour.

    Who set out the seven dimensions of ABA?

    Baer, Wolf and Risley (1968).

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the meaning and techniques of behaviour modification. 10 marks
    1. Definition and basis; ABC (draw).
    2. Skill-building techniques (table); prompt hierarchy.
    3. Problem behaviour: functions, techniques, ethics.
    Write notes on applied behaviour analysis. 5 marks
    1. Meaning; seven dimensions.
    2. Process; Lovaas; criticism.
    Disabilities & Rehabilitation · Unit IV

    Rehabilitation Techniques

    Habilitation vs rehabilitation

    Rehabilitation aims to restore a person to the highest possible level of physical, mental, social and vocational functioning and to full participation in society.

    PointHabilitationRehabilitation
    MeaningHelping a person develop skills for the first timeHelping a person regain skills that were lost
    Skills before?Never acquired (disability from birth or early childhood)Existed earlier, then lost (injury, illness, stroke)
    Typical clientsIntellectual disability, autism, cerebral palsy from birthSpinal cord injury, accident, stroke, mental illness
    ExampleTeaching a child with ID to dress and speakTeaching an adult to walk again after a stroke

    In practice the word "rehabilitation" is used for both. The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) uses it for the whole field.

    Components of rehabilitation

    Medical

    Treatment, surgery, aids and appliances, physiotherapy

    Psychological

    Counselling, behaviour therapy, adjustment

    Educational

    Special education, inclusion

    Social

    Family, community participation, rights

    Vocational

    Training and employment

    Basic principles of intervention

    Early

    Start as early as possible: the brain is most flexible in childhood.

    Individualised

    Plan based on each person's strengths, needs and goals.

    Family-centred

    Parents are partners, trained and supported.

    Multidisciplinary team

    Psychologist, doctor, therapists, special educator, social worker.

    Normalisation

    Make life conditions as close as possible to those of others (Nirje; Wolfensberger).

    Least restrictive environment and inclusion

    Support in the ordinary school and community wherever possible.

    Strengths and self-determination

    Build on abilities; involve the person in decisions.

    Continuous evaluation

    Review goals and data regularly.

    Types of intervention

    Individual
    • One-to-one therapy and training
    • Behaviour modification, speech therapy, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, counselling
    • Individualised education programme (IEP) with clear goals
    • Best for specific skills and sensitive problems
    Group
    • Social skills groups, life-skills and self-help groups, peer support
    • Sensory-play and recreation groups, group counselling for adolescents
    • Builds friendship, confidence and practice of social skills
    • Efficient: many people per therapist
    Family-based
    • Parent training: teach parents behaviour methods and how to teach at home
    • Counselling for grief, stress and siblings
    • Parent support groups; respite care; home-based programmes
    • Family is the main and lifelong support
    Early intervention

    For infants and young children (0–6 years), often at home or in centres: stimulation, therapies, parent coaching. In India, District Early Intervention Centres (DEIC) under the National Health Mission screen and support young children.

    Community-based rehabilitation (CBR)

    WHO strategy to deliver services in the community through trained local workers, families and volunteers. Useful in villages. Covers health, education, livelihood, social and empowerment.

    Parent roles

    • Accept the disability; seek early help; learn skills; be consistent
    • Treat the child as a whole person; keep high but realistic expectations; plan for the future (guardianship, trusts)

    Vocational rehabilitation and counselling

    Vocational counselling helps a person with disability choose, prepare for, find and keep a suitable job matched to their abilities, interests and the job market.

    1Assessment

    Abilities, interests, aptitude, personality, work skills and limits; medical fitness; a work sample or trial.

    2Counselling and guidance

    Explore options; set realistic goals; correct myths; involve family.

    3Training

    Skills at an ITI, vocational centre or on the job; job-specific and social skills.

    4Placement

    Find a job through employers, employment exchanges and special programmes; job coaching.

    5Follow-up

    Support after placement; solve problems; adapt workplace.

    Work settingMeaningFor whom
    Open (competitive) employmentRegular job with the same payMild disability
    Supported employmentRegular job with a job coach and supportModerate disability
    Sheltered workshopProtected setting with supervisionModerate to severe
    Self-employmentOwn business with loans and training (e.g. NHFDC loans)Varied
    Home-based workWork at homeSevere mobility limits

    Employers: the RPWD Act 2016 requires reasonable accommodation, reservation in government jobs and non-discrimination (see Unit V). Counsellors should challenge employers' misconceptions about productivity and cost.

    Unit IV self-test

    Habilitation vs rehabilitation?

    Habilitation develops skills never acquired; rehabilitation restores lost skills.

    What is normalisation?

    Making living conditions of people with disabilities as close as possible to those of others.

    What is an IEP?

    An individualised education programme with goals planned for one child.

    Three types of intervention by setting?

    Individual, group and family-based.

    What is CBR?

    Community-based rehabilitation: services delivered in the community by local workers and families.

    Steps of vocational counselling?

    Assessment, counselling, training, placement, follow-up.

    Supported employment?

    A regular job with help from a job coach.

    Long-answer outlines

    Differentiate habilitation and rehabilitation and explain principles of intervention. 10 marks
    1. Table of differences; components.
    2. Principles; team diagram.
    Discuss types of intervention and vocational counselling. 10 marks
    1. Individual, group, family; early intervention; CBR.
    2. Vocational steps and work settings.
    Disabilities & Rehabilitation · Unit V

    Rehabilitation Services, Schemes and Laws

    Settings and agencies

    SettingServices
    Hospitals and clinicsDiagnosis, medical care, physiotherapy, psychological assessment, early intervention
    Special schools and resource roomsEducation tailored to the disability; inclusive education with support
    Rehabilitation and day-care centresTherapy, skills training, daycare, respite
    Vocational training centres and sheltered workshopsSkills and employment
    Residential homes and group homesLong-term living with care (e.g. National Trust's Gharaunda)
    Home and communityCBR, home training, parent groups

    National institutes and bodies

    • Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD), Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment: the nodal department
    • National institutes, e.g. NIEPID (intellectual disabilities, Secunderabad), NIEPVD (visual), AYJNISHD (hearing, Mumbai), NIEPMD (multiple disabilities, Chennai), plus composite regional centres and District Disability Rehabilitation Centres (DDRC)
    • Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI), National Trust, NHFDC (loans), Artificial Limbs Manufacturing Corporation (ALIMCO)
    • Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities and State Commissioners: monitor the law and hear complaints

    Role of NGOs

    Service delivery

    Run special schools, therapy, daycare and workshops, especially in places government services do not reach.

    Awareness and advocacy

    Change attitudes, press for rights, help families.

    Innovation and training

    Pilot new methods, train parents and workers.

    Funding link

    Receive grants under schemes such as DDRS (below).

    Government schemes for rehabilitation

    SchemeWhat it does
    Deendayal Disabled Rehabilitation Scheme (DDRS)Grants to NGOs to run projects: special schools, early intervention, vocational training, community-based rehabilitation
    ADIP schemeAssistance to Disabled Persons for purchase and fitting of aids and appliances
    Unique Disability ID (UDID)One national ID and online certificate
    Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan, 2015)Make buildings, transport and information accessible
    Scholarships and NHFDC loansEducation support; loans for self-employment
    Disability pension and concessionsPension, travel concessions, tax benefits

    National Trust schemes

    Disha

    Early intervention and school-readiness centres.

    Vikaas

    Day-care centres for skill development.

    Samarth

    Respite homes for short stays.

    Gharaunda

    Group homes for adult residential care.

    Niramaya
