    Health insurance (cover up to ₹1 lakh).

    Sahyogi

    Caregiver training.

    Prerna and Gyan Prabha

    Marketing of products; educational support.

    Legal guardianship

    Local level committees appoint guardians.

    Timeline of key laws

    Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPWD) Act, 2016

    Replaced the PwD Act, 1995 and brought India's law in line with the UNCRPD. It came into force in April 2017.

    21 disabilities

    Raised from 7. Includes intellectual disability, specific learning disability, autism spectrum disorder, mental illness, speech and language disability, blood disorders (haemophilia, thalassemia, sickle cell), acid attack victims, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, in addition to blindness, low vision, hearing impairment, locomotor disability, cerebral palsy, leprosy cured, dwarfism, muscular dystrophy, chronic neurological conditions, multiple disabilities, and deaf-blindness.

    Benchmark disability

    At least 40% of a specified disability, or a person with a certified disability. Many benefits are for this group.

    Rights and entitlements
    • Equality and non-discrimination; right to life with dignity
    • Free education for ages 6–18 for children with benchmark disability; 5% reservation in higher education
    • 4% reservation in government jobs (up from 3%)
    • Accessibility, reasonable accommodation
    • Legal capacity and limited guardianship
    Institutions and penalties
    • Chief Commissioner and State Commissioners; Special Courts
    • Penalties for discrimination, abuse and violence
    • National and State Funds

    National Trust Act, 1999

    "National Trust for Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act". It set up the National Trust.

    • Provides legal guardianship for those who cannot manage their own affairs
    • Promotes independent living, support for parents, and services through registered organisations
    • Runs schemes: Niramaya, Disha, Vikaas, Samarth, Gharaunda, Sahyogi

    RCI Act, 1992 (amended 2000)

    Created the Rehabilitation Council of India as a statutory body.

    • Regulates training of rehabilitation professionals (e.g. clinical and rehabilitation psychologists, special educators, therapists)
    • Recognises courses and institutions
    • Maintains the Central Rehabilitation Register; only registered persons may practise
    • The 2000 amendment widened powers and punishment for unqualified practice

    Also relevant

    • Mental Healthcare Act, 2017: right to access mental health care, informed consent, advance directives; an attempt at suicide is presumed to be due to severe stress and is not to be punished
    • Right to Education Act, 2009 and inclusive education policy

    Ethical issues in rehabilitation

    Respect and dignity

    Treat the person as an adult with rights; avoid pity and infantilising.

    Informed consent and assent

    Explain in simple words; get guardian consent plus the person's assent; allow supported decision-making.

    Autonomy vs protection

    Balance choice with safety; avoid unnecessary guardianship or restriction.

    Confidentiality

    Protect records; share only what is necessary (with team and family).

    Competence

    Practise only within training; be RCI-registered; keep learning.

    Non-discrimination and justice

    Equal access for girls, rural and poor families; fair use of scarce services.

    Least restrictive, non-harmful methods

    No abuse, restraint or harsh punishment; avoid unproven "cures".

    Avoiding labels and stigma

    Use person-first language; protect from exploitation and abuse.

    Research ethics

    Consent, safety and benefit when studying vulnerable people.

    Unit V self-test

    How many disabilities in the RPWD Act 2016?

    21 (up from 7 in 1995).

    What does "benchmark disability" mean?

    At least 40% of a specified disability.

    Reservation in government jobs under RPWD?

    4% (and 5% in higher education).

    Four conditions covered by the National Trust Act 1999?

    Autism, cerebral palsy, intellectual disability (mental retardation), multiple disabilities.

    What does the RCI Act do?

    Regulates training and registration of rehabilitation professionals.

    What is DDRS?

    Deendayal Disabled Rehabilitation Scheme: grants to NGOs.

    What is ADIP?

    Scheme for aids and appliances.

    Which National Trust scheme gives health insurance?

    Niramaya.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain settings, agencies and government schemes for rehabilitation. 10 marks
    1. Settings table; national institutes.
    2. Role of NGOs.
    3. DDRS, ADIP, UDID, National Trust schemes.
    Describe the RPWD Act 2016, National Trust Act 1999 and RCI Act 1992. 10 marks
    1. Timeline (draw).
    2. Each Act: aims, key provisions.
    Discuss ethical issues in rehabilitation. 5 marks
    1. Dignity, consent, autonomy, confidentiality, competence, justice, non-harm.
    Health Psychology · Unit I

    Introduction to Health Psychology

    What is health?

    WHO definition (1948)

    "Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity."

    Later view (Ottawa Charter, 1986)

    Health is a resource for everyday life, not the object of living. WHO later added the ability to lead a socially and economically productive life.

    What is health psychology?

    Joseph Matarazzo (1980): health psychology is the aggregate of educational, scientific and professional contributions of psychology to the promotion and maintenance of health, the prevention and treatment of illness, the identification of causes and correlates of health and illness, and the improvement of the health care system and health policy.

    Promotion

    Encourage exercise, healthy diet, sleep.

    Prevention

    Reduce risks (smoking, unsafe sex), screening.

    Treatment and adjustment

    Help patients cope, follow treatment and recover.

    Causes

    Study how stress, personality and behaviour affect disease.

    Health system

    Improve doctor–patient communication and policy.

    Why it grew: the main killers changed from infectious diseases to chronic, lifestyle-related diseases (heart disease, diabetes, cancer) in which behaviour matters; and awareness that the mind affects the body. Related fields: behavioural medicine, medical psychology, psychosomatic medicine.

    The mind–body relationship

    Ancient viewsGreek, Indian, Chinese

    Hippocrates: balance of humours. Ayurveda: balance of doshas and mind–body unity. Yoga treats mind and body together.

    DualismDescartes, 17th c.

    Mind and body are separate. Medicine then focused on the body only.

    Psychosomatic medicine1930s–40s

    Dunbar and Alexander linked conflicts and personality to illnesses (ulcers, asthma, hypertension). Too simple, but opened the door.

    Stress research1930s–50s

    Cannon's fight or flight; Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome.

    Behavioural medicine1970s

    Behaviour and biomedical knowledge combined.

    Psychoneuroimmunology (PNI)1975 onward

    Ader and Cohen showed the immune system can be conditioned. See Unit II.

    Mind affects body

    Stress raises blood pressure and suppresses immunity; worry causes headaches; placebos relieve pain; positive emotions protect health.

    Body affects mind

    Chronic illness leads to depression; thyroid disease changes mood; pain alters thinking; exercise lifts mood.

    GE
    George L. Engel (1913–1999)American psychiatrist. His 1977 paper "The need for a new medical model" proposed the biopsychosocial model.

    Biomedical vs biopsychosocial model

    PointBiomedical modelBiopsychosocial model
    Cause of illnessSingle biological cause (germ, gene)Many interacting causes: biological, psychological, social
    Mind and bodySeparate (dualism)Inseparable
    PatientPassive recipientActive participant
    TreatmentDrugs, surgeryMedicine plus behaviour change, support, therapy
    FocusIllness and cureHealth, prevention and the whole person
    WeaknessCannot explain chronic, lifestyle diseasesBroad; harder to test; some factors hard to measure
    Example · type 2 diabetes

    All three layers

    Biological: genes, insulin resistance. Psychological: stress eating, beliefs, depression, self-efficacy. Social: income, access to healthy food, family habits, cultural diets. Effective care targets all three.

    RememberB-P-S: Body, Psychology, Society together shape health.

    Unit I self-test

    WHO definition of health (1948)?

    A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

    Who defined health psychology (1980)?

    Joseph Matarazzo.

    Four aims of health psychology?

    Promote health, prevent illness, treat and help adjust to illness, improve the health care system.

    What is mind-body dualism?

    Descartes' view that mind and body are separate.

    Who proposed the biopsychosocial model?

    George Engel (1977).

    One limitation of the biomedical model?

    It cannot explain chronic, lifestyle-related diseases, and ignores psychological and social factors.

    Long-answer outlines

    Define health and health psychology. Why did health psychology develop? 10 marks
    1. WHO definition; continuum (draw).
    2. Matarazzo's definition and aims.
    3. Reasons for growth.
    Compare the biomedical and biopsychosocial models. 10 marks
    1. Mind-body history.
    2. Model diagram; comparison table; diabetes example.
    Health Psychology · Unit II

    Body Systems and Psychological Relations

    How the mind reaches the body

    Short bursts of this response help us cope (Cannon's fight or flight). Chronic activation wears down the heart, gut and immune system (Selye). Reactivity: people differ in how strongly their body reacts to stress, and high reactors are at higher risk.

    Cardiovascular system

    Structure and function

    Heart, blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) and blood. The heart pumps blood to deliver oxygen and nutrients and remove waste. Blood pressure is the force of blood on artery walls (systolic over diastolic).

    Main disorders
    • Atherosclerosis: fatty plaque narrows arteries
    • Coronary heart disease (CHD): heart's arteries narrowed; angina, heart attack
    • Hypertension: high blood pressure
    • Stroke: blocked or burst brain artery

    Psychological links

    Stress

    Raises heart rate, blood pressure and clotting; encourages smoking and overeating.

    Hostility, anger

    Strongest personality risk (Type A, see Unit V).

    Depression

    Doubles the risk of heart disease and worsens recovery after a heart attack.

    Social isolation

    Low support increases risk; strong support protects.

    Behaviour

    Smoking, diet, inactivity, medicine adherence.

    Digestive system

    Structure and function

    Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small and large intestines, liver, pancreas. Breaks down food, absorbs nutrients and removes waste. The gut has its own nervous system (the "second brain") and strong links with the brain (gut–brain axis).

    Stress-related disorders
    • Peptic ulcer: sore in stomach or duodenum lining. Mainly Helicobacter pylori bacteria and painkillers (Marshall and Warren, Nobel 1982); stress, alcohol and smoking make it worse
    • Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS): pain with diarrhoea or constipation, strongly stress-linked
    • Acid reflux, indigestion, ulcerative colitis flares
    • Eating disorders: anorexia, bulimia, binge eating

    Psychological help: relaxation, CBT and gut-directed hypnotherapy for IBS; stress management; regular meals. Note: Brady's "executive monkey" ulcer study (1958) is now seen as flawed, but showed a stress link.

    Immune system

    Structure and function

    Defends against germs and cancer cells. Innate (non-specific): skin, mucus, inflammation, natural killer (NK) cells. Adaptive (specific): B cells (make antibodies) and T cells (destroy infected cells), with memory.

    Problems
    • Weak immunity: frequent infections, slower healing, HIV/AIDS (CD4 T cells destroyed)
    • Autoimmune disease: attacks own body (rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes)
    • Allergy: over-reaction to harmless substances

    Psychoneuroimmunology (PNI)

    The study of the links between psychological factors, the nervous system and the immune system. Chronic stress raises cortisol, which suppresses immune cells and slows wound healing; short stress can boost immunity.

    StudyFinding
    Ader & Cohen (1975)Rats were given saccharin water paired with an immune-suppressing drug. Later, saccharin alone suppressed immunity: conditioned immunosuppression.
    Kiecolt-Glaser et al. (1984)Medical students had lower natural killer cell activity during exams than during a calm time.
    Cohen et al. (1991)Volunteers were exposed to cold viruses; those with more life stress were more likely to develop colds (dose-response).
    Kiecolt-Glaser (1995)Wounds healed more slowly in people caring for relatives with dementia.

    Protective factors: social support, optimism, exercise, sleep, relaxation and meditation are linked to better immune functioning.

    Unit II self-test

    Two stress pathways?

    Sympathetic–adrenal-medullary (fast, adrenaline) and HPA axis (slower, cortisol).

    What is atherosclerosis?

    Narrowing of arteries by fatty plaque.

    Main cause of peptic ulcer?

    Helicobacter pylori infection (and painkillers); stress aggravates.

    What do NK cells do?

    Natural killer cells destroy virus-infected and cancer cells (innate immunity).

    What is PNI?

    Psychoneuroimmunology: study of links between psychology, nervous and immune systems.

    What did Ader and Cohen show?

    The immune system can be classically conditioned.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the relationship between psychological factors and the cardiovascular, digestive and immune systems. 10 marks
    1. Stress pathways (draw).
    2. Each system: structure, disorders, psychological links.
    3. PNI studies (table).
    Health Psychology · Unit III

    Health Behaviours and Changing Health Habits

    Health behaviours

    Health behaviour is any activity undertaken to maintain, protect or improve health (or, for risk behaviours, to harm it).

    Health-promoting

    Exercise, healthy diet, enough sleep, hygiene, relaxation.

    Preventive (Kasl & Cobb)

    Done by healthy people to prevent illness: screening, vaccination, brushing teeth.

    Illness behaviour

    Done when symptoms appear: seeing a doctor, resting.

    Sick-role behaviour

    Following treatment after diagnosis: taking medicines, rest (Parsons).

    Health-compromising

    Smoking, heavy drinking, junk food, unsafe sex, inactivity.

    Health habits

    A health habit is a health behaviour that has become automatic through repetition, often triggered by cues without thought (brushing teeth after waking). Habits start in childhood, are shaped by family and culture, and are hard to change because they are practised daily and rewarded.

    Why habits are hard to break: immediate rewards vs delayed harm; peer and cultural pressure; addiction; stress; feeling invulnerable (optimistic bias: "it won't happen to me"); lack of knowledge or skills.

    Attitude change and health behaviour

    Persuasive communication (Yale model)

    Credible and attractive communicator + clear, relevant message + receptive audience. Example: doctors' warnings, anti-tobacco advertisements.

    Fear appeals (Rogers: protection motivation)

    Fear works only when the message also gives an effective, doable action and builds confidence. Fear alone makes people avoid the message.

    Framing

    Gain-framed messages ("exercise keeps you healthy") work better for prevention; loss-framed ("not screening risks cancer") for detection.

    Cognitive dissonance

    Inconsistency between belief ("smoking is harmful") and behaviour creates tension that can motivate change, or be reduced by excuses.

    Attitudes alone do not change behaviour. That is why models such as the HBM and TPB (below) add beliefs about risk, norms and control.

    Health Belief Model (HBM)

    IR
    Irwin Rosenstock (1966), later Hochbaum, BeckerCreated in the 1950s by US public health psychologists to explain why people did not take up TB screening and vaccination.

    People take health action when they believe they are at risk, the problem is serious, the action will work and the costs are acceptable.

    ComponentMeaningExample: mammogram
    Perceived susceptibility"Could I get it?""My mother had breast cancer, so I may too"
    Perceived severity"How serious would it be?""It can be fatal"
    Perceived benefits"Will the action help?""Early detection saves lives"
    Perceived barriers"What does it cost me?""Pain, cost, embarrassment, fear of result"
    Cues to actionTrigger to actA doctor's reminder, a friend's diagnosis
    Self-efficacy"Can I do it?""I can arrange the visit"

    Evaluation: + simple, widely used for screening, vaccination, adherence; barriers are the best predictor. − ignores emotions, habits, social norms; does not explain how to change.

    Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB)

    IA
    Icek Ajzen (1991)Extended Fishbein and Ajzen's Theory of Reasoned Action (1975) by adding perceived behavioural control.
    • Attitude: beliefs about the outcome and how much it is valued
    • Subjective norm: what important others expect, and wish to comply with
    • Perceived behavioural control: how easy or hard the behaviour seems (similar to self-efficacy)
    • Predicts intention, which predicts behaviour. Limit: the "intention–behaviour gap" (we do not always do what we plan)

    Self-Determination Theory (SDT)

    Edward Deci and Richard Ryan (1985, 2000)People have three basic psychological needs; meeting them gives lasting motivation.Photo: Center for Self-Determination Theory, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
    Autonomy

    Feeling that I choose my actions.

    Competence

    Feeling effective and able to master the task.

    Relatedness

    Feeling connected and supported.

    Autonomous motivation (I want to exercise because I enjoy it or value health) lasts longer than controlled motivation (I exercise because my doctor scolds me). Health professionals should support autonomy: offer choices, explain reasons, avoid pressure.

    Self-regulation and health behaviour

    Self-regulation is directing one's own thoughts, feelings and actions toward goals (Carver & Scheier's feedback-loop model).

    Goal setting

    Specific, measurable, realistic goals ("walk 30 min, 5 days a week").

    Self-monitoring

    Track behaviour: food diary, step counter.

    Feedback and comparison

    Compare with the goal; adjust.

    Implementation intentions (Gollwitzer)

    "If X, then I will do Y": "If it is 6 am, I walk."

    Self-reward and coping plans

    Reward progress; plan for relapse.

    Self-efficacy (Bandura)

    Belief "I can do it" is the strongest predictor of change. Built by mastery, role models, encouragement.

    Stages of Change (Transtheoretical) Model

    JP
    James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente (1983)Studied how smokers quit on their own and found that change is a process in stages, not a single event.
    RememberP-C-P-A-M: "Please Change Poor Activity Modes." (Precontemplation, Contemplation, Preparation, Action, Maintenance; termination is sometimes added)

    Processes of change include consciousness raising, self-re-evaluation, social support, counter-conditioning, reinforcement management. Also decisional balance (pros vs cons) and self-efficacy. Evaluation: + practical, matches advice to readiness; − stages are arbitrary, change may be continuous.

    Unit III self-test

    Preventive, illness and sick-role behaviour?

    Preventive: by healthy people; illness: when symptoms appear; sick-role: after diagnosis, following treatment.

    Six components of the HBM?

    Susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, cues to action, self-efficacy.

    Three predictors of intention in TPB?

    Attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioural control.

    Three needs in SDT?

    Autonomy, competence, relatedness.

    What is an implementation intention?

    An if-then plan linking a cue to an action.

    Five stages of change?

    Precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance.

    Who proposed the stage model?

    Prochaska and DiClemente.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the Health Belief Model with its evaluation. 10 marks
    1. Origin; six components (draw and table).
    2. Example; strengths and weaknesses.
    Discuss theories for changing health habits. 10 marks
    1. Habits and attitude change.
    2. HBM, TPB (draw), SDT.
    3. Self-regulation; stages of change (draw).
    Health Psychology · Unit IV

    Health-Promoting and Health-Compromising Behaviours

    Exercise

    Benefits
    • Lowers risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, some cancers, osteoporosis
    • Controls weight and blood pressure; raises "good" HDL cholesterol
    • Improves mood, sleep, self-esteem; lowers depression and anxiety
    • Helps thinking and slows cognitive decline; lengthens life
    Recommendations (WHO)
    • Adults: 150 minutes a week of moderate activity (e.g. brisk walking) or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, plus muscle-strengthening on 2 days
    • Children and adolescents: about 60 minutes a day
    • Reduce sitting time

    Why people do not exercise: lack of time, low self-efficacy, no facilities or safe space, low enjoyment. Help: start small, choose enjoyable activities, goal setting and self-monitoring, social support (partner or group), implementation intentions. Yoga has well-documented benefits for stress and fitness.

    Sleep

    Need and cycle

    Adults need about 7–9 hours; teenagers 8–10; children more. Sleep cycles last about 90 minutes, moving through light sleep, deep (slow-wave) sleep and REM (dreaming).

    Effects of poor sleep

    Poor attention and memory, low mood, irritability, accidents, weaker immunity, higher risk of obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease. Insomnia is a common problem.

    RememberSleep hygiene: fixed bedtime and wake time; dark, cool, quiet room; no screens, caffeine or heavy meals before bed; daytime exercise and light; use the bed only for sleep; get up if awake for 20 minutes. CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment.

    Healthy diet

    • Balanced: fruits, vegetables, whole grains, pulses, nuts, adequate protein; limit salt, sugar, fried and processed food and saturated fat
    • Enough water; regular meals; portion control. In India: the Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI) promotes "Eat Right"
    • Benefits: lower risk of obesity, heart disease, diabetes, some cancers; better mood and energy
    • Problems: undernutrition and obesity side by side; eating disorders (anorexia, bulimia, binge eating)
    • Psychology of eating: eating is shaped by habits, stress (emotional eating), culture, family, advertising and availability. Dieting by strict rules often backfires; lasting change comes from small steps, self-monitoring and support

    Health-compromising behaviours

    Behaviours that increase the risk of illness, injury or early death: smoking, heavy drinking and drug use, unsafe sex, junk-food diets, inactivity, risky driving, non-adherence to treatment. Also called health risk behaviours or behavioural pathogens (Matarazzo).

    Characteristics

    Immediate reward, delayed cost

    Pleasure now; harm comes after years, so it is easy to ignore.

    Often begin in adolescence

    Linked to curiosity, identity, risk-taking and peer influence.

    Habit and dependence

    Become automatic and physically or psychologically addictive.

    Social and cultural support

    Shaped by peers, family, advertising, norms.

    Optimistic bias

    "It will not happen to me" (unrealistic optimism, Weinstein).

    Stress coping

    Used to cope with stress, boredom or negative mood.

    Cluster together

    Smoking, drinking and drug use often occur together.

    Changeable, but relapse-prone

    Quitting often takes several attempts.

    Remember"Immediate pleasure, Habit, Peers, Optimism, Stress": the reasons risk behaviours persist.

    Smoking: facts

    • Tobacco is the leading preventable cause of death. Smoking causes lung cancer, heart disease, stroke, chronic lung disease (COPD) and many other cancers; secondhand smoke harms others
    • India: more than a quarter of adults use tobacco in some form (GATS-2, 2016–17: 28.6%), including smoked (bidi, cigarette) and smokeless (gutka, khaini, paan masala) tobacco
    • Nicotine is highly addictive: it releases dopamine; withdrawal causes craving, irritability, poor concentration, anxiety, increased appetite

    Factors associated with smoking

    Biological

    Nicotine addiction; genetic differences in nicotine metabolism and receptors.

    Psychological

    Smoking to cope with stress or depression, to control weight, for pleasure; beliefs ("it relaxes me"); low self-efficacy to quit.

    Social and learning

    Modelling by parents, peers; advertising; classical conditioning (cues such as tea, alcohol and the end of a meal trigger craving); operant reinforcement.

    Socio-economic

    Higher in low-income and low-education groups; weak laws; cheap loose cigarettes and bidis.

    Interventions to reduce smoking

    LevelInterventions
    Prevention (before starting)School-based life-skills programmes (resisting peer pressure); parent education; media campaigns; ban on tobacco advertising; no sale to minors
    Brief adviceDoctor or health worker asks, advises, assesses, assists and arranges follow-up (the 5 A's); even 3 minutes helps
    MedicationNicotine replacement therapy (patch, gum, lozenge), bupropion, varenicline; roughly doubles quit rates
    Psychological therapyCBT (identify triggers, coping skills, relapse prevention), motivational interviewing (stages of change), contingency management, hypnosis, group programmes, aversion therapy (rapid smoking, now rare)
    Quitlines and appsTelephone and text support (India's National Tobacco Quitline)
    PolicyHigher tobacco taxes, pictorial health warnings, smoke-free public places (India: COTPA 2003, the Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act), plain packaging, the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) and MPOWER measures
    Remember5 A's: Ask about tobacco, Advise to quit, Assess readiness, Assist with a plan and medicine, Arrange follow-up.

    Relapse prevention: expect lapses; identify high-risk situations (alcohol, stress, other smokers); coping plans; do not treat a slip as total failure. Combined medicine + counselling works best.

    Unit IV self-test

    WHO exercise guideline for adults?

    At least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity (or 75 vigorous), plus muscle strengthening twice a week.

    How many hours of sleep do adults need?

    About 7–9 hours.

    Why do risk behaviours persist?

    Immediate rewards, delayed costs, habit, peers, optimistic bias and stress coping.

    What is optimistic bias?

    Believing that bad things are less likely to happen to oneself than to others.

    Why is nicotine addictive?

    It releases dopamine and causes withdrawal when stopped.

    What is COTPA?

    Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act, 2003 (India).

    The 5 A's?

    Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange.

    Long-answer outlines

    Discuss health-promoting behaviours: exercise, sleep and diet. 10 marks
    1. Exercise: benefits, WHO guidelines, barriers.
    2. Sleep: need, effects, hygiene.
    3. Diet: balanced diet, psychology of eating.
    Explain health-compromising behaviour with reference to smoking and its reduction. 10 marks
    1. Characteristics of risk behaviours.
    2. Smoking factors (biological, psychological, social); stages (draw).
    3. Interventions: drugs, therapy, policy.
    Health Psychology · Unit V

    Chronic Diseases: CHD, Hypertension and Diabetes

    Coronary heart disease (CHD)

    CHD (coronary artery disease) is the condition in which the arteries that supply the heart muscle become narrowed by atherosclerosis (fatty plaque). Reduced blood flow causes angina (chest pain) and, when a clot blocks an artery, a myocardial infarction (heart attack). It is the leading cause of death worldwide, and India has high rates, often at younger ages.

    Personality and CHD: Type A behaviour

    MF
    Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman (1959)Two cardiologists who noticed the "hurry sickness" of their heart patients and defined the Type A behaviour pattern.
    Type AType B
    Competitive, ambitious, achievement-drivenRelaxed, patient, easy-going
    Time urgency: always hurrying, impatientDoes not feel rushed
    Hostile, easily angered, irritableRarely angry
    Key study · Western Collaborative Group Study, 1960–69

    3,154 healthy men followed for 8.5 years

    Type A men had about twice the rate of CHD of Type B men, even after controlling for smoking, blood pressure and cholesterol.

    Later research found that being busy and ambitious is not the toxic part; hostility (cynicism, anger, mistrust) is the main risk. Type D (distressed personality: negative emotions plus social inhibition; Denollet) also predicts poor heart outcomes. Mechanisms: stronger stress reactivity, high blood pressure, more smoking and poorer coping and support.

    Prevention and psychological management

    Prevention
    • Primary: stop smoking, healthy diet, exercise, weight control, limit alcohol, manage stress, screen BP, cholesterol and sugar
    • Secondary: after a heart attack, prevent another
    Psychological management
    • Cardiac rehabilitation: supervised exercise, education, counselling
    • Stress management and relaxation; anger and hostility reduction (CBT); changing Type A behaviour (Friedman's Recurrent Coronary Prevention Project reduced second heart attacks)
    • Treat depression and anxiety; support adherence to medicines; family involvement
    • Lifestyle programmes (Ornish: diet, yoga, meditation, support)

    Hypertension (high blood pressure)

    A condition in which blood pressure remains persistently high, forcing the heart to work harder and damaging arteries. It is a "silent killer" because it usually has no symptoms, and a major risk for heart attack, stroke, kidney failure and dementia.

    Measurement

    With a sphygmomanometer (cuff) or digital monitor, in mmHg. Systolic pressure (heart contracting) is written over diastolic (heart relaxing), e.g. 120/80.

    Category (AHA/ACC 2017)SystolicDiastolic
    Normalbelow 120and below 80
    Elevated120–129and below 80
    Stage 1 hypertension130–139or 80–89
    Stage 2 hypertension140 or higheror 90 or higher
    Hypertensive crisisabove 180and/or above 120

    Many countries, including India, still use 140/90 as the cut-off. Diagnosis needs repeated readings. White-coat hypertension: BP rises only in the clinic (anxiety). Ambulatory monitoring checks BP over 24 hours.

    Causes
    • Essential (primary) hypertension: about 90–95%, no single cause; genes plus lifestyle
    • Secondary: kidney disease, hormone problems, drugs
    • Risk factors: high salt, obesity, inactivity, alcohol, smoking, ageing, family history
    • Psychological: chronic stress and high reactivity, anger suppression and hostility, anxiety, job strain
    Psychological management
    • Relaxation and meditation, yoga; biofeedback for BP and heart rate
    • Stress and anger management; CBT
    • Lifestyle: DASH diet, less salt, exercise, weight loss, quit smoking, limit alcohol
    • Adherence: reminders, simple regimens, patient education, self-monitoring at home

    Type 2 diabetes mellitus

    A chronic condition in which the body either becomes resistant to insulin or does not make enough, so blood glucose stays high. Insulin, made by the pancreas, moves glucose from blood into cells.

    PointType 1Type 2
    CauseAutoimmune destruction of insulin-making cellsInsulin resistance plus reduced insulin; lifestyle and genes
    OnsetChildhood or youthUsually adults (now also younger)
    ShareAbout 5–10%About 90%
    TreatmentInsulin alwaysLifestyle, tablets, insulin if needed
    Diagnosis (ADA)
    • Fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or more
    • HbA1c 6.5% or more (average over 2–3 months)
    • Random glucose 200 mg/dL or more with symptoms
    • Pre-diabetes: fasting 100–125 mg/dL; HbA1c 5.7–6.4%
    Symptoms

    Frequent urination, thirst, hunger, tiredness, blurred vision, slow wound healing, recurrent infections. Often silent for years. India has one of the largest numbers of people with diabetes (the "diabetes capital").

    Health implications

    Heart and vessels

    Heart attack, stroke, high blood pressure.

    Eyes

    Retinopathy: leading cause of blindness.

    Kidneys

    Nephropathy, kidney failure.

    Nerves and feet

    Neuropathy, foot ulcers, amputation.

    Mind and mood

    Depression (about twice as common), anxiety, diabetes distress, eating problems, cognitive decline.

    Psychological factors, prevention and management

    Psychosocial risk
    • Chronic stress raises cortisol and glucose and promotes overeating
    • Depression increases risk and worsens control (two-way link)
    • Poverty, urban lifestyle, low support, poor self-efficacy
    Prevention (Diabetes Prevention Program)
    • 5–7% weight loss and 150 minutes a week of activity reduced new diabetes by about 58% in high-risk people, more than medicine
    • Healthy diet, no smoking, screening
    Part of managementWhat and how psychology helps
    Self-managementDaily glucose monitoring, diet, exercise, foot care; self-efficacy and self-regulation (goal setting, self-monitoring)
    Medication adherenceReminders, simple regimens, address fears of insulin and side effects
    EducationDiabetes self-management education; family involvement
    Coping and emotionsTreat depression and diabetes distress; stress management; CBT; motivational interviewing
    Social supportFamily, peer groups; reduce stigma

    Unit V self-test

    What causes CHD?

    Atherosclerosis: narrowing of coronary arteries by fatty plaque.

    Who identified the Type A pattern?

    Friedman and Rosenman (1959).

    Which Type A component is most harmful?

    Hostility.

    What is Type D personality?

    Distressed: negative emotions plus social inhibition (Denollet).

    BP cut-off for stage 2 hypertension (AHA 2017)?

    140/90 mmHg or higher.

    Share of essential hypertension?

    About 90–95%.

    Fasting glucose and HbA1c cut-offs for diabetes?

    126 mg/dL or more; 6.5% or more.

    Type 1 vs type 2 diabetes?

    Type 1 is autoimmune and needs insulin; type 2 is insulin resistance, strongly lifestyle-linked.

    Long-answer outlines

    Discuss coronary heart disease: risk factors, personality and management. 10 marks
    1. Meaning; risk factors (draw).
    2. Type A, Western Collaborative Group Study, hostility, Type D.
    3. Prevention and psychological management.
    Explain hypertension and type 2 diabetes: causes and psychological management. 10 marks

    2. Diabetes: meaning, types, implications, prevention, self-management.
    Stress Management · Unit I

    Concept of Stress and Health

    What is stress?

    Hans Selye defined stress as "the non-specific response of the body to any demand made upon it". Lazarus and Folkman: stress arises when a person judges that the demands of a situation exceed their resources and endanger wellbeing.

    Stressor

    Anything that triggers stress: exam, noise, loss, a deadline.

    Stress response

    The body and mind's reaction: racing heart, worry, irritability.

    Stress as transaction

    The meaning a person gives the event. The same exam stresses one student and challenges another.

    Eustress vs distress (Selye)

    Eustress: positive, motivating stress (a wedding, a promotion, a competition). Distress: negative, harmful stress (bereavement, long unemployment).

    Acute vs chronic

    Acute: short and sharp (an argument). Episodic acute: frequent crises. Chronic: long-lasting (poverty, a bad job, caring for a sick relative). Chronic stress does the most harm.

    Sources of stress

    Life events

    Major changes: death, divorce, job loss, moving.

    Daily hassles

    Traffic, queues, arguments, deadlines (Lazarus): often more harmful than rare big events.

    Chronic strain

    Poverty, discrimination, illness, caregiving.

    Work and study

    Overload, little control, exams, role conflict.

    Conflict and frustration

    Approach–avoidance conflicts, blocked goals.

    Traumatic events

    Accidents, violence, disasters.

    Health and wellbeing

    Health (WHO)

    Complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, not only the absence of disease.

    Wellbeing

    Hedonic (feeling good, life satisfaction) and eudaimonic (meaning, growth, purpose; Ryff's six dimensions). Stress that is managed well can build wellbeing; unmanaged stress erodes it.

    Hans Selye (1907–1982)Hungarian-Canadian endocrinologist, the "father of stress research". Found that rats exposed to different harmful agents all showed the same pattern, which he published in 1936 and named the General Adaptation Syndrome in The Stress of Life (1956).Photo: Jean-Paul Rioux, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

    General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS)

    StageWhat happensBody
    1 Alarm reactionStressor perceived. Shock phase (resistance drops), then counter-shock (defences mobilised)Sympathetic arousal, adrenaline, fight or flight; heart rate and BP up
    2 ResistanceBody adapts and copes if the stress continues. Signs of stress seem to disappear, but resources are quietly used upHigh cortisol; resistance above normal to this stressor but lowered to others
    3 ExhaustionStress is prolonged or too severe; adaptation energy is gone. "Diseases of adaptation"Weak immunity, ulcers, high blood pressure, heart disease, depression, burnout; in extreme cases, death
    RememberA-R-E: Alarm → Resistance → Exhaustion.

    Evaluation: + showed the body-wide effects of chronic stress and laid the base for stress medicine. − Based on animals; ignores psychological appraisal (Lazarus); stress responses differ between people and stressors (not fully "non-specific").

    Walter Cannon (1871–1945)Harvard physiologist who coined "fight or flight" (1915, 1929) and "homeostasis".Photo: CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

    Fight-or-flight response

    An automatic emergency reaction that prepares the body to fight a threat or flee from it. It evolved to help our ancestors survive predators, but is triggered today by exams, traffic and arguments.

    Pathway 1: sympathetic–adrenal-medullary (seconds)

    Brain's threat centres (amygdala) → hypothalamus → sympathetic nervous system → adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline.

    Pathway 2: HPA axis (minutes)

    Hypothalamus releases CRH → pituitary releases ACTH → adrenal cortex releases cortisol, which keeps energy high and later switches off the response.

    Body changePurpose
    Heart beats faster, BP risesPump blood to muscles
    Breathing quickensMore oxygen
    Blood sugar released from liverQuick energy
    Blood flow diverted from gut and skin to musclesDigestion slows; skin pales
    Pupils dilate; senses sharpenSee and hear better
    Sweating; muscle tensionCool the body; ready to act
    Clotting increases; pain sensitivity fallsLimit bleeding and pain

    Beyond fight or flight: some people freeze, and Shelley Taylor (2000) proposed "tend and befriend" as a typical female response: protect offspring and seek social support.

    Stress and illness

    Stress contributes to illness directly (through hormones and the nervous and immune systems) and indirectly (smoking, drinking, poor sleep, comfort eating, skipping treatment).

    Effects of long-term stress

    Physical
    • High blood pressure, heart disease, stroke
    • Weak immunity: more infections, slower healing
    • Ulcers, IBS, headaches, back pain
    • Diabetes, weight gain; sleep problems
    Emotional
    • Anxiety, irritability, anger
    • Depression, feeling overwhelmed
    • Burnout (Maslach): exhaustion, cynicism, reduced achievement
    Cognitive
    • Poor concentration and memory
    • Indecision, negative thinking
    • Chronic cortisol can shrink the hippocampus
    Behavioural
    • Smoking, alcohol, drugs
    • Over- or under-eating
    • Withdrawal, accidents, work or study decline
    Key study · Holmes & Rahe, 1967

    Life events and illness

    People with a high total of life-change scores in the past year had a higher chance of illness in the next year. See Unit II for the scale.

    Key study · Cohen, Tyrrell & Smith, 1991

    Stress and the common cold

    Healthy volunteers dripped with a cold virus caught colds more often the higher their stress score.

    Moderators: perceived control, social support, coping style, personality (hardiness, optimism, Type A) and the nature of the stressor decide who becomes ill.

    Unit I self-test

    Selye's definition of stress?

    The non-specific response of the body to any demand made upon it.

    Eustress vs distress?

    Eustress is positive, motivating stress; distress is harmful stress.

    Three stages of GAS?

    Alarm, resistance, exhaustion.

    Who coined fight or flight?

    Walter Cannon.

    Two stress pathways?

    Sympathetic–adrenal-medullary (adrenaline, fast) and HPA axis (cortisol, slower).

    What is "tend and befriend"?

    Shelley Taylor's idea that women often respond to stress by protecting offspring and seeking social support.

    Name three effects of chronic stress.

    High blood pressure, weaker immunity and depression (also ulcers, burnout, poor memory).

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the concept of stress, its types and sources. 10 marks
    1. Definitions; stressor and response; eustress and distress.
    2. Acute, episodic, chronic; sources.
    3. Health and wellbeing.
    Describe Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome and fight-or-flight. 10 marks
    1. GAS graph (draw) and table; evaluation.
    2. Fight or flight: two pathways, body changes.
    3. Long-term effects of stress.
    Stress Management · Unit II

    Emotions, Stress and Coping

    RL
    Richard Lazarus (1922–2002) and Susan FolkmanStress, Appraisal and Coping (1984). Stress depends on how a person appraises a situation and whether they believe they can cope.

    Transactional model of stress and coping

    Coping strategies

    Problem-focused coping

    Act on the problem to change or remove the stressor: plan, seek information, study more, ask for help. Works best when the situation can be changed.

    Emotion-focused coping

    Manage the feelings: relax, talk to a friend, reappraise, pray, accept. Works best when the situation cannot be changed. Can be harmful if it becomes denial.

    Adaptive copingMaladaptive coping
    Active coping, planning, seeking social support, positive reframing, acceptance, humour, exercise, relaxation, religion or spirituality (when it brings comfort)Denial, avoidance, substance use, self-blame, behavioural disengagement, venting without change, rumination, self-harm

    Other classifications: approach vs avoidance (Roth & Cohen); meaning-focused coping. Best coping is flexible: matching the strategy to the situation. Defence mechanisms (Freud) are unconscious; coping is usually conscious.

    Social support

    Help and comfort from others. It both reduces stress and protects health. Evidence: people with strong social ties live longer (Berkman & Syme, 1979, Alameda County study).

    Emotional

    Care, empathy, listening ("I'm here for you").

    Instrumental (tangible)

    Practical help: money, time, a lift.

    Informational

    Advice and facts.

    Appraisal (esteem)

    Feedback and encouragement.

    Companionship

    Belonging and shared activity.

    Buffering hypothesis (Cohen & Wills, 1985)

    Support protects mainly when stress is high, by changing how the stressor is appraised and by providing help.

    Main-effect hypothesis

    Support benefits health at all stress levels through belonging and meaning.

    Perceived support (feeling that help is available) predicts wellbeing better than received support. Sources: family, friends, colleagues, community, faith groups, online groups. Indian family and community ties are a major strength.

    Negative emotions and stress

    Anxiety

    Anticipating threat; worry, tension. Chronic anxiety strains the heart and sleep.

    Anger and hostility

    Strongest emotional risk for heart disease. Both suppressed and explosive anger are harmful.

    Depression and helplessness

    Follows loss and uncontrollable stress; weakens immunity and motivation.

    Guilt, shame, loneliness

    Increase stress and lower health.

    Negative emotions affect health through stress hormones and through behaviour. They are also signals: the aim is to regulate, not to eliminate them.

    JG
    James Gross (1998)Process model of emotion regulation: we can regulate emotion at five points, from before the emotion starts to after it has begun.

    Emotion regulation

    Emotion regulation is the set of processes by which we influence which emotions we have, when we have them, and how we experience and express them.

    Coping resources

    Resilience

    The ability to adapt and bounce back after stress, adversity or trauma. Linked to a supportive relationship, self-efficacy, problem-solving, a sense of purpose and flexible thinking. It can be learned.

    Optimism

    Expecting good outcomes (Scheier & Carver, dispositional optimism; measured by the Life Orientation Test, LOT-R). Optimists cope actively, seek support and recover faster after heart surgery. Also the explanatory style (Seligman): attributing bad events to temporary, specific, external causes.

    Hardiness (Kobasa, 1979)

    The "3 C's": commitment, control, challenge. Hardy executives stayed healthier under stress.

    Others

    Self-efficacy, sense of coherence (Antonovsky), perceived control, hope, humour, spirituality.

    Assessment of stress and coping

    ToolWhat it measures
    Social Readjustment Rating Scale (Holmes & Rahe, 1967)43 life events with life-change units. Total over a year predicts illness
    Perceived Stress Scale (Cohen, 1983)10 items, how unpredictable, uncontrollable and overloaded life felt in the last month (0–4 scale)
    Hassles and Uplifts Scale (Lazarus)Daily minor stressors and positive events
    COPE / Brief COPE (Carver)Coping strategies, from problem-focused to avoidance
    Ways of Coping Questionnaire (Folkman & Lazarus)Thoughts and acts used in a specific stressful event
    DASS-21, GHQ-12Depression, anxiety, stress; general psychological distress
    Physiological measuresCortisol (saliva), heart rate and variability, blood pressure, skin conductance

    Examples from the Holmes–Rahe scale (life-change units)

    Unit II self-test

    Primary vs secondary appraisal?

    Primary: is the event a threat? Secondary: do I have the resources to cope?

    Problem-focused vs emotion-focused coping?

    Problem-focused tackles the stressor; emotion-focused manages feelings.

    Four types of social support?

    Emotional, instrumental, informational, appraisal.

    Buffering hypothesis?

    Social support protects mainly when stress is high.

    Best-supported strategy in Gross's model?

    Cognitive reappraisal.

    Kobasa's three C's of hardiness?

    Commitment, control, challenge.

    Which scale gives life-change units?

    Social Readjustment Rating Scale (Holmes and Rahe, 1967).

    How many items in the Perceived Stress Scale (Cohen)?

    10.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model and coping strategies. 10 marks
    1. Model (draw): primary and secondary appraisal.
    2. Problem-focused vs emotion-focused; adaptive vs maladaptive.
    Discuss social support, emotional regulation and coping resources. 10 marks
    1. Types of support; buffering vs main effect.
    2. Gross's model (draw).
    3. Resilience, optimism, hardiness; assessment tools.
    Stress Management · Unit III

    Relaxation and Biofeedback

    What is biofeedback?

    Biofeedback is a technique in which a person is given real-time information (feedback) about a body process they are normally unaware of, and learns to control it voluntarily. The screen or sound shows a change as it happens, so the person learns which thoughts and actions bring it about.

    Theory

    Operant conditioning

    A desired body change (lower heart rate) is reinforced by the feedback and the sense of success. Neal Miller (1960s) showed that rats could learn to change heart rate and blood flow, a result that began biofeedback; Joe Kamiya trained people to recognise alpha brain waves (1958–62).

    Awareness and self-efficacy

    Seeing the body respond builds awareness and the belief "I can control my stress".

    Relaxation response

    Feedback guides the person into a low-arousal state that opposes the stress response.

    Placebo and attention

    Part of the effect may come from expectation and focused attention. Evidence is best for headaches, hypertension and incontinence.

    Uses: stress, anxiety, tension and migraine headache, high blood pressure, Raynaud's disease, chronic pain, ADHD (neurofeedback), insomnia, urinary incontinence. Advantages: non-drug, no side effects, active role. Limits: needs equipment and training; takes many sessions; some people respond poorly.

    Biofeedback modalities

    ModalityMeasuresHow it relates to stressGoal
    GSR (galvanic skin response) or EDA (electrodermal activity)Skin conductance from sweat in the fingers or palmSweat glands are driven by the sympathetic system; conductance rises with arousal and emotionLower conductance
    Pulse / heart rate and HRV (ECG, photoplethysmography)Heart rate; heart rate variability (variation between beats)Stress raises rate and lowers HRV; relaxed breathing raises HRVLower rate; higher HRV (resonance breathing at about 6 breaths a minute)
    RespirationBreathing rate and pattern (belt sensor)Stress makes breathing fast, shallow and from the chestSlow, deep, diaphragmatic breathing
    Thermal (temperature)Fingertip skin temperatureStress narrows blood vessels in the hands, so fingers cool; relaxation warms themWarmer hands (for migraine, Raynaud's)
    EMG (electromyography)Muscle tensionTight muscles (forehead, neck) with stressReduced tension (headache, back pain)
    EEG (neurofeedback)Brain wavesAlpha (relaxed), beta (alert), theta, deltaTrain brain-wave patterns (ADHD, anxiety)
    RememberStress = GSR up, pulse up, breathing fast, hands cold, muscles tight. Biofeedback trains all of these in the opposite direction.

    Procedure: (1) explain and get consent; (2) attach sensors; (3) 2–5 minute baseline; (4) stress profile (mental arithmetic or a recalled stress) and recovery; (5) training with feedback; (6) home practice and generalisation. Typically 8–12 sessions.

    Relaxation techniques

    EJ
    Edmund Jacobson (1888–1983)Developed progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) in the 1920s–30s at the University of Chicago, in Progressive Relaxation (1938).
    TechniqueHow it works
    Progressive muscle relaxationTense, hold for about 5–7 seconds, then release each muscle group in turn (hands, arms, face, neck, shoulders, chest, abdomen, legs, feet) while noticing the contrast. Wolpe shortened it for desensitisation. Reduces muscle tension and anxiety.
    Diaphragmatic (deep) breathingSlow breath through the nose into the belly, longer exhale (e.g. 4 seconds in, 6 out). Activates the parasympathetic system. Related: pranayama (e.g. anulom vilom, bhramari).
    Autogenic training (Schultz, 1932)Repeat self-suggestions about heaviness and warmth in the limbs, calm heartbeat and breathing, cool forehead.
    Relaxation response (Benson, 1975)Four elements: a quiet place, a comfortable position, a mental device (a word or sound repeated), and a passive attitude. 10–20 minutes daily lowers heart rate, BP and oxygen use. A Western version of meditation.
    Guided imageryPicture a calm place with all senses (see Unit V).
    Yoga and yoga nidraPostures, breathing and guided deep relaxation; lowers stress and BP.
    Effects

    Slower heart rate and breathing, lower blood pressure, less muscle tension and cortisol, better sleep. The opposite of the stress response.

    Tips

    Practise daily, not only in crisis; choose a quiet time; start with 10 minutes; do not force relaxation. Caution in some medical conditions (e.g. avoid tensing injured muscles).

    Meditation

    Meditation is a family of practices that train attention and awareness to produce calm, clarity and emotional balance. It has roots in Indian and Buddhist traditions (dhyana in the eight-limbed yoga of Patanjali).

    Focused attention

    Rest attention on one object (breath, a mantra, a candle) and gently return when it wanders. E.g. concentrative meditation, Transcendental Meditation (TM), mantra and japa.

    Open monitoring

    Observe thoughts, feelings and sensations as they arise without judgement. E.g. mindfulness and Vipassana.

    Loving-kindness

    Cultivate goodwill toward self and others.

    Findings
    • Lowers anxiety, stress, depression and blood pressure
    • Better attention and emotion regulation
    • Brain scans show changes in the prefrontal cortex and a calmer amygdala
    • Experienced meditators show higher alpha and theta waves
    Cautions

    Effects are moderate; quality of research varies; a few people feel more anxious or distressed, so beginners with trauma need guidance. It supplements, not replaces, medical care.

    Unit III self-test

    Define biofeedback.

    Giving a person real-time information about a body process so they can learn to control it.

    Which learning theory underlies biofeedback?

    Operant conditioning (Neal Miller).

    What does GSR measure and how does it change with stress?

    Skin conductance from sweat; it rises with arousal.

    How does temperature change with stress and relaxation?

    Fingers cool with stress and warm with relaxation.

    Who developed progressive muscle relaxation?

    Edmund Jacobson.

    Four elements of Benson's relaxation response?

    Quiet place, comfortable position, mental device, passive attitude.

    Focused attention vs open monitoring meditation?

    Focus on one object vs observe all experience without judgement.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the concept, theory and modalities of biofeedback. 10 marks
    1. Meaning; loop (draw).
    2. Theory: Miller, operant conditioning.
    3. GSR, pulse, respiration, thermal, EMG, EEG (table); procedure.
    Describe relaxation and meditation techniques for stress. 10 marks
    1. PMR, breathing, autogenic, relaxation response (table).
    2. Meditation types; findings; cautions.
    Stress Management · Unit IV

    Psychological Approaches for Stress Management

    Psychoeducation

    Psychoeducation is the systematic teaching of information about a problem and ways to manage it, to people and their families, in a way that builds understanding and skills. It treats the client as an active learner.

    What is taught

    What stress is; how it affects body, thinking and behaviour; signs of overload; myths ("stress is weakness"); when to seek help.

    Skills taught

    Relaxation, time management, assertiveness, problem solving, sleep hygiene, healthy habits.

    Who and where

    Individuals, groups, schools, workplaces, patients and caregivers; workshops, leaflets, apps.

    1Assess

    Needs, current knowledge and beliefs.

    2Teach

    Simple, clear information; examples; visual aids.

    3Practise

    Role-play and exercises; home tasks.

    4Review

    Check understanding; address barriers; follow up.

    Benefits: reduces fear and stigma, improves adherence, builds self-efficacy and prevents relapse. Used widely in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, diabetes and heart disease as well.

    TD
    Thomas D'Zurilla and Marvin Goldfried (1971)Problem-solving therapy: stress often comes from how we handle problems, so teach a clear method.

    Problem-solving approach

    RememberD-B-E-A-R: Define, Brainstorm, Evaluate, Act, Review.

    Useful when: the stressor can be changed (money, conflict at work, study load). Evidence: effective for depression, anxiety and stress, including in primary care and older adults. Not enough alone for problems that cannot be changed; combine with emotion-focused skills.

    SD
    Steve de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg (1980s)Developed Solution-Focused Brief Therapy (SFBT) at the Brief Family Therapy Center, Milwaukee.

    Solution-focused brief therapy (SFBT)

    Instead of analysing the problem, SFBT builds solutions using what is already working. Therapy is brief (often 3–8 sessions) and centred on the client's goals.

    Miracle question

    "Suppose tonight a miracle happened and the problem was solved. What would be the first small sign tomorrow?"

    Scaling questions

    "On a scale of 0 to 10, where are you now? What would move you from 4 to 5?"

    Exceptions

    "When was the problem absent or less? What was different?" Spot and repeat times that went well.

    Coping questions

    "How have you managed so far?" Highlights strengths.

    Goal setting

    Small, specific, positive, realistic, behavioural goals.

    Compliments and tasks

    Affirm effort; give small experiments to do.

    Principles
    • If it works, do more of it; if not, do something different
    • Clients are the experts on their own lives
    • Small change leads to bigger change
    • Focus on the future, not the past
    Evaluation
    • + Brief, respectful, hopeful, suits school and workplace counselling
    • − Little attention to causes; evidence is moderate
    Jon Kabat-Zinn (b. 1944)Developed MBSR in 1979 at the University of Massachusetts Medical School for patients with chronic pain and stress. His definition: mindfulness is "paying attention in a particular way: on purpose, in the present moment, and non-judgmentally."Photo: ExperienceLifeMag, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

    MBSR

    Programme
    • 8 weeks, one weekly group session of 2–2.5 hours
    • Plus a full-day retreat and about 45 minutes of daily home practice
    • Taught in groups of 20–30 people
    Core practices
    • Body scan: attention moves slowly through the body
    • Sitting meditation: attention on the breath
    • Mindful movement (gentle hatha yoga)
    • Walking meditation; informal mindfulness in daily tasks (eating, listening)
    Seven attitudes (Kabat-Zinn)

    Non-judging · Patience · Beginner's mind · Trust · Non-striving · Acceptance · Letting go.

    How it helps

    Observing thoughts as passing events reduces rumination and automatic reactions; it changes our relationship to stress ("de-centring"), and calms the amygdala while strengthening prefrontal control.

    Evidence
    • Lowers stress, anxiety, depression and chronic pain; improves sleep and wellbeing
    • Related: MBCT (Segal, Williams and Teasdale) halves relapse in recurrent depression
    • Effects are moderate; mixed quality studies; not suited to everyone in acute crisis
    RememberMBSR = 8 weeks · body scan · sitting · yoga · retreat day, founded by Kabat-Zinn (1979).

    Unit IV self-test

    Define psychoeducation.

    Systematic teaching of information and skills about a problem to clients and families.

    Five steps of problem solving?

    Define, brainstorm, evaluate and choose, act, review.

    Who developed solution-focused therapy?

    Steve de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg.

    What is the miracle question?

    "If a miracle solved your problem tonight, what would be the first sign tomorrow?"

    Who developed MBSR and when?

    Jon Kabat-Zinn, 1979.

    Length and core practices of MBSR?

    8 weeks; body scan, sitting meditation, mindful yoga; plus a day-long retreat.

    Kabat-Zinn's definition of mindfulness?

    Paying attention on purpose, in the present moment, non-judgementally.

    Long-answer outlines

    2. Problem solving: five steps (draw), example, evaluation.
    Describe solution-focused therapy and MBSR. 10 marks
