    Stress Management · Unit V

    Other Approaches to Stress Management

    Coping skills training

    A structured programme that teaches and rehearses specific skills for handling stressful situations, usually in groups, with practice and feedback.

    Cognitive skills

    Spot and challenge negative thoughts; reframing; positive self-talk.

    Behavioural skills

    Time management, assertiveness, communication, relaxation, problem solving.

    Social skills

    Asking for help, building support.

    Lifestyle skills

    Exercise, sleep, diet, leisure.

    Stress Inoculation Training (SIT)

    Donald Meichenbaum (1985)Like a vaccine, gives the person small, safe "doses" of stress while building skills for larger ones.Photo: Rosiestep, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

    Self-observation, self-monitoring and self-control

    FK
    Frederick Kanfer (1970)Three-stage model of self-regulation: self-monitoring, self-evaluation, self-reinforcement.
    Self-observation / self-monitoring

    Deliberately recording one's own behaviour, thoughts and feelings with time, place and trigger. Example: a stress diary with situation, thought, body signs, 0–10 intensity, coping used. Shows patterns; often reduces the behaviour itself (reactivity).

    Self-evaluation

    Compare behaviour with the goal or standard.

    Self-control (self-reinforcement)

    Reward success; change triggers (stimulus control); make commitments; delay gratification. Includes thought stopping, scheduling worry time and goal setting.

    Self-instructional training

    Meichenbaum's method of teaching people to talk themselves through a stressful task with helpful inner statements. Based on Vygotsky's idea that children first regulate behaviour with spoken self-talk.

    PhaseSelf-statement example
    Preparing"What do I have to do? I have a plan. I can take it one step at a time."
    Confronting and handling"Relax, breathe slowly. One step at a time. It's not as bad as I thought."
    Coping with feeling overwhelmed"My heart is racing: that's a signal to use my skills. Pause and breathe."
    Reinforcing"I did it. Well done. I handled that better than last time."
    Modelling

    Therapist does the task and speaks aloud.

    Overt guidance

    Client does it while therapist instructs aloud.

    Overt self-guidance

    Client talks self through aloud.

    Faded overt

    Whispers.

    Covert self-instruction

    Silent inner speech.

    Guided imagery

    Using the imagination to create calming mental pictures, led by a guide, a recording or oneself. The brain responds to vivid imagery much as to real experience, so imagining a peaceful scene lowers arousal.

    1. Sit comfortably, close the eyes and relax with slow breathing
    2. Imagine a safe, calm place (beach, hill, garden) using all five senses: sights, sounds, smells, touch, taste
    3. Stay for 10–20 minutes, noticing how the body feels more relaxed
    4. Return slowly, then open the eyes

    Types: relaxation imagery; mental rehearsal of a performance (sport, interview, exam); healing imagery in pain and cancer care. Use in stress, anxiety, pain and sleep, and with desensitisation.

    Psychological immunity

    The idea that the mind has a "psychological immune system" that, like the body's, protects against stress and helps recovery. The concept is developed by Attila Oláh, and relates to the "psychological immune system" described by Gilbert and colleagues (1998): automatic mental processes that restore wellbeing after bad events.

    Components

    Optimism, sense of coherence, self-efficacy, hardiness, emotional regulation, social support, creativity and humour, spirituality and meaning.

    Building it

    Sleep, exercise, nutrition, relationships, gratitude and positive emotions (Fredrickson's broaden-and-build), mindfulness, meaning-making, learning from setbacks.

    Link to resilience

    Strong psychological immunity means quicker recovery and growth after adversity.

    Grounding techniques

    Simple exercises that bring attention back to the present moment and the senses during panic, flashbacks or intense distress, when the mind races or feels unreal.

    5-4-3-2-1 method

    Name 5 things you see, 4 you can touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste.

    Physical grounding

    Feel your feet on the floor; hold something cold or textured; splash water; press your palms together.

    Mental grounding

    Say your name, date and place; count backwards from 100 by 7; describe an object in detail.

    Breathing

    Slow breath with a longer exhale.

    Soothing

    Say kind words to yourself; think of a safe person or place.

    Common in treatment of panic, PTSD and dissociation. Choose methods that suit the person; avoid anything that feels like a trigger.

    Psychological first aid (PFA)

    A humane, supportive response to people in distress just after a crisis (disaster, accident, violence), given by trained helpers. WHO (2011) guide, based on research. It is not counselling or compulsory debriefing.

    Do
    • Be calm, kind and honest; respect privacy and choices
    • Provide basic needs (water, food, safety), information, contact with loved ones
    • Encourage use of own strengths and social support
    Don't
    • Force people to talk; push for details of the event
    • Promise what you cannot deliver; say "you'll be fine"; judge
    • Give false reassurance, advice or share private details

    Refer people with severe symptoms (suicidal thoughts, psychosis, severe panic or substance withdrawal) to professionals. India: NDMA guidelines include psychosocial support in disasters. Also look after the helper's own stress.

    Unit V self-test

    Three phases of stress inoculation training?

    Conceptualisation, skills acquisition and rehearsal, application and follow-through.

    Who developed SIT and self-instructional training?

    Donald Meichenbaum.

    What is self-monitoring?

    Deliberately recording one's own behaviour, thoughts and feelings, e.g. in a stress diary.

    Kanfer's three stages of self-regulation?

    Self-monitoring, self-evaluation, self-reinforcement.

    What does guided imagery use?

    Vivid, calming mental pictures involving all five senses.

    Explain the 5-4-3-2-1 technique.

    Name 5 things you see, 4 touch, 3 hear, 2 smell, 1 taste.

    The core actions of psychological first aid?

    Look, listen, link (after preparing).

    Is psychological debriefing part of PFA?

    No. PFA does not push people to talk about the event.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain coping skills training and stress inoculation. 10 marks
    1. Coping skills: cognitive, behavioural, social, lifestyle.
    2. SIT: three phases (draw).
    Describe self-monitoring, self-instructional training and guided imagery. 10 marks
    1. Kanfer's stages; stress diary.
    2. Self-instruction: phases and example statements.
    3. Guided imagery; psychological immunity.
    Write notes on grounding techniques and psychological first aid. 5 marks
    1. 5-4-3-2-1 and other grounding.
    2. PFA: look, listen, link (draw); do's and don'ts.
    Indian Psychology · Unit I

    Introduction to Indian Psychology

    What is Indian psychology?

    Indian psychology is the psychology that grows out of Indian thought and practice: its ideas about the self, mind, consciousness and well-being, found in the Vedas, Upanishads, the Gita, Yoga, Buddhism, Jainism and Ayurveda. It studies the whole person and sees growth as moving toward self-realisation.

    Psychology in India

    Western psychology (theories, tests) taught and practised in India. Largely imported.

    Indian psychology

    Psychology from the Indian tradition, using its own concepts (Atman, chitta, guna, karma) and methods (meditation, self-observation).

    AP
    Key scholarsJadunath Sinha (Indian Psychology, 3 volumes, 1933–58); K. Ramakrishna Rao and Anand Paranjpe (Psychology in the Indian Tradition, Handbook of Indian Psychology); Durganand Sinha, J. B. P. Sinha, Girishwar Misra, Ajit Dalal, Janak Pandey (Psychology for India); Indra Sen (integral psychology).

    History

    Vedic periodto about 500 BCE

    Rig Veda and Upanishads: the self (Atman), consciousness, four states of consciousness, the five sheaths (kosha).

    Classical period500 BCE–500 CE

    Six orthodox schools (Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta); Buddhism, Jainism; Patanjali's Yoga Sutras; the Bhagavad Gita; Ayurveda (Charaka, Sushruta).

    Medieval period

    Bhakti saints (Kabir, Mirabai, Tulsidas), Sufi mystics, Shankara, Ramanuja: devotion and inner transformation.

    Modern thinkers19th–20th c.

    Vivekananda (Raja Yoga), Sri Aurobindo (integral yoga), Gandhi, Tagore, Radhakrishnan, Krishnamurti.

    Academic psychology1915 onward

    First psychology department at Calcutta University (1915) with a laboratory (1916), under N. N. Sen Gupta. Indian Psychological Association formed in 1924. Girindrasekhar Bose founded the Indian Psychoanalytic Society (1922), an early Asian psychoanalyst who corresponded with Freud and proposed the "opposite wish" idea.

    Indigenisation1970s onward

    Indian psychologists question borrowed theories and develop culture-sensitive research and tools.

    Why indigenise psychology?

    Indigenisation means making psychology fit the culture it studies: its concepts, problems, methods and applications.

    Colonial imitation

    Indian psychology copied British and American models without checking whether they fit.

    Cultural mismatch

    Western ideas of an independent, separate self, individual achievement and happiness differ from Indian ideas of interdependence, duty and inner peace.

    WEIRD samples

    Most research uses participants from Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic societies (Henrich et al., 2010), who are not typical of humanity.

    Relevance to local problems

    Poverty, caste, joint family, migration, spirituality, traditional healing and the mental health treatment gap.

    Rich native resources

    Detailed theories of mind and methods of self-change already exist in the tradition.

    Better tools

    Scales and therapies need Indian norms, language and examples.

    Two routes (Kim & Berry, 1993)

    Indigenisation from without

    Take Western theories and tests and adapt them to India: translate, re-norm, modify.

    Indigenisation from within

    Start from local concepts and practices to build new theories (e.g. triguna personality, nishkama karma, atma-based self).

    Caution: indigenisation should not become narrow nationalism, nor reject all Western science. The aim is a global psychology enriched by many traditions (Durganand Sinha called for such a psychology).

    Core assumptions

    1 · Consciousness is basic

    Consciousness (chit) is not just a by-product of the brain. It is the ground of experience.

    2 · The person is more than body and mind

    A deeper Self (Atman) lies beyond the ego, and can be realised.

    3 · Holism

    Body, life-energy, mind, intellect and spirit are one connected system (five koshas).

    4 · Karma and continuity

    Actions have lasting effects (karma); impressions (samskaras) shape personality.

    5 · Goal: liberation and fulfilment

    Life aims at the four purusharthas and ultimately moksha (freedom).

    6 · First-person methods are valid

    Knowledge comes from direct experience (pratyaksha), inference (anumana) and reliable testimony (shabda), and from yogic self-observation.

    7 · Interconnectedness

    The self is related to family, society and cosmos; well-being is shared.

    8 · Human potential for transformation

    The mind can be trained and refined through practice (sadhana).

    Ashramas (stages of life)

    Brahmacharya (student), Grihastha (householder), Vanaprastha (gradual withdrawal), Sannyasa (renunciation). Like a life-span development model, each with its tasks.

    Pramanas (valid knowing)

    Pratyaksha (perception), anumana (inference), upamana (analogy), shabda (testimony). See Unit IV.

    RememberPurusharthas = D-A-K-M: Dharma, Artha, Kama, Moksha. Ashramas = B-G-V-S: Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha, Sannyasa.

    Schools of Indian philosophy (darshanas)

    SchoolFounder (traditional)Main ideaPsychological relevance
    NyayaGautamaLogic; four pramanasTheory of knowledge, perception and error
    VaisheshikaKanadaAtomism; categories of realitySoul and mind as substances; mind is atomic
    SamkhyaKapilaDualism of Purusha (consciousness) and Prakriti (matter); three gunasStructure of mind (antahkarana), personality, suffering and release
    YogaPatanjaliCalming the fluctuations of the mind; eight limbsPractical psychology of mental training and therapy
    MimamsaJaiminiDuty (dharma), ritual action, karmaAction, motivation and obligation
    VedantaBadarayana; Shankara (Advaita), Ramanuja, MadhvaAtman = Brahman; the world is illusion (maya) in AdvaitaSelf, ego vs Self, liberation by knowledge
    Charvaka (Lokayata)BrihaspatiMaterialism; only perception is valid; consciousness arises from matterAn early materialist, empirical view
    JainismMahavira (24th Tirthankara)Soul (jiva) and non-soul; ahimsa; anekantavada (many-sidedness)Non-violence, many perspectives, karma as matter
    BuddhismGautama BuddhaNo permanent self (anatta); suffering and its endMindfulness, craving, emotion and compassion

    Indian psychology and modern psychology

    PointModern (Western) psychologyIndian psychology
    AimDescribe, predict, control behaviour; adjustment, mental healthUnderstand consciousness; self-realisation, freedom (moksha), as well as adjustment
    View of the personIndividual with ego, personality, brainEgo plus a deeper Self; body–mind–spirit whole
    Mind and consciousnessMind from the brain; consciousness studied as a processConsciousness is basic; mind (manas, chitta) is its instrument
    MethodExperiment, tests, third-person observationFirst-person: introspection, meditation, yoga; also reasoning and texts
    Well-beingHappiness, life satisfaction, absence of disorderInner peace, ananda, equanimity, meaning
    EmotionRegulate, expressUnderstand and transform; detachment, witnessing
    SelfIndependent, autonomous (Western); self-esteemRelational and transcendent; reduce ego-centredness
    TimeThis life, evidence-basedIncludes karma and continuity beyond one life
    Points of contact
    • Mindfulness (MBSR, MBCT) from Buddhist practice
    • Yoga therapy in stress, depression and hypertension
    • Self-regulation; positive psychology (gratitude, compassion)
    • Humanistic, transpersonal and existential ideas (Maslow, Jung, May)
    Limits and criticisms
    • Some ideas (rebirth, subtle bodies) are hard to test
    • Texts are old, diverse, and sometimes contradictory
    • Risk of mixing religion and science, or of idealising the past
    • Needs empirical research with modern methods

    Relation: the two are best seen as complementary: Western psychology for rigorous methods and symptoms; Indian psychology for depth, meaning and growth.

    Unit I self-test

    Psychology in India vs Indian psychology?

    Psychology in India is Western psychology practised in India; Indian psychology draws on Indian concepts and practices.

    Who set up the first psychology department in India?

    Calcutta University (1915), led by N. N. Sen Gupta; the lab followed in 1916.

    What does WEIRD stand for?

    Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic.

    Indigenisation from within vs without?

    Within: build theory from local concepts. Without: adapt Western theories and tests.

    The four purusharthas?

    Dharma, artha, kama, moksha.

    Four ashramas?

    Brahmacharya, grihastha, vanaprastha, sannyasa.

    Astika vs nastika schools?

    Astika accept the authority of the Vedas (six schools); nastika do not (Charvaka, Jainism, Buddhism).

    Which school gave the Purusha–Prakriti dualism?

    Samkhya (Kapila).

    Long-answer outlines

    What is Indian psychology? Discuss its history and need for indigenisation. 10 marks
    1. Definition; psychology in India vs Indian psychology.
    2. Historical timeline; early academic psychology.
    3. Reasons for indigenisation; two routes; cautions.
    Explain the assumptions of Indian psychology and the schools of Indian philosophy. 10 marks
    1. Assumptions; purusharthas (draw); ashramas.
    2. Astika and nastika schools (tree and table).
    Compare Indian psychology with modern psychology. 5 marks
    1. Comparison table; points of contact; limitations.
    Indian Psychology · Unit II

    Yogic Psychology

    Antahkarana: the inner instrument

    In Samkhya, Yoga and Vedanta the mind is an inner instrument (antahkarana) with four functions that work together. It takes in what the senses bring, stores it, judges it and claims it as "mine".

    PartFunctionEveryday example
    ManasThe sensory mind: gathers data from the senses, forms options, doubts (sankalpa and vikalpa); links the senses to the intellect. Also called the "sixth sense"You hear a noise and wonder "what is that?"
    ChittaThe storehouse: memory, past impressions (samskaras), habits, the subconscious. In Yoga it is the whole "mind-stuff"You recall the voice from last week
    BuddhiThe intellect: judges, discriminates, decides, understands; the highest of the mind-instruments"It is a neighbour's radio, ignore it"
    AhankaraThe ego ("I-maker"): sense of "I" and "mine"; identity"My peace is disturbed"
    RememberM-C-B-A: "Many Clever Brains Ask": Manas (senses), Chitta (memory), Buddhi (decide), Ahankara (ego). Sometimes only three are counted (manas, buddhi, ahankara) with chitta as the base.

    Behind all of them stands Atman / Purusha, the pure witness. Suffering arises when we identify with the ego and mind rather than the witness.

    Pancha kosha: five sheaths of the person

    From the Taittiriya Upanishad: the Self is covered by five layers, from the grossest to the subtlest, like layers of an onion.

    KoshaMeaningDisturbanceYoga practice
    AnnamayaPhysical body, made of foodIllness, fatigueAsana, healthy diet
    PranamayaVital energy, breathLow energy, shallow breathPranayama
    ManomayaMind, emotion, sensory mindAnxiety, restless thoughtsPratyahara, chanting, devotion
    VijnanamayaIntellect and wisdomWrong views, confusionSelf-study, discrimination, jnana
    AnandamayaBliss, deep contentmentLack of meaningMeditation, samadhi

    A holistic model of well-being: illness or distress in one sheath affects the others; therapy can work on any layer. Compare with the biopsychosocial model.

    Prakriti and Purusha (Samkhya)

    Purusha

    Pure consciousness; the witness (sakshi). Eternal, unchanging, inactive, not made of the gunas. Many Purushas (one in each being).

    Prakriti

    Primal matter and energy: active, ever-changing, unconscious. Composed of three gunas: sattva, rajas, tamas. All of body, mind and ego are Prakriti.

    • Bondage comes from aviveka: not discriminating Purusha from Prakriti, i.e. taking "I am the body, mind or ego".
    • Liberation (kaivalya) comes from viveka-khyati: clear knowledge that Purusha is separate; suffering then ends.
    • Three gunas: sattva (light, clarity), rajas (energy, passion), tamas (inertia, dullness). Personality and mood reflect the dominant guna (see Units III–V).
    • Three types of suffering and their remedies appear in Unit V.
    PY
    PatanjaliCompiler of the Yoga Sutras (about 200 BCE–400 CE), 196 short aphorisms in four chapters (Samadhi, Sadhana, Vibhuti, Kaivalya). He defined yoga as "yogas chitta-vritti-nirodhah" (1.2): yoga is the stilling of the modifications of the mind.

    Vrittis: the five modifications of mind

    Pramana

    Valid knowledge (perception, inference, testimony).

    Viparyaya

    Misconception, wrong knowledge.

    Vikalpa

    Imagination, verbal delusion.

    Nidra

    Sleep.

    Smriti

    Memory.

    Chitta bhumis: five states of mind

    Panchkleshas: five afflictions

    Avidya

    Ignorance: seeing the impermanent as permanent, the non-self as Self. The root of all kleshas.

    Asmita

    Egoism: identifying with the body-mind.

    Raga

    Attachment to pleasure.

    Dvesha

    Aversion to pain.

    Abhinivesha

    Clinging to life; fear of death.

    RememberA-A-R-D-A: "All Ants Run, Don't Ask": Avidya, Asmita, Raga, Dvesha, Abhinivesha. Avidya is the soil from which the other four grow.

    Chitta prasadanam: clarity of mind (YS 1.33)

    The mind becomes clear and serene by cultivating attitudes (the four brahmaviharas) toward different kinds of people:

    Maitri

    Friendliness toward the happy (instead of envy).

    Karuna

    Compassion toward the suffering (instead of indifference).

    Mudita

    Joy toward the virtuous (instead of jealousy).

    Upeksha

    Equanimity toward the wicked (instead of anger).

    Also in the same chapter: breath regulation, focus on the senses, a luminous inner state, a steady object of meditation. The antarayas (obstacles): disease, dullness, doubt, carelessness, laziness, craving, false perception, failure to reach a stage and instability.

    Ashtanga yoga: the eight limbs

    LimbMeaningContents and psychological effect
    1 YamaRestraints (social ethics)Ahimsa (non-violence), satya (truth), asteya (non-stealing), brahmacharya (self-control), aparigraha (non-possessiveness). Reduce guilt, conflict and anger
    2 NiyamaObservances (personal discipline)Shaucha (cleanliness), santosha (contentment), tapas (discipline), svadhyaya (self-study), Ishvara pranidhana (surrender). Build contentment and resilience
    3 AsanaPosture: "steady and comfortable" (sthira-sukham)Physical health, body awareness, less tension
    4 PranayamaRegulation of breathCalms the autonomic nervous system; lowers anxiety and blood pressure
    5 PratyaharaWithdrawal of senses from objectsReduces distraction, over-stimulation
    6 DharanaConcentration: holding attention on one pointAttention control (ekagrata)
    7 DhyanaMeditation: unbroken flow of attentionStillness, clarity, insight
    8 SamadhiAbsorption; union of observer and objectHighest state; liberation from afflictions
    RememberY-N-A-P-P-D-D-S: "Your New Aunt Practises Peaceful Deep Dream Sleep." Dharana + dhyana + samadhi together are called samyama.

    Kriya yoga (YS 2.1)

    The "yoga of action", a practical path for ordinary people with a restless mind. It has three parts that weaken the kleshas:

    Tapas

    Disciplined effort; austerity; bearing discomfort.

    Svadhyaya

    Self-study and study of scriptures.

    Ishvara pranidhana

    Surrender of the fruits of action to a higher Reality.

    SA
    Sri Aurobindo (1872–1950)Philosopher-yogi, once a revolutionary. Founded an ashram in Pondicherry (1926) with Mirra Alfassa, "The Mother", and Auroville (1968). Works: The Life Divine, The Synthesis of Yoga, Savitri.

    Integral yoga

    Other paths aim to escape the world. Aurobindo's integral yoga aims to transform the whole of human nature and life through the descent of a higher consciousness ("All life is Yoga"). It synthesises karma, jnana and bhakti yoga.

    Three transformations
    1. Psychic: the inner soul comes forward and guides
    2. Spiritual: higher consciousness descends and calms the mind
    3. Supramental: full change of mind, life and body
    Method

    Three movements: aspiration (call), rejection (of ego, desire, doubt) and surrender (to the Divine). Work in daily life, not by withdrawing.

    Psychological ideas

    Psychic being vs ego; integral personality (physical, vital, mental, psychic); psychological transformation. Indra Sen developed integral psychology from this base.

    Implications for counselling and psychotherapy

    ConceptCounselling use
    Witness (sakshi bhava)Teach clients to observe thoughts and feelings without identifying with them: like mindfulness and cognitive defusion
    KleshasTreat attachment, aversion and fear of death as targets: grief, anxiety, addiction work
    Maitri-karuna-mudita-upekshaBuild compassion, reduce envy and anger; loving-kindness training
    Asana and pranayamaBody-based relaxation, stress and anxiety control, sleep
    Yamas and niyamasValues clarification, ethical living, self-discipline
    Pancha koshaHolistic assessment of the person on five levels
    Integral yogaPersonal growth, meaning, life-purpose work

    Evidence: yoga and pranayama reduce anxiety, depression and blood pressure in trials, and India's NIMHANS offers integrated yoga programmes. Use alongside evidence-based care, not as a substitute in severe illness.

    Unit II self-test

    Four parts of antahkarana?

    Manas, chitta, buddhi, ahankara.

    Five koshas from outer to inner?

    Annamaya, pranamaya, manomaya, vijnanamaya, anandamaya.

    Purusha vs Prakriti?

    Purusha is passive pure consciousness; Prakriti is active matter-energy made of three gunas.

    Patanjali's definition of yoga?

    Yogas chitta-vritti-nirodhah: yoga is the stilling of the modifications of the mind.

    Five chitta bhumis?

    Kshipta, mudha, vikshipta, ekagra, niruddha.

    Five kleshas?

    Avidya, asmita, raga, dvesha, abhinivesha.

    Four attitudes in chitta prasadanam?

    Maitri, karuna, mudita, upeksha.

    Three parts of kriya yoga?

    Tapas, svadhyaya, Ishvara pranidhana.

    Who proposed integral yoga?

    Sri Aurobindo.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the yogic concept of mind: antahkarana, pancha kosha, Prakriti and Purusha. 10 marks
    1. Antahkarana (draw and table).
    2. Pancha kosha (draw).
    3. Samkhya dualism; gunas; liberation.
    Discuss Patanjali's Yoga Sutras: chitta bhumis, kleshas, chitta prasadanam, ashtanga and kriya yoga. 10 marks
    1. Definition; vrittis; chitta bhumis (draw).
    2. Kleshas; four attitudes.
    3. Eight limbs (table); kriya yoga.
    Explain integral yoga and implications of yogic psychology for counselling. 10 marks
    1. Aurobindo's aim; levels of being; three transformations.
    2. Counselling applications (table); evidence.
    Indian Psychology · Unit III

    The Bhagavad Gita and Buddhism

    The Bhagavad Gita as psychology

    The Bhagavad Gita ("Song of the Lord", 700 verses in 18 chapters, part of the Mahabharata) opens with Arjuna's collapse on the battlefield: trembling, dry mouth, confusion, wanting to give up. Krishna acts like a counsellor, helping him restore clarity and act. Many psychologists treat it as a manual of coping, motivation and personality.

    Atman (the Self)

    The real Self is eternal, unborn and unchanging: "it is not born, nor does it ever die" (2.20). The body is like a garment that is changed (2.22). Grief arises from identifying with the body. Realising the Atman gives freedom from fear.

    Mind (manas)

    The mind is restless, turbulent and hard to control (6.34), yet can be trained by abhyasa (practice) and vairagya (detachment) (6.35). It can be a friend or an enemy of the self (6.5–6.6). Senses pull the mind like a ship in a storm (2.67).

    Personality: the three gunas (triguna)

    All beings are shaped by the three gunas of Prakriti (chapters 14, 17, 18). Everyone has all three, but one usually dominates.

    QualitySattvaRajasTamas
    NaturePurity, light, balancePassion, activity, cravingInertia, darkness, delusion
    MindCalm, clear, wiseRestless, greedy, ambitiousDull, confused, careless
    EffectBinds by happiness and knowledgeBinds by attachment to actionBinds by ignorance and sleep
    ActionDone as duty without attachmentDone for reward, with ego and strainDone without thought, harmful, or neglected
    Food preferenceFresh, nourishing, lightSpicy, salty, very hotStale, impure, heavy
    ResultHigher states, health, peacePain, restlessnessIgnorance, lower states
    RememberS-R-T = Sereneity, Restlessness, Torpor. The aim is to rise toward sattva and finally go beyond all three (gunatita).

    Svabhava and svadharma

    Svabhava

    One's inborn nature, formed by the gunas and past impressions. Like temperament and traits; it drives behaviour (3.33).

    Svadharma

    The duty and role that suits one's own nature. "Better is one's own dharma, though imperfect, than the dharma of another well performed" (3.35, 18.47). Psychologically: person–environment fit and authentic living.

    The Gita links gunas and action to four types of duty (guna-karma); later history turned this into a rigid caste system, which modern readers criticise. The psychological core is: find work that fits your nature and do it with the right attitude.

    The three yogas of the Gita

    Karma Yoga (ch. 3, 5)
    • Nishkama karma: act without attachment to results
    • "You have a right to action alone, never to its fruits" (2.47)
    • "Yoga is skill in action" (2.50): equanimity in success and failure
    • Work as yajna: an offering, not for ego
    • Psychology: reduces performance anxiety, burnout and outcome-attachment; links with intrinsic motivation and flow
    Jnana Yoga (ch. 4, 13)
    • Knowledge that the Self is separate from body, mind and ego (viveka, discrimination)
    • The sthitaprajna (steady-minded person, 2.54–72) is unmoved by pain and pleasure, free from desire, fear and anger; sense-control like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs
    • Psychology: cognitive restructuring, insight, equanimity
    Bhakti Yoga (ch. 12)
    • Love and devotion; surrender (sharanagati, 18.66)
    • Qualities of the devotee: friendly, compassionate, free from ego, even-minded in pain and pleasure
    • Psychology: faith, hope, meaning and social support; emotion channelled toward a higher purpose
    PointKarmaJnanaBhakti
    Faculty usedWill and actionIntellectEmotion, heart
    Core practiceSelfless dutyStudy, reflection, discriminationPrayer, devotion, surrender
    RemovesAttachment to resultsIgnorance (avidya)Ego and separateness
    Modern parallelIntrinsic motivation, acceptanceCognitive therapy, insightSpirituality, social bonding

    Chapter 6 teaches dhyana yoga: a steady seat, moderation in food and sleep ("yoga is not for one who eats too much or too little", 6.16–17) and meditation. Evidence for Gita-based counselling is growing but mostly small studies.

    GB
    Gautama Buddha (about 563–483 BCE; some scholars give later dates)Prince Siddhartha of the Shakya clan, born at Lumbini. He renounced palace life, attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, and taught at Sarnath ("first sermon") and elsewhere for about 45 years.

    Concept of anatta (no-self)

    Buddhism denies a permanent, independent Self. What we call a "person" is a changing process of five aggregates (skandhas):

    Rupa

    Material form, the body.

    Vedana

    Feeling: pleasant, unpleasant, neutral.

    Sanna (samjna)

    Perception, recognition, labelling.

    Sankhara (samskara)

    Mental formations: habits, intentions, will.

    Vinnana (vijnana)

    Consciousness, awareness of objects.

    The three marks of existence: anicca (impermanence), dukkha (suffering, unsatisfactoriness) and anatta (no-self). Clinging to a fixed "I" and to permanent things causes suffering. The chariot analogy (Milinda Panha): a chariot is only parts, not something separate; so is the self.

    Dependent origination (paticca-samuppada): everything arises from conditions: a chain of 12 links from ignorance to craving, clinging, becoming and suffering. Break the chain at craving.

    The Four Noble Truths

    The Noble Eightfold Path

    GroupFactorMeaning
    Prajna (wisdom)1 Right viewUnderstand the Four Noble Truths, impermanence, karma
    2 Right intentionResolve for renunciation, goodwill, non-harm
    Sila (ethical conduct)3 Right speechTruthful, kind, helpful; no lying, gossip or harsh words
    4 Right actionNo killing, stealing or sexual misconduct
    5 Right livelihoodEarn a living without harming others
    Samadhi (mental discipline)6 Right effortPrevent and abandon unwholesome states; cultivate wholesome ones
    7 Right mindfulnessPresent-moment awareness of body, feelings, mind and mental objects (satipatthana)
    8 Right concentrationOne-pointed meditation (jhana)
    RememberV-I-S-A-L-E-M-C: View, Intention, Speech, Action, Livelihood, Effort, Mindfulness, Concentration. Grouped as W-E-M: Wisdom (1–2), Ethics (3–5), Mind training (6–8).

    Schools of Buddhism

    SchoolKey ideasPsychological relevance
    TheravadaEarliest surviving school; follows the Pali canon; ideal is the arhat who frees himself; vipassana (insight) meditationBasis of mindfulness practice and MBSR
    MahayanaIdeal is the bodhisattva who delays nirvana to help all beings; compassion (karuna) and wisdom (prajna). Schools: Madhyamaka (Nagarjuna: all things are empty, sunyata); Yogachara (Vijnanavada: only mind/consciousness is real); Zen (sudden insight by sitting meditation); Pure LandCompassion training; emptiness of self; mind-only theories relevant to perception; Zen influence on therapy
    VajrayanaTibetan Buddhism; tantra, mantra, visualisation, guruVisualisation and mantra techniques; Tibetan models of mind and death

    Four classical Indian philosophical schools: Vaibhashika and Sautrantika (realist), Madhyamika (Shunyavada) and Yogachara (Vijnanavada). Councils (Rajgir, Vaishali, Pataliputra, Kashmir) shaped the sects.

    Implications for counselling and psychotherapy

    Buddhist ideaApplication
    Mindfulness (sati)MBSR (Kabat-Zinn), MBCT (relapse prevention in depression), DBT (mindfulness and radical acceptance), ACT (acceptance and present-moment awareness)
    Dukkha and acceptanceNormalise suffering; accept what cannot be changed; reduce the "second arrow" (suffering added by resisting pain)
    Craving and attachmentWork with addiction (mindfulness-based relapse prevention), perfectionism, and grief
    ImpermanenceGrief and loss; coping with illness and ageing. Story of Kisa Gotami and the mustard seed: she learns that every household knows death
    AnattaLoosen rigid identity ("I am a failure"); self-compassion
    Loving-kindness and compassion (metta, karuna)Reduce anger and shame; improve relationships and empathy
    Right speech, action, livelihoodEthical living, communication skills, work-life balance
    Eightfold PathA complete treatment plan: view, ethics and mental training

    Comparison with the Gita: both seek freedom from suffering and equanimity; the Gita affirms an eternal Atman, Buddhism denies a permanent self.

    Unit III self-test

    Three gunas?

    Sattva, rajas, tamas.

    Svabhava vs svadharma?

    Svabhava is one's inborn nature; svadharma is the duty suited to that nature.

    Gita verse on action and fruits?

    2.47: right to action alone, never to its fruits.

    Who is the sthitaprajna?

    The steady-minded person, unmoved by pain, pleasure, desire, fear or anger (2.54–72).

    Three yogas of the Gita?

    Karma (action), jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion).

    Five skandhas?

    Rupa, vedana, sanna, sankhara, vinnana.

    Four Noble Truths?

    Dukkha, its origin (craving), its cessation (nirvana), the path (Eightfold).

    Three groups of the Eightfold Path?

    Wisdom (prajna), ethics (sila), mental discipline (samadhi).

    Three main schools of Buddhism?

    Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana.

    Indian Psychology · Unit IV

    Indian Psychological Thoughts

    The self in Indian thought

    TraditionView of the self
    Upanishads / VedantaAtman is the real Self, pure consciousness (sat-chit-ananda: being, awareness, bliss). Advaita (Shankara): Atman = Brahman ("tat tvam asi", "that thou art"; "aham brahmasmi"). Method of "neti, neti" (not this, not this): remove what is not the Self (body, mind, ego)
    Samkhya / YogaPurusha: pure witness, distinct from Prakriti (mind and body)
    Nyaya-VaisheshikaThe self is an eternal substance; consciousness is its quality that appears with the body
    BuddhismAnatta: no permanent self; a stream of aggregates
    JainismJiva: the soul, conscious, eternal, many, with infinite potential covered by karma
    CharvakaThe self is only the body with consciousness

    Self and ego: the Indian view separates the ego (ahankara: "I" and "mine", the small self) from the Self (Atman). Growth means reducing ego-centredness. Compare with Western ideas of an independent self (Markus and Kitayama) and Jung's Self.

    Mind (manas) and consciousness

    Mind

    In Nyaya the mind is the inner sense organ (antarindriya) that links the soul with the senses; it is atomic and only one thing can be attended to at a time. In Samkhya and Yoga it is the antahkarana (Unit II). In Buddhism the mind is the sixth sense.

    Consciousness

    The Vedanta view: consciousness (chit) is fundamental and self-luminous; mind and matter appear in it. Buddhism: vinnana is conditioned and arises dependent on contact. Samkhya: Purusha is consciousness; Prakriti is unconscious.

    Four states of consciousness (Mandukya Upanishad)

    The Mandukya Upanishad analyses the sacred syllable AUM as the three states plus the silence of turiya. Modern link: waking, REM dreaming, NREM deep sleep, and meditative awareness; turiya has no modern equivalent.

    Spirituality

    In the Indian tradition, spirituality is the search for and realisation of one's deepest Self and its unity with all, expressed in ethical living, inner discipline and compassion. It is wider than organised religion.

    Sadhana

    Spiritual practice: meditation, prayer, yoga, service, study.

    Moksha

    Liberation: freedom from suffering, ego and ignorance.

    Ananda

    Deep joy and peace independent of circumstances.

    Seva

    Selfless service as a path.

    Dharma

    Living by values and duties.

    Satsang and guru

    Company of the wise; guidance by a teacher.

    Spirituality and mental health

    Research links spiritual practice to lower stress and depression, better coping, meaning in life and social support. Risks: spiritual bypassing (avoiding real problems) and harmful guru dependency. A counsellor should respect the client's beliefs, assess their role in coping, and refer when needed (see Pant, 2023).

    Modern Indian thinkers
    • Vivekananda: each soul is potentially divine; Raja Yoga; strength and service
    • Aurobindo: integral yoga; evolution of consciousness
    • Gandhi: truth (satya) and non-violence (ahimsa) as spiritual action
    • Tagore: harmony with nature and humanity
    • Krishnamurti: choiceless awareness
    • Radhakrishnan: philosophy as a way of life

    Indian models of personality

    No single theory; several traditions give models that stress inner qualities and development, not only traits.

    SourceModel
    Samkhya / GitaTriguna: sattva, rajas, tamas. Personality = the mix of gunas; svabhava = inborn nature
    YogaPersonality is shaped by samskaras (impressions) and kleshas; development = purifying the mind and moving toward the witness
    Vedanta (pancha kosha)Personality as five layers from body to bliss
    AyurvedaPrakriti (Vata, Pitta, Kapha) plus mental constitution by gunas (Unit V)
    AurobindoPhysical, vital, mental, psychic being; the true personality emerges from the psychic centre
    VivekanandaCharacter = the sum of one's tendencies (samskaras); change by new habits and thoughts
    AshramasDevelopmental stages with different tasks across the life span

    Research on triguna

    • Indian psychologists built triguna scales (e.g. work by Sandhu, Mohan, and Kapur in the 1980s–90s) and Wolf's Vedic Personality Inventory (1998) to measure sattva, rajas and tamas.
    • Findings are mixed: sattva tends to go with well-being, conscientiousness and agreeableness; rajas with achievement and also stress; tamas with low mood and indifference. These links are approximate, not a proven match with Big Five traits.
    PointWestern trait modelsIndian triguna model
    Nature of traitsFairly fixed dispositionsChangeable by practice; guna balance can be shifted
    IdealAdjustment; healthy range of traitsRise toward sattva and beyond the gunas
    Includes spiritual dimension?No (usually)Yes
    MeasurementFactor-analytic scales (e.g. NEO)Triguna scales, VPI; still developing

    Cognition: sources of valid knowledge (pramanas)

    A pramana is a valid means of knowing. Schools differ in how many they accept.

    PramanaMeaningExample
    PratyakshaDirect perceptionSeeing a pot
    AnumanaInferenceSmoke on the hill, so there is fire
    UpamanaComparison or analogyA gavaya (wild ox) is like a cow
    ShabdaReliable testimony (speech of an expert, scripture)A doctor's word about a disease
    ArthapattiPresumptionDevadatta is fat but does not eat by day, so he eats at night
    AnupalabdhiNon-perceptionKnowing a pot is absent from the table
    SchoolAccepts
    CharvakaPerception only
    Buddhists and VaisheshikaPerception and inference
    Samkhya and YogaPerception, inference, testimony (3)
    NyayaPerception, inference, comparison, testimony (4)
    Mimamsa (Prabhakara, Bhatta) and Advaita VedantaAll six
    RememberP-A-U-S-A-A: Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana, Shabda, Arthapatti, Anupalabdhi.

    Process of perception (Nyaya)

    Perception happens through a chain of contact: Self (Atman) ↔ Mind (manas) ↔ Sense organ ↔ Object. First there is nirvikalpaka (indeterminate, bare awareness of "something"), then savikalpaka (determinate: "this is a pot", with name and class). Compare with sensation and perception in cognitive psychology.

    Memory (smriti)

    Recall of earlier impressions (samskaras). Seen as a mental vritti in Yoga.

    Error (khyati)

    Illusions such as taking a rope for a snake; theories of error differ by school (anyathakhyati, anirvachaniya-khyati). Advaita uses the rope–snake example for ignorance of the Self.

    Emotions in Indian thought

    Rasa theory (Bharata, Natyashastra)

    Bharata's Natyashastra (about 200 BCE–200 CE), the Indian treatise on drama, describes rasa, the "flavour" of emotion felt by an audience. Each rasa grows from a stable emotion (sthayi bhava).

    RasaMeaningStable emotion (sthayi bhava)
    ShringaraLove, beautyRati (love)
    HasyaHumourHasa (laughter)
    KarunaCompassion, pathosShoka (sorrow)
    RaudraAngerKrodha (anger)
    VeeraHeroism, courageUtsaha (energy)
    BhayanakaTerrorBhaya (fear)
    BibhatsaDisgustJugupsa (disgust)
    AdbhutaWonderVismaya (surprise)
    ShantaPeace, serenity (added later; Abhinavagupta)Shama / nirveda (calm)

    Compare with Ekman's six basic emotions. The Indian view adds a ninth, peace (shanta), as the final aim of emotional life.

    Emotions and the self

    Six enemies (shadripu / arishadvarga)

    Kama (lust, desire), krodha (anger), lobha (greed), moha (delusion, infatuation), mada (pride), matsarya (envy). Unregulated passions that disturb the mind.

    Kleshas and vrittis

    Emotions are modifications of the mind; raga and dvesha are the root of emotional suffering (Unit II).

    Regulation

    Not suppressing but witnessing (sakshi), detachment (vairagya), equanimity (samatva in the Gita), pranayama, meditation, and cultivating maitri, karuna, mudita.

    Sthitaprajna

    The ideal: emotionally stable, "the same in pleasure and pain" (Gita 2.56).

    Sleep and dreams

    Upanishadic view

    Three states: waking, dreaming, deep sleep. In dreams the mind creates its own world from impressions (samskaras) of waking life (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad); in deep sleep the mind rests and the person is united with the Self without knowing it, which explains refreshment. Turiya is awareness that witnesses all three.

    Yoga

    Nidra (sleep) is one of the five vrittis: a mental state with no content. Yoga nidra is guided deep relaxation between waking and sleep. A yogi aims to remain aware (witness) even in sleep.

    Ayurveda

    Sleep (nidra) is one of the three pillars of life (trayopastambha) with ahara (food) and brahmacharya (regulated living). Tamas promotes sleep; excess Vata causes insomnia; excess Kapha, oversleep. Charaka describes seven kinds of dreams: seen, heard, experienced, desired, imagined, premonitory and those caused by a disturbed body.

    Compare with modern psychology

    Freud: dreams are wish-fulfilment from the unconscious; Indian: dreams reflect samskaras and the mind's creative power, and may carry meaning. Sleep research: NREM and REM stages.

    Sleep hygiene in the tradition: early to bed and rising before dawn (brahma muhurta), light dinner, fixed routine.

    Unit IV self-test

    What is "neti neti"?

    "Not this, not this": the Upanishadic method of negating what is not the Self.

    Four states of consciousness (Mandukya)?

    Jagrat, svapna, sushupti, turiya.

    Which sound corresponds to waking, dream and deep sleep?

    A, U and M of AUM.

    Ego vs Self in Indian thought?

    Ahankara is the small self ("I and mine"); Atman is the real Self.

    Six pramanas?

    Pratyaksha, anumana, upamana, shabda, arthapatti, anupalabdhi.

    Nirvikalpaka vs savikalpaka perception?

    Indeterminate (bare awareness) vs determinate (named, classified).

    Who gave the rasa theory? How many rasas?

    Bharata (Natyashastra); eight, with shanta added as the ninth.

    Six enemies of the mind?

    Kama, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, matsarya.

    How many types of dreams in Charaka?

    Seven.

    Long-answer outlines

    Discuss notions of self, mind, consciousness and spirituality in Indian thought. 10 marks
    1. Self in each tradition (table); ego vs Self.
    2. Mind; consciousness; four states (draw).
    3. Spirituality; links to mental health.
    Explain Indian views on personality and cognition. 10 marks
    1. Personality models; triguna and VPI; compare with Western traits.
    2. Pramanas (table); Nyaya perception.
    Write notes on emotions, sleep and dreams in Indian psychology. 10 marks
    1. Rasa theory (table); six enemies; regulation.
    2. Sleep and dream in Upanishads, Yoga, Ayurveda.
    Indian Psychology · Unit V

    Ayurveda and Psychology

    Ayurveda: the science of life

    Ayurveda (ayus life + veda knowledge) is India's traditional system of medicine, systematised in the Charaka Samhita (medicine) and Sushruta Samhita (surgery), with Ashtanga Hridaya (Vagbhata). It treats the person as body, senses, mind and soul together.

    Definition of health (Sushruta)

    One is healthy whose doshas, digestive fire (agni), tissues (dhatus) and wastes (malas) are in balance, and whose soul, senses and mind are cheerful (prasanna atmendriya manah). So mental well-being is part of the definition of health.

    The mind (manas) in Ayurveda

    • The mind is a sense organ (the 11th indriya) and also the controller of the other senses; it is the link between the soul and the body
    • Its seat is the heart (hridaya); it is one (ekatva: one thought at a time) and subtle (anutva)
    • Functions: cintya (thinking), vicharya (reasoning), uhya (imagination), dhyeya (aim), sankalpya (resolve): sense control, self-control, reasoning, memory
    • Mental qualities come from the gunas: sattva (pure), rajas and tamas. Rajas and tamas are called the manasika doshas (mental doshas)
    • Mental illness (unmada: psychosis; apasmara: epilepsy; atattvabhinivesha: false belief) arises from imbalance of doshas, bad conduct, emotional shock and stress (chittodvega)

    Three kinds of treatment (Charaka)

    Daivavyapashraya

    Spiritual or faith therapy: mantras, rituals, charity, pilgrimage, prayer, wearing of gems.

    Yuktivyapashraya

    Rational therapy: diet, medicines (including herbs), cleansing (panchakarma), lifestyle.

    Sattvavajaya

    Psychotherapy: restraining the mind from unwholesome objects by knowledge, patience, memory, concentration and counselling (jnana, vijnana, dhairya, smriti, samadhi).

    RememberD-Y-S: Daiva (faith), Yukti (rational), Sattvavajaya (psychological).

    Tridosha: the three bodily humours

    Everything in the body works through three functional principles made from the five elements (mahabhutas): Vata (air + space), Pitta (fire + water), Kapha (earth + water).

    Prakriti (constitution)

    Your natural dosha mix, fixed at conception, giving body type and temperament (e.g. Vata-Pitta). Like a personality-plus-body typology.

    Vikriti

    The current imbalance that causes illness. Treatment aims to return to prakriti.

    Triguna: the mental constitution

    Mind types are described by the dominant guna (manasa prakriti). Charaka lists sixteen types: seven sattvic, six rajasic and three tamasic, named after qualities of gods, humans and animals.

    GunaSattvaRajasTamas
    Mental traitsClarity, compassion, truthful, self-controlledAmbitious, impulsive, angry, greedyDull, lazy, fearful, ignorant
    Mental healthResilientProne to anxiety, maniaProne to depression, dementia
    RolePureMental doshaMental dosha

    Link between the two systems: Vata and Pitta go with rajas; Kapha goes with tamas in a rough way. Physical doshas (vata, pitta, kapha) vs mental doshas (rajas, tamas) is a key exam point.

    Three kinds of suffering (tapatraya)

    Samkhya opens with the question: how do we end the threefold suffering? Ayurveda and Yoga take the same classification.

    TypeModern parallelCounselling response
    AdhyatmikBiological and psychological stressorsTreatment, coping skills, mindfulness
    AdhibhautikSocial and interpersonal stress (violence, discrimination, family conflict)Safety, social support, assertiveness, community action
    AdidaivikEnvironmental stress and disasters; existential limitsDisaster preparedness, psychological first aid, meaning and acceptance
    RememberAdhi + Atma / Bhuta / Daiva = self / other beings / nature and fate. Inside → people around → forces beyond.

    Yajna

    Yajna (from yaj, to worship, give, unite) is the Vedic ritual of offering, usually oblations of ghee and herbs into a sacred fire (havan, Agnihotra) with chanting of mantras. In the Gita (ch. 3 and 4) it widens to any selfless action done as an offering for the common good (karma yajna, jnana yajna, dravya yajna).

    Rhythmic mantra chanting

    Slow, steady chanting calms breathing and heart rate and focuses attention (like meditation).

    Focused attention and ritual

    Following a fixed sequence reduces rumination and gives a sense of order.

    Group participation

    Shared ritual builds belonging, social support and identity.

    Giving without expectation

    Selfless giving lowers ego-centredness; helping others is linked to well-being.

    Sensory aspects

    Warmth, light and fragrant herbs create a calming atmosphere (compare aromatherapy).

    Meaning and gratitude

    Acknowledging debts to gods, sages, ancestors, people and nature (the five yajnas) fosters gratitude and connectedness.

    Research

    Studies, including work from Indian institutions such as Gurukula Kangri, report that yajna and mantra chanting reduce anxiety and stress and improve mood and attention. Evidence is limited: studies are small and often lack controls, and benefits may come from relaxation, expectation and social contact rather than any special property of the fire.

    Five daily yajnas (pancha mahayajna)
    • Brahma: study and teaching
    • Deva: worship, havan
    • Pitri: honouring parents and ancestors
    • Manushya: hospitality, service
    • Bhuta: care of animals and nature

    Implications for counselling and psychotherapy

    Ayurvedic ideaHow a counsellor can use it
    Prakriti and gunaUnderstand the client's temperament; tailor advice (e.g. calming routines for Vata, anger management for Pitta, activation for Kapha)
    Dinacharya (daily routine) and ritucharya (seasonal)Regular sleep, meals, exercise: a lifestyle intervention
    Ahara (diet), nidra (sleep), brahmacharyaThe "three pillars": nutrition, sleep hygiene, regulated living
    Sadvritta (good conduct)Values, ethics, healthy relationships; truthfulness, non-violence, cleanliness
    Achara rasayanaConduct that rejuvenates the mind: compassion, patience, service
    SattvavajayaTalk-based psychotherapy: reassurance, reasoning, memory and concentration training
    Yoga, pranayama, meditationStress, anxiety and sleep problems
    Medhya rasayana (herbs such as brahmi, ashwagandha)Traditionally used for the mind; evidence is limited, so never replace prescribed medicine, check safety with a doctor
    Tapatraya frameworkSort problems into inner, social and environmental, and plan accordingly
    Cultural sensitivity

    Many Indian clients explain distress in terms of doshas, karma, fate, evil eye or possession. Ask about these beliefs, respect them, and combine them with evidence-based care.

    Cautions
    • Refer for severe illness, suicidality or psychosis
    • Do not claim cures; be honest about evidence
    • Avoid promoting unregulated products
    • Practitioners must stay within their training (RCI/NMC rules)

    Sushruta's definition of health?

    Balanced doshas, agni, dhatus and malas, with a cheerful soul, senses and mind.

    What are the manasika doshas?

    Rajas and tamas.

    Three kinds of therapy in Charaka?

    Daivavyapashraya (faith), yuktivyapashraya (rational), sattvavajaya (psychological).

    Elements of Vata, Pitta, Kapha?

    Air + space; fire + water; earth + water.

    Prakriti vs vikriti?

    Prakriti: natural constitution; vikriti: current imbalance.

    How many mental types does Charaka list?

    Sixteen: 7 sattvic, 6 rajasic, 3 tamasic.

    Three kinds of dukkha?

    Adhyatmik, adhibhautik, adidaivik.

    Give one remedy for adhibhautik dukkha.

    Care and protection, social support, law and ethical conduct.

    What is yajna?

    Ritual of offering, and more widely selfless action done for the common good.

    2. Remedies and modern parallels.
