    Western Thoughts and Psychology · Unit I

    Associationism

    Where Western psychology came from

    Before 1879 psychology was part of philosophy. The questions were old: Where does knowledge come from? How do ideas join together? Two answers competed:

    Rationalism

    Reason and innate ideas are the source of knowledge (Descartes, Leibniz, Kant).

    Empiricism

    All knowledge comes from sense experience; the mind begins blank (Locke, Berkeley, Hume). Associationism grew out of this.

    What is associationism?

    Associationism is the view that mental life is built from simple ideas joined by association. Complex thoughts are made from simple elements (sensations and ideas), the way molecules are made from atoms. Learning, memory and thought all depend on associations.

    Contiguity

    Ideas that occur together in time or place become linked ("thunder" evokes "lightning").

    Similarity (resemblance)

    Similar ideas evoke each other (a photograph reminds you of the person).

    Contrast

    Opposites evoke each other (hot and cold).

    Cause and effect

    Hume: ideas linked as cause and effect (a wound and pain).

    Frequency and vividness

    Associations strengthen with repetition, recency and intensity.

    The roots go back to Aristotle, who named three laws of recall: similarity, contrast and contiguity.

    TH
    Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679)English philosopher; Leviathan (1651). A materialist who said everything, including thought, is matter in motion.
    • All ideas come from sensation: external objects press on the sense organs, causing motion that travels to the brain
    • Imagination and memory are "decaying sense": fading traces of sensation
    • Thoughts follow each other in a train of thought: sometimes unregulated (like dreams), sometimes guided by desire and purpose
    • Behaviour is guided by pursuit of pleasure and avoidance of pain; mind is the product of the body (materialism, mechanism)
    JL
    John Locke (1632–1704)An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690). Founder of British empiricism.
    • Tabula rasa: the mind at birth is a "blank slate" (white paper); no innate ideas
    • Two sources of ideas: sensation (outer experience) and reflection (the mind noticing its own operations)
    • Simple ideas (a colour, a taste) combine into complex ideas (an apple, justice)
    • Primary qualities (size, shape, motion) are in objects; secondary qualities (colour, taste, sound) depend on the perceiver
    • Introduced the phrase association of ideas (4th edition, 1700) mainly to explain odd, irrational connections (like an unreasoned fear)
    GB
    George Berkeley (1685–1753)Irish bishop and philosopher; A New Theory of Vision (1709).
    • "Esse est percipi": to be is to be perceived. We know only our ideas, not matter itself (idealism)
    • In his New Theory of Vision, distance and depth are learned by associating visual cues with touch and movement. This is an early learning theory of perception (opposed to nativism)
    • Showed that associations can explain complex perception
    DH
    David Hume (1711–1776)Scottish philosopher; A Treatise of Human Nature (1739).
    • All mental contents are impressions (vivid, direct sensations and feelings) or ideas (fainter copies of impressions)
    • Three laws of association: resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect
    • Scepticism about cause: we never observe causation, only repeated succession; the belief in cause comes from habit (association)
    • Bundle theory of the self: there is no separate "self", only a bundle of perceptions in constant flux. (Compare with the Buddhist anatta.)
    DH2
    David Hartley (1705–1757)English physician; Observations on Man (1749). The first systematic associationist.
    • Gave association a physiological basis: sensations are vibrations in the nerves and brain; repeated vibrations leave traces (vibratiuncles) that can be set off together
    • Main law: contiguity (frequent joint occurrence). Complex ideas form from simple ones by association
    • Believed association could explain memory, emotion and even moral development
    • Often called the founder of associationism as a school and an early physiological psychologist
    JM
    John Stuart Mill (1806–1873)English philosopher and economist; System of Logic (1843). Son of James Mill (1773–1836), whose "mental mechanics" held that complex ideas are just the sum of simple ones.
    • Mental chemistry: simple ideas combine to form something new and different (like hydrogen and oxygen make water), not just their sum. The whole may differ from its parts. (A step toward Gestalt thinking.)
    • Argued that psychology could be a science of mental laws and proposed a science of character (ethology)
    • Supported studying the mind through observation and experiment

    Summary of contributions

    ThinkerKey ideaLasting influence
    HobbesThought = motion; sensation is the source; materialismMind as natural, mechanical; scientific psychology
    LockeTabula rasa; sensation + reflection; simple and complex ideasRole of experience and learning; environmentalism
    BerkeleyEsse est percipi; visual depth is learned by associationPerception is learned (empiricist theory)
    HumeImpressions and ideas; three laws of association; bundle theory of selfLaws of association; scepticism about cause
    HartleyNerve vibrations; contiguity; physiological associationismLink between brain and mind
    J. S. MillMental chemistry; psychology as a scienceWhole more than sum of parts; critique of mechanism

    Evaluation

    Strengths

    • Gave a testable principle for learning and memory
    • Basis of Ebbinghaus's memory research, Pavlov's conditioning, Thorndike's connectionism and behaviourism
    • Stressed the role of experience and moved psychology toward natural science
    • Still alive in neural networks and word-association studies

    Criticisms

    • Passive, atomistic mind: ignores the active, organising role of the mind (Kant, Gestalt psychologists)
    • Cannot explain why one association is chosen over another (no role for motivation or purpose)
    • Ignores innate structures (e.g. language)
    • Based on armchair reasoning, not experiment
    • The whole is more than the sum of parts (Gestalt)
    RememberBritish empiricists in order of birth: H-L-B-H-H-M: Hobbes (1588), Locke (1632), Berkeley (1685), Hartley (1705), Hume (1711), Mill (1806).

    Unit I self-test

    What is associationism?

    The view that complex mental life is built from simple ideas linked by association.

    Three laws of recall from Aristotle?

    Similarity, contrast, contiguity.

    What is tabula rasa?

    Locke's idea that the mind is a blank slate at birth.

    Locke's two sources of ideas?

    Sensation and reflection.

    What does "esse est percipi" mean?

    To be is to be perceived (Berkeley).

    Hume's three laws of association?

    Resemblance, contiguity, cause and effect.

    Who gave association a physiological basis?

    David Hartley (nerve vibrations).

    What is "mental chemistry"?

    J. S. Mill's idea that combined ideas can form something new, not just their sum.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain associationism and the contributions of Hobbes, Locke and Berkeley. 10 marks
    1. Rationalism vs empiricism; meaning and laws of association.
    2. Hobbes, Locke, Berkeley: key ideas.
    Describe the contributions of Hume, Hartley and J. S. Mill, and evaluate associationism. 10 marks
    1. Hume, Hartley, Mill (table).
    2. Strengths and criticisms.
    Western Thoughts and Psychology · Unit II

    Structuralism

    What is structuralism?

    Structuralism is the first school of experimental psychology. Its aim: analyse consciousness into its basic elements and find how they combine, as chemists analyse matter. The name was given by Edward Titchener to the system he built from Wundt's ideas.

    Subject matter

    Immediate conscious experience: what we feel and sense right now, not what things mean.

    Aim

    Find the elements of consciousness, how they combine, and the laws of combination.

    Method

    Introspection: trained observers report their own sensations under controlled conditions.

    Question

    "What?": what is the structure of the mind?

    Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920)German physician and philosopher. Principles of Physiological Psychology (1873–74). Founded the first experimental psychology laboratory at Leipzig in 1879 and the first journal (Philosophische Studien, 1881).Photo: public domain, Wikimedia Commons
    • Psychology as an independent science: the study of immediate experience (what it is directly, not what it refers to)
    • Experimental introspection (inner perception): observers trained to report simple sensations to controlled stimuli (e.g. a metronome's beats, lights, tones), repeated many times. Different from casual self-reflection
    • Elements: pure sensations and simple feelings. Feelings vary on three dimensions (tridimensional theory): pleasant–unpleasant, excitement–calm, strain–relaxation
    • Apperception: the active process of focusing attention and organising experience (creative synthesis): the mind is more than a passive collection of elements (this makes Wundt less mechanical than later structuralists)
    • Mental chronometry: measured reaction times (extending Donders and Helmholtz) to study the speed of mental processes
    • Two psychologies: experimental (for basic sensory processes) and Völkerpsychologie (folk or cultural psychology: language, myth, custom, studied by historical, non-experimental methods; 10 volumes)
    • Trained many students: Titchener, Cattell, Hall, Külpe, Münsterberg, Spearman and others, who spread psychology to America and elsewhere

    Lasting legacy: established psychology as a separate discipline with its own laboratory, journals and training. 1879 is the usual "birth of scientific psychology".

    ET
    Edward Bradford Titchener (1867–1927)English-born student of Wundt at Leipzig; moved to Cornell University (USA) in 1892, where he led structuralism until his death. Experimental Psychology (1901–05) was his four-volume lab manual.
    • Defined psychology as the study of the structure of the generalised, normal, adult human mind: "the sum total of experiences"
    • Strict introspection: highly trained observers (thousands of trials) report only the sensory elements, not meanings
    • Stimulus error: naming the object ("an orange") instead of the sensations (colour, shape): must be avoided
    • Three kinds of elements: sensations (elements of perception), images (elements of ideas) and affections (elements of emotion), reported about 43,000 sensory elements (about 32,000 visual and 12,000 auditory)
    • Four (later five) attributes of every element: quality, intensity, duration, clarity (and extensity)
    • Context theory of meaning (later): meaning of an experience is the context of images and sensations it brings with it
    • Pure science only: rejected applied, child, animal and abnormal psychology as outside "pure" structure

    Titchener's rejection of Wundt's apperception made structuralism more rigid. He saw psychology as like physics or chemistry: describing what exists.

    Wundt vs Titchener

    PointWundtTitchener
    CountryGermany (Leipzig)England to USA (Cornell)
    Scope of psychologyExperimental + cultural psychology (Völkerpsychologie)Pure structure of the individual normal adult mind only
    Active mindYes: apperception and creative synthesisNo: elements combine passively
    FeelingsThree dimensions of feelingAffections as elements with attributes
    Applied psychologyAllowed someRejected

    Criticisms of structuralism

    1 · Unreliable introspection

    Reports were private and unverifiable; trained observers in different labs gave different answers (the Leipzig vs Cornell disagreement over whether thought needs images).

    2 · Imageless thought

    The Würzburg school (Külpe, 1900s) found that thoughts could occur without any sensations or images, which contradicted Titchener.

    3 · Ignores function

    Asked only what the mind is, not what it is for (functionalists: James, Dewey).

    4 · Narrow scope

    Left out animals, children, abnormal behaviour, individual differences, the unconscious (Freud) and applied problems.

    5 · Atomistic

    Breaking experience into elements loses the whole (Gestalt: "the whole is different from the sum of its parts").

    6 · Subjective

    Watson: psychology must study objective behaviour, not inner experience.

    Decline: structuralism faded after Titchener's death in 1927, but its experimental method, emphasis on laboratory control and measurement and training of the first generation of psychologists remain important. Its questions about sensation and perception returned in cognitive psychology.

    RememberStructuralism's flaws: U-I-F-N-A-S: Unreliable, Imageless thought, Function ignored, Narrow, Atomistic, Subjective.

    Unit II self-test

    When and where was the first psychology lab?

    Wundt, University of Leipzig, 1879.

    Aim of structuralism?

    To analyse consciousness into elements and find how they combine.

    Wundt's tridimensional theory of feeling?

    Pleasant–unpleasant, excitement–calm, strain–relaxation.

    What is apperception?

    The active organising of experience by focused attention (Wundt).

    Titchener's three kinds of elements?

    Sensations, images, affections.

    What is the stimulus error?

    Describing the object instead of the raw sensations.

    What did the Würzburg school find?

    Imageless thought: thinking can occur without images or sensations.

    Which two schools replaced structuralism?

    Functionalism and behaviourism (also Gestalt psychology).

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain structuralism with reference to Wundt and Titchener. 10 marks
    1. Aim, subject matter, method; analysis diagram.
    2. Wundt's contributions; Titchener's contributions.
    3. Comparison table.
    Critically evaluate structuralism. 10 marks
    1. Contributions.
    2. Six criticisms; decline; legacy.
    Western Thoughts and Psychology · Unit III

    Functionalism and Behaviourism

    What is functionalism?

    Functionalism (United States, late 1800s) asked what the mind is for: how mental processes help a person adapt to the environment. It was a reaction against the narrow, elementist structuralism, and it was shaped by Darwin's theory of evolution and pragmatism.

    Focus

    Mental processes and functions (thinking, learning, habit) rather than static elements.

    Question

    "What for?" and "Why?"

    Methods

    Introspection plus objective methods: tests, questionnaires, observation, animal studies, physiological recording.

    Subjects

    Everyone: children, animals, the abnormal, individual differences.

    Applied

    Welcomed practical use in education, industry and clinics.

    Functionalism was not a single organised school. Main centres: Harvard (James), Chicago (Dewey, Angell, Carr) and Columbia (Cattell, Woodworth, Thorndike).

    William James (1842–1910)Harvard physician-philosopher-psychologist. The Principles of Psychology (1890), written over 12 years, still readable today. Also The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902).Photo: Notman Studios, public domain, Wikimedia Commons
    • Stream of consciousness: consciousness is not a chain of elements but a continuous, flowing stream: personal, always changing, continuous, selective (attention chooses)
    • Function of consciousness: helps the organism choose and adapt
    • Habit: a "great flywheel of society"; habits free the mind for higher tasks
    • Self: the "I" (self as knower) and the "Me" (self as known: material, social, spiritual self)
    • Emotion: the James–Lange theory (we are afraid because we tremble)
    • Instincts and will: humans have many instincts, modified by habit
    • Pragmatism: the truth of an idea lies in its practical consequences
    • Taught the first psychology course in the USA (1875) and set up an early demonstration lab at Harvard
    GH
    G. Stanley Hall (1844–1924)American psychologist. First American to earn a PhD in psychology (Harvard, 1878, under James), then studied with Wundt.
    • Founded the first American psychology laboratory at Johns Hopkins University (1883)
    • Started the first American psychology journal, American Journal of Psychology (1887)
    • Founder and first president of the American Psychological Association (APA), 1892
    • President of Clark University; invited Freud and Jung to the USA (1909)
    • Child study movement and developmental psychology: used questionnaires to study children; Adolescence (1904) described the period as "storm and stress", and he applied recapitulation theory (individual development repeats the evolution of the species)
    • Also studied old age (Senescence, 1922)
    Other functionalists

    John Dewey: reflex arc paper (1896), the organism as a whole acting. J. R. Angell: The Province of Functional Psychology (1907). Harvey Carr. J. M. Cattell: mental tests, individual differences. Thorndike: learning.

    Angell's three claims (1907)

    Psychology studies mental operations not contents; function is mediating between environment and needs; it studies the mind–body as a whole.

    Structuralism vs functionalism

    PointStructuralismFunctionalism
    QuestionWhat is the mind made of?What is the mind for?
    UnitElements: sensations, images, affectionsMental processes, activities; stream of consciousness
    MethodStrict introspectionIntrospection plus tests, observation, animal studies
    InfluencePhysics and chemistry; WundtDarwin; pragmatism
    SubjectsNormal adult humanChildren, animals, abnormal, individuals
    Applied useRejectedWelcomed
    HomeLeipzig, CornellHarvard, Chicago, Columbia

    Criticisms of functionalism

    • Not a unified school: no single clear definition or system; hard to say what was "functional"
    • Vague concept of function and still based on consciousness and introspection, which behaviourists later rejected
    • Lacked a precise method and a systematic theory: many descriptive studies
    • Behaviourists said it was still mentalistic; psychoanalysts said it ignored the unconscious

    Contributions: broadened psychology to include learning, motivation, individual differences, child and animal psychology and applied fields (education, industry, tests); influenced behaviourism and modern cognitive and evolutionary psychology.

    What is behaviourism?

    Behaviourism holds that psychology should study only observable behaviour, not consciousness. Behaviour is explained by stimuli (S) and responses (R) and by learning from the environment.

    Subject matter

    Observable, measurable behaviour.

    Method

    Objective experiments, mainly on animals; no introspection.

    Explanation

    Learning through conditioning; the environment shapes behaviour (nurture).

    Aim

    Prediction and control of behaviour.

    Mind

    Treated as a "black box": unobservable and unnecessary.

    JW
    John B. Watson (1878–1958)American psychologist at Johns Hopkins; founder of behaviourism. His 1913 paper "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It" (the "behaviourist manifesto") launched the movement. Behaviorism (1925).
    • Psychology is "a purely objective experimental branch of natural science"; its goal is the prediction and control of behaviour
    • Rejected consciousness, introspection, instincts and mentalistic terms
    • Behaviour = stimulus–response habits built by conditioning; even thinking is subvocal speech (laryngeal movements)
    • Environment over heredity: "Give me a dozen healthy infants … and I'll guarantee to take any one at random and train him to become any type of specialist I might select" (1924)
    • Little Albert study (Watson and Rayner, 1920): an infant conditioned to fear a white rat, then other furry objects (stimulus generalisation). It showed emotions can be learned; ethically unacceptable today
    • Applied psychology to advertising, and to child-rearing (advised parents to avoid too much affection: since criticised)
    • Left academia in 1920 after a scandal, and worked in advertising
    Ivan Pavlov (1849–1936)Russian physiologist; Nobel Prize 1904 for work on digestion. Discovered classical conditioning and laid the basis of behaviourism, though he saw himself as a physiologist.Photo: public domain, Wikimedia Commons
    • Dogs began to salivate to a bell (neutral stimulus) after it was repeatedly paired with food: conditioned reflex
    • Concepts: unconditioned stimulus and response (UCS, UCR), conditioned stimulus and response (CS, CR), acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination, higher-order conditioning
    • Studied the nervous system: excitation and inhibition; "experimental neurosis"; types of nervous system
    • Influence: Watson built on it; basis of behaviour therapy (desensitisation)
    B. F. Skinner (1904–1990)Harvard psychologist, the most influential behaviourist. The Behavior of Organisms (1938), Science and Human Behavior (1953), Verbal Behavior (1957), Walden Two (1948), Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971).Photo: Silly rabbit, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons
    • Radical behaviourism: internal states exist, but are not causes; behaviour is explained by its consequences (unlike Watson's methodological behaviourism)
    • Operant conditioning: behaviour (operant) is strengthened by reinforcement and weakened by punishment. Built the Skinner box
    • Schedules of reinforcement (fixed and variable ratio and interval), shaping, extinction
    • Applications: programmed instruction and teaching machines, behaviour modification, token economies, applied behaviour analysis
    • Argued that free will is an illusion and society should be designed by reinforcement (Walden Two)
    PointPavlovWatsonSkinner
    FieldPhysiologyPsychology (founder)Psychology
    Main ideaClassical conditioning: reflexesS–R habits; environment shapes everythingOperant conditioning: consequences
    LearnerPassive: respondsPassiveActive: operates on the environment
    SubjectsDogsHumans (Little Albert), animalsRats, pigeons
    Inner statesStudied physiologyRejectedNot causes

    Evaluation of behaviourism

    Strengths

    • Made psychology objective and scientific
    • Precise concepts, laboratory experiments
    • Very practical: behaviour therapy, education, ABA, animal training
    • Dominant in American psychology from about 1913 to the 1950s

    Criticisms

    • Ignores thinking, emotion, consciousness and the inner life
    • Over-generalises from animals to humans; humans are not only passive responders
    • Environmental determinism ignores heredity, free will
    • Chomsky (1959) showed language is not explained by reinforcement (review of Verbal Behavior)
    • Bandura: learning by observation without reinforcement; Tolman: cognitive maps, latent learning
    • Ethical issues in control of behaviour

    Decline: after the 1950s the cognitive revolution (Unit V) replaced behaviourism as the main approach, but conditioning remains central to learning theory and therapy.

    Unit III self-test

    What question did functionalism ask?

    What is the mind for? How does it help the organism adapt?

    Which theory influenced functionalism?

    Darwin's theory of evolution (and pragmatism).

    James's "stream of consciousness"?

    Consciousness is a continuous, flowing, personal and selective stream, not a set of elements.

    G. Stanley Hall's firsts?

    First US psychology lab (Johns Hopkins, 1883), first journal (1887), founder and first president of the APA (1892).

    What is the behaviourist manifesto?

    Watson's 1913 paper "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It".

    Little Albert showed that…?

    Emotions such as fear can be classically conditioned.

    Skinner vs Pavlov?

    Skinner studied operant behaviour shaped by consequences; Pavlov studied classical conditioning of reflexes.

    Who criticised Skinner's Verbal Behavior?

    Noam Chomsky (1959).

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain functionalism and the contributions of William James and G. Stanley Hall. 10 marks
    1. Meaning; difference from structuralism (table).
    2. James, Hall.
    3. Criticisms and contributions.
    Discuss behaviourism with the contributions of Watson, Pavlov and Skinner. 10 marks
    1. Meaning and assumptions (draw S–R).
    2. Watson, Pavlov, Skinner (table).
    3. Evaluation.
    Western Thoughts and Psychology · Unit IV

    Gestalt and Transpersonal Psychology

    What is Gestalt psychology?

    Gestalt is a German word meaning form, shape or configuration. The Gestalt school (Germany, 1912) argued that experience is organised into meaningful wholes. Its slogan: "The whole is other than (different from) the sum of its parts" (Koffka; often misquoted as "greater than").

    Against elementism

    Rejects Wundt's and Titchener's analysis into sensations and the behaviourist S–R chain.

    Holism

    We perceive patterns, not pieces. A melody is more than a list of notes (and it stays the same if transposed to another key).

    Active mind

    The brain organises experience by its own principles.

    Phenomenology

    Study experience as it appears directly (naive observation).

    Isomorphism

    Experience and brain activity have the same structure (Köhler).

    Field theory

    Brain and behaviour are organised as dynamic fields (Köhler, Lewin).

    MW
    Max Wertheimer (1880–1943)Founder of Gestalt psychology. In 1912 he published his experiments on apparent movement. Later at the New School (New York); Productive Thinking (1945, posthumous).
    • Phi phenomenon (1912): on a train, he bought a toy stroboscope and tested at Frankfurt. Two lights flashed one after the other at the right interval look like one light moving, although nothing moves. Movement cannot be explained by adding sensations, so the "whole" is more than its parts
    • Collaborators and subjects: Koffka and Köhler
    • Formulated the laws of perceptual organisation (1923): proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, etc.
    • Productive thinking: problem solving by restructuring the whole situation (insight), not by drill and association
    KK
    Kurt Koffka (1886–1941)German psychologist who brought Gestalt ideas to the USA (Smith College). The Growth of the Mind (1921), Principles of Gestalt Psychology (1935).
    • Spread Gestalt psychology in English-speaking countries; applied it to child development, perception and learning
    • Geographical vs behavioural environment: the world as it is vs the world as we experience it; behaviour responds to the behavioural environment
    • Stressed the dynamic "field" and the organising role of the brain
    WK
    Wolfgang Köhler (1887–1967)Director of the Prussian Academy's anthropoid station on Tenerife (1913–20); The Mentality of Apes (1917), Gestalt Psychology (1929). Later at Swarthmore.
    • Insight learning: the chimpanzee Sultan joined two bamboo sticks to reach a banana, and piled boxes to reach hanging fruit. After a pause, the solution came suddenly ("Aha!" experience), by seeing the whole relationship, not by trial and error (Thorndike)
    • Features of insight: sudden, smooth, reusable in new situations, based on perception of relations
    • Isomorphism: the structure of experience matches the structure of the brain's field processes
    • Transposition: animals respond to the relation between stimuli (e.g. the darker of two greys), not to absolute stimuli

    Laws of perceptual organisation (Prägnanz)

    The master principle is the law of Prägnanz (good form, simplicity): we perceive the simplest, most stable and regular organisation possible.

    LawMeaningExample
    Figure–groundWe separate an object (figure) from its backgroundRubin's vase and two faces; text on a page
    ProximityThings near each other are groupedDots in pairs look like pairs
    SimilaritySimilar things (shape, colour, size) are groupedRows of circles and squares
    ClosureWe fill gaps to see complete shapesA broken circle is still seen as a circle
    Continuity (good continuation)We follow smooth, continuous linesTwo crossing lines are seen as two lines, not four
    Common fateThings moving together are groupedA flock of birds
    Symmetry and simplicity (Prägnanz)We prefer symmetrical, simple formsInterlocking Olympic rings seen as five circles
    RememberF-P-S-C-C-C: "Five Pink Snakes Came, Crawled, Collapsed": Figure-ground, Proximity, Similarity, Closure, Continuity, Common fate.

    Evaluation of the Gestalt school

    Contributions

    • Showed the importance of organisation and the whole in perception
    • Insight learning and productive thinking: problem solving research
    • Influenced cognitive psychology, social psychology (Lewin's field theory, Asch), and Gestalt therapy (Perls), design, art and visual computing
    • Used phenomenological observation and carefully planned experiments

    Criticisms

    • Descriptive, not explanatory: laws describe grouping but do not say why
    • Vague concepts (Prägnanz, isomorphism) that are hard to test
    • Nativist bias: underplayed the role of learning and experience
    • Limited quantitative methods; weak on development, personality, motivation
    • Insight explanation cannot say how the solution arises
    Founders: Abraham Maslow, Anthony Sutich, Stanislav Grof (1968–69)They named a "fourth force" in psychology, after psychoanalysis, behaviourism and humanistic psychology. Journal of Transpersonal Psychology began in 1969; the Association for Transpersonal Psychology followed in 1972.Photo: William Carter, public domain, Wikimedia Commons

    Overview

    Transpersonal psychology studies experiences, development and potentials that go beyond ("trans") the personal ego: mystical and peak experiences, altered states, meditation, self-transcendence, spirituality, and the highest human potential.

    Topics

    Consciousness, meditation, peak and mystical experiences, near-death experiences, altruism, wisdom, creativity, unity of all beings, spiritual crises.

    Roots

    William James (religious experience), Jung (collective unconscious), Assagioli (psychosynthesis), Maslow (peak experiences and, in 1969, self-transcendence above self-actualisation), Frankl, and Eastern traditions (yoga, Buddhism, Vedanta).

    Methods

    First-person study of experience, meditation, interviews, physiological and brain research, case studies; increasingly empirical research on mindfulness and contemplative practice.

    Applications

    Transpersonal psychotherapy: psychosynthesis, holotropic breathwork (Grof), mindfulness, meditation, dream work, work with spiritual emergencies and meaning.

    Strengths

    • Widened psychology to include spirituality and meaning
    • Brought Eastern practice and psychology together
    • Stimulated research on meditation and consciousness

    Criticisms

    • Hard to define and measure; often unscientific
    • Risk of blending science and religion; vague terms
    • Western focus on "peak" and mystical experience may be elitist
    KW
    Ken Wilber (b. 1949)American writer on consciousness and philosophy. Key books: The Spectrum of Consciousness (1977), The Atman Project (1980), Sex, Ecology, Spirituality (1995), A Theory of Everything (2000). Founder of integral theory.

    The spectrum of consciousness

    • Consciousness is a spectrum of levels, from the simple identification with the body to the unity of all things (Atman/Brahman, non-dual), drawing on Vedanta, Buddhism and Western psychology
    • Three broad stages: prepersonal (before ego formation), personal (ego, reason), transpersonal (beyond ego)
    • Pre/trans fallacy: mixing up pre-rational states (regression, infantile fusion) with trans-rational states (mystical unity), so that some reduce mysticism to regression (Freud) and others glorify regression as spiritual
    • Atman project: humans seek wholeness (Atman), but mistake substitutes (food, sex, power, ego) for it until they find the real Self
    • Great Chain of Being: matter, body, mind, soul, spirit

    Integral theory: AQAL

    AQAL ("ah-qwul") = All Quadrants, All Levels (plus lines, states and types): a map that includes every aspect of reality.

    Levels, lines, states, types

    Levels: stages of development; lines: separate abilities (cognitive, emotional, moral, spiritual); states: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, meditative states; types: personality types and gender.

    Significance

    Offers a framework to integrate science, psychology and spirituality, and to fit psychotherapies on one map (each works in a different quadrant). Critics: broad and speculative; hard to test; claims of completeness.

    Unit IV self-test

    What does Gestalt mean?

    Form, shape or configuration (a meaningful whole).

    Phi phenomenon?

    Apparent movement from two lights flashed in sequence (Wertheimer, 1912).

    Köhler's study of insight?

    Chimpanzee Sultan on Tenerife: sudden solution, e.g. joining sticks or piling boxes.

    Law of Prägnanz?

    We perceive the simplest, most stable organisation.

    Name four Gestalt laws.

    Proximity, similarity, closure, continuity (also figure-ground, common fate).

    Why is transpersonal psychology the "fourth force"?

    It followed psychoanalysis, behaviourism and humanistic psychology.

    Wilber's three broad stages?

    Prepersonal, personal, transpersonal.

    What does AQAL stand for?

    All Quadrants, All Levels (with lines, states, types).

    What is the pre/trans fallacy?

    Confusing pre-rational states with trans-rational states.

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the Gestalt school with the contributions of Wertheimer, Koffka and Köhler, and evaluate it. 10 marks
    1. Meaning and principles.
    2. Three founders; laws of organisation (draw).
    3. Evaluation.
    Give an overview of transpersonal psychology and Ken Wilber's contribution. 10 marks
    1. Fourth force; roots; topics; evaluation.
    2. Spectrum of consciousness (draw); pre/trans fallacy; AQAL quadrants (draw).
    Western Thoughts and Psychology · Unit V

    Cognitive Revolution and Multiculturalism

    The cognitive revolution

    From the mid-1950s, psychology shifted from studying only behaviour to studying mental processes: attention, memory, language, thinking and problem solving. This shift, so large that it is called a "revolution", made the cognitive approach dominant.

    Causes

    Failures of behaviourism

    Could not explain language, insight, planning or observational learning.

    Computers and information theory

    The computer gave a new model of mind: input, storage, processing, output (Turing, Shannon, Newell and Simon's "Logic Theorist", 1956).

    Linguistics

    Noam Chomsky's Syntactic Structures (1957) and his 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior.

    Wartime human-factors research

    Attention and performance of radar operators and pilots (Broadbent).

    Earlier cognitive ideas

    Gestalt psychology, Tolman's cognitive maps, Piaget, Bartlett's schema theory, Vygotsky.

    Key figures

    PersonContribution
    George Miller (1956)"The magical number seven, plus or minus two": limits of short-term memory; chunking
    Jerome Bruner (1956)A Study of Thinking: concept formation and strategies; "New Look" in perception
    Noam Chomsky (1957, 1959)Innate universal grammar; showed that behaviourism cannot explain language
    Newell and Simon (1956)Logic Theorist, General Problem Solver; mind as symbol-processing system
    Donald Broadbent (1958)Filter model of attention; information-processing diagrams
    Ulric Neisser (1967)Gave the field its name in Cognitive Psychology

    Features, comparison and evaluation

    PointBehaviourismCognitive approach
    Subject matterObservable behaviourMental processes (inferred)
    ModelStimulus → Response ("black box")Stimulus → mental processing → Response (S–O–R)
    MetaphorMachine, reflexComputer (information processing)
    MethodsAnimal experimentsHuman experiments, reaction time, modelling, later brain imaging
    LearnerPassiveActive processor

    Strengths

    • Rigorous experiments on mental processes
    • Applied in education, therapy (CBT), design, AI, eyewitness testimony
    • Links to neuroscience and artificial intelligence

    Criticisms

    • Computer metaphor is limited: people have emotion, bodies and culture
    • Lab tasks lack ecological validity (Neisser's later critique)
    • Mental processes are inferred, not seen
    • Neglect of culture and context

    What is multiculturalism?

    Multiculturalism is the view that a society is made up of many cultural groups (ethnic, religious, linguistic) and that this diversity should be recognised, respected and supported. It is both a fact (diverse societies) and a policy or ideal (how to treat diversity).

    Recognition

    Cultural identity is important for dignity (Charles Taylor: the "politics of recognition").

    Equality and rights

    All groups have equal status; protection from discrimination.

    Respect for difference

    Languages, customs, religions are valued, not just tolerated.

    Participation and integration

    Groups take part in the common civic life.

    Link with psychology

    • Cultural psychology and cross-cultural psychology grew from the cognitive revolution's recognition that thinking is shaped by culture: East Asians tend to think more holistically, Westerners more analytically (Nisbett, 2003); independent vs interdependent self (Markus and Kitayama, 1991); Vygotsky: thought develops through cultural tools
    • WEIRD critique (Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan, 2010): most research uses Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic samples and cannot be assumed universal
    • Multicultural counselling: Paul Pedersen (1991) called multiculturalism the "fourth force" in counselling; counsellors need cultural competence (awareness, knowledge, skills)
    • In India: "unity in diversity", a constitution that protects minority language and religion rights, and many cultures within one country

    Three models of multiculturalism

    ModelCore ideaKey thinkersExample
    Liberal multiculturalismProtect individual rights and freedom of culture, language and religion in private and public life. Same civic rights for all; diversity is allowed within shared liberal values. Groups get fair treatment, not special powerWill Kymlicka (and earlier liberal tradition: Mill)Freedom of worship; multilingual schools in a common legal system
    Pluralist multiculturalismSociety is a mosaic of distinct cultural groups. Groups have collective (group) rights to preserve and govern their culture; the state recognises each group's identityCharles Taylor (recognition); communitarian thinkers; the "salad bowl" imageCommunity-specific personal laws; separate schools or language rights
    Cosmopolitan multiculturalismCultures are fluid and mixing. People can belong to several cultures and choose and blend identities; loyalty is to humanity as a wholeKwame Anthony Appiah, Jeremy Waldron, Ulrich BeckGlobal citizens; mixed-heritage and migrant identities; fusion food and music
    RememberL-P-C = Liberal: Like (individuals) · Pluralist: Parts (groups) · Cosmopolitan: Combining (blends).

    Limitations of multiculturalism

    1 · Essentialism and stereotyping

    Treats cultures as fixed, uniform blocks; ignores differences within groups and change over time.

    2 · Group rights vs individual rights

    Group rights can restrict individuals inside the group (women, children, dissenters, LGBT members) (Susan Okin, Is Multiculturalism Bad for Women?).

    3 · Segregation and weak cohesion

    Separate communities may share little; "parallel lives", mistrust, a weak shared identity.

    4 · Tokenism and symbolic politics

    Celebrating food and festivals while real inequality in jobs, education and power continues.

    5 · Neglect of class and economy

    Focus on cultural identity can hide poverty and structural discrimination.

    6 · Identity politics and conflict

    Competition between groups for recognition and resources; backlash. Several European leaders (e.g. Angela Merkel in 2010) declared multiculturalism had "failed".

    7 · Cultural relativism problem

    Hard to criticise harmful practices if all cultures must be respected equally.

    8 · Weak fit with cognitive science of culture

    Culture is not a simple block but a flexible set of ideas that people use differently in different situations (cultural cognition). Cognitive research warns against treating culture as one cause of behaviour.

    Response: interculturalism (dialogue and mixing), civic integration with equal rights, critical multiculturalism that tackles inequality, and cosmopolitan models that allow multiple belongings.

    Schools of psychology at a glance

    SchoolSubject matterMethodKey names
    StructuralismElements of consciousnessIntrospectionWundt, Titchener
    FunctionalismFunction of mind in adaptationIntrospection + objectiveJames, Hall, Dewey, Angell
    BehaviourismObservable behaviourExperiments, conditioningWatson, Pavlov, Skinner
    GestaltWholes in perception, insightPhenomenological experimentsWertheimer, Koffka, Köhler
    CognitiveMental processesExperiments, modellingMiller, Chomsky, Broadbent, Neisser
    TranspersonalConsciousness beyond egoFirst-person, meditationMaslow, Grof, Wilber

    Unit V self-test

    What triggered the cognitive revolution?

    Failures of behaviourism, the computer metaphor, information theory, and Chomsky's linguistics.

    Who wrote "The magical number seven"?

    George Miller (1956).

    Who named the field "cognitive psychology"?

    Ulric Neisser (1967).

    What did Chomsky's 1959 review show?

    Reinforcement cannot explain language.

    Three models of multiculturalism?

    Liberal, pluralist, cosmopolitan.

    Pluralist vs liberal multiculturalism?

    Pluralist stresses group rights and distinct groups; liberal stresses equal individual rights.

    One limitation of multiculturalism?

    Essentialism, group rights conflicting with individual rights, segregation, tokenism, or neglect of class.

    What does WEIRD stand for?

    Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic.

    Long-answer outlines

    Give an overview of the cognitive revolution. 10 marks
    1. Causes; timeline (draw).
    2. Key figures; features; comparison with behaviourism.
    3. Evaluation.
    Explain multiculturalism, its models and limitations. 10 marks
    1. Meaning; link with cultural psychology and the cognitive turn.
    2. Liberal, pluralist, cosmopolitan (draw and table).
    3. Limitations and responses.
    Practical (Semester 3) · Part A

    Lab Basics: Protocol, Scoring and Report

    What the paper expects

    You do any five practicals from the list, administer tests on others, score and interpret them, write a practical record (report) and answer a viva. The learning outcomes: skill with biofeedback; evaluating stress and coping; test protocols; administering tests ethically; reporting results.

    Part A (this part)

    Protocol, ethics, scoring and norms, and how to write the report.

    Part B

    Biofeedback, anxiety, depression, hopelessness, mental health, stress, coping, social support, emotion regulation.

    Part C

    Quality of life, optimism, self-efficacy, Vedic personality, job anxiety, job satisfaction, occupational stress, leadership, medico-psychological and neuropsychological tests.

    Important: test names and exact scoring differ between versions. Follow the manual of the test your lab uses. The numbers here are standard published values for common tools, for revision.

    The seven steps of every practical

    Before the session
    • Read the manual; check the test, answer sheet, scoring key, stopwatch, pencils
    • Choose a quiet, well-lit, private room; same conditions for all
    • Pick suitable participants: age, language and education matching the test; no one in acute distress for sensitive tests
    During
    • Greet, build rapport, explain purpose in simple words
    • Get informed consent (voluntary, can stop at any time)
    • Read the standard instructions exactly; give practice items if the manual says so
    • Observe behaviour: anxiety, fatigue, effort, distractions; record it
    • Stay available but do not hint or help with answers

    Ethical principles in testing

    Informed consent

    Explain the aim, what you will do and what happens to the data. Written consent for adults; parent consent plus child assent for minors.

    Voluntary and right to withdraw

    No pressure; the person can stop at any time without penalty.

    Confidentiality

    Use code numbers, not names, in the record; store sheets safely; share only with those who need to know.

    No harm

    Avoid distressing items for vulnerable people; be ready to stop and support. Know the referral pathway.

    Competence

    Students administer under supervision; never diagnose from one test.

    Feedback and debriefing

    Give results kindly, in simple language, as scores on a scale, not labels ("you are depressed"). Offer help if the score is high.

    Suicide and high-risk responses

    If a person scores very high on hopelessness or depression, or mentions harming themselves, stop, stay calm, do not leave them alone, and tell your supervisor immediately. Screening scores are not a diagnosis.

    Common problems in self-report tests

    ProblemMeaningWhat to do
    Social desirabilityAnswering to look goodEnsure anonymity; reassure there are no right answers
    AcquiescenceAgreeing with everything ("yes-saying")Use scales with reverse-worded items
    Extreme or central respondingAlways choosing end points or the middleCheck the pattern while scoring
    FakingDeliberately false answersLook at lie scales or consistency
    Examiner and situation effectsExaminer's tone, noise, time of dayStandardise conditions
    Language and literacyItems not understoodUse a suitable language version; read aloud only if allowed

    Scoring and interpretation

    Raw score

    The sum of item scores according to the key. Meaningless alone; compare with norms or cut-offs.

    Reverse scoring

    For negatively worded items so that a high score always means more of the trait.

    Reversed score = (highest option + lowest option) − the answer given

    Example: on a 1–5 scale, an answer of 2 on a reversed item becomes (5 + 1) − 2 = 4. On a 0–4 scale: (4 + 0) − 1 = 3.

    Converting scores

    TermMeaningFormula or example
    Mean and SDAverage and spread of the norm groupUse the manual's values
    z-scoreDistance from the mean in SD unitsz = (X − M) ÷ SD
    T-scoreScaled score, mean 50, SD 10T = 50 + 10z
    PercentilePercentage of the norm group scoring at or below you60th percentile = higher than 60%
    Sten / stanineStandard scores with 10 and 9 bandsSten mean 5.5; stanine mean 5
    Cut-offA score above which the problem is likelyPHQ-9 ≥ 10; PSS-10 ≥ 27 (high)
    Worked example

    Test mean 60, SD 10; raw score 75. z = (75 − 60) ÷ 10 = 1.5; T = 50 + 10 × 1.5 = 65; about the 93rd percentile. Interpretation: a clearly above-average score. Say what it means in words, for example "high anxiety compared with peers", and add the limits.

    Reliability and validity (what to quote from the manual)

    • Reliability: consistency (test–retest, split-half, Cronbach's alpha). A good scale has alpha of about .70 or more
    • Validity: measures what it claims (content, criterion, construct)
    • Norms: group on which the scores are based; use the right norm table (age, sex, culture)

    Practical record format

    #SectionWhat to write
    1Title and dateName of the test or experiment; date; your name and roll number
    2Aim"To measure the level of [variable] in [participant] using [test]."
    3IntroductionShort background: meaning of the variable, why it matters, key theory or research (5–10 lines)
    4ParticipantCode number, age, sex, education, occupation (no name); consent obtained
    5Material and test descriptionAuthor, year, language version, items, response format, dimensions, reliability and validity, norms
    6ProcedureSetting, rapport, instructions given, time taken, any problems (past tense, short)
    7ScoringKey used, reverse-scored items, how totals are found
    8ResultsRaw scores per dimension in a table; converted scores or levels from norms
    9Interpretation and discussionWhat the scores mean; behavioural observations; link to theory; limits (one respondent, self-report, mood on the day)
    10Conclusion and precautionsOne-line result; steps taken to ensure accuracy
    11References and appendixAPA-style reference of the manual; attach the filled sheet and scoring
    RememberA-I-P-M-P-S-R-D-C: "All Intelligent Psychologists Make Perfect Scores Right, Definitely Correct": Aim, Introduction, Participant, Material, Procedure, Scoring, Results, Discussion, Conclusion.

    General viva questions

    Why did you choose this test?

    Because it measures the variable, has good reliability and validity, suits the age and language of the participant, and has norms.

    What are reliability and validity?

    Reliability is consistency; validity is whether the test measures what it should.

    What is reverse scoring and why is it used?

    Reversing the score of negatively worded items so that a higher total always means more of the trait; it also reduces yes-saying.

    How did you ensure ethics?

    Informed consent, voluntary participation, confidentiality with a code number, no harm, and feedback.

    Why can one score not diagnose a disorder?

    Self-report screening tools show risk, not diagnosis, and are affected by mood, honesty and the situation. Diagnosis needs a full clinical assessment.

    What is a norm?

    A reference table of scores from a representative group, used to interpret an individual's score.

    What are the limits of your findings?

    One participant, self-report bias, social desirability, state on the day, norms may not fit.

    What precautions did you take?

    Quiet room, standard instructions, clear rapport, checked all items answered, accurate scoring, double-checked totals.

    Practical (Semester 3) · Part B

    Biofeedback, Emotion, Stress and Mental Health Tests

    Biofeedback (any parameter)

    Aim

    To show how a physiological response (e.g. skin conductance) changes under stress and relaxation, and to train voluntary reduction with feedback.

    Parameters

    GSR / EDA (µS), EMG (µV, forehead or trapezius), thermal (°C, fingertip), pulse / HRV (bpm; ms), respiration (breaths a minute), EEG.

    Equipment

    Biofeedback device with sensors and software, electrode gel or finger bands, alcohol swab, chair, quiet room (22–25 °C).

    Procedure

    1Prepare

    Explain; get consent; ask about caffeine, medicines, pacemaker or skin conditions. Seat the person comfortably; clean the skin; attach sensors.

    2Adaptation

    3–5 minutes of quiet sitting so readings settle.

    3Baseline

    2–5 minutes eyes open or closed; record mean value.

    4Stress profile

    A mild stressor for 1–2 minutes (serial subtraction, e.g. 1000 minus 7; or recall a stress). Record peak.

    5Recovery

    Rest for 2–3 minutes; record how fast the value returns to baseline.

    6Training

    With visual or sound feedback, guide slow breathing or muscle relaxation for 10–15 minutes; record the trend.

    7Post-test

    Final baseline; compare. Ask how the person felt.

    PhaseReading (example)What it shows
    BaselineGSR 4.0 µSResting level
    StressGSR 7.2 µS (+80%)Arousal rises
    TrainingGSR 3.1 µSLearned reduction (below baseline)

    Interpretation: change = (phase − baseline) ÷ baseline × 100. A fall in GSR, EMG and heart rate and a rise in finger temperature indicate relaxation. Precautions: no talking or movement of the sensor hand, same time of day, no recent exercise or caffeine, clean skin. Limits: one participant, short training, and expectation effects.

    Viva points

    Define biofeedback; theory (operant conditioning, Neal Miller); why GSR rises with arousal (sweat glands, sympathetic); difference between GSR and EMG; why fingers cool in stress.

    Anxiety

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation
    Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI), Beck et al., 198821 items, symptoms in the past week; 0–3Total 0–63: 0–7 minimal, 8–15 mild, 16–25 moderate, 26–63 severe
    State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI), Spielberger40 items: 20 state ("how you feel now") + 20 trait ("how you generally feel"); 4-point; Form YEach scale 20–80; compare with age and sex norms; some items reverse-scored
    GAD-7, Spitzer, 20067 items, 0–30–21: 5, 10, 15 = mild, moderate, severe
    Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale14 items, clinician-rated0–56; interview, for clinical use
    Sinha's Comprehensive Anxiety Test (SCAT)Indian tool: yes/no itemsUse the manual's norms
    Viva points

    State vs trait anxiety (Spielberger); difference between fear and anxiety; why BAI emphasises somatic symptoms.

    Depression

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation
    Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II), Beck, Steer and Brown, 199621 items; each 4 statements scored 0–3 (past two weeks)Total 0–63: 0–13 minimal, 14–19 mild, 20–28 moderate, 29–63 severe. Item 9 is suicide: always check
    PHQ-99 items from DSM criteria, 0–3 (past two weeks)0–27: 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 moderately severe, 20–27 severe; 10 or more is the common cut-off
    CES-D, Radloff, 197720 items, 0–3, last week0–60; 16 or more suggests risk
    Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS)17 items, clinician-ratedInterview; severity bands
    Viva points

    Beck's cognitive triad; difference between sadness and depression (duration of 2 weeks, impairment); why screening is not diagnosis; what to do if item 9 is endorsed.

    Hopelessness

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation
    Beck Hopelessness Scale (BHS), Beck et al., 197420 true/false statements about the future; 9 are keyed "false" and 11 "true"0–20: 0–3 minimal, 4–8 mild, 9–14 moderate, 15–20 severe. A high score is a predictor of suicide risk

    Care: hopelessness is a stronger predictor of suicide than depression itself. If the score is 9 or more, or any item suggests risk, inform the supervisor and make sure the person gets follow-up.

    Mental health

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation
    General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-12), Goldberg12 items on recent distress, 4 options; screens for common mental disordersGHQ scoring (0-0-1-1): 0–12; cut-off about 3 or more suggests distress. Likert scoring (0-1-2-3): 0–36
    WHO-5 Well-Being Index5 positive statements about the last 2 weeks, 0–5Raw 0–25, × 4 = 0–100. Below 50 suggests low well-being; screen for depression
    Mental Health Inventory, Jagdish and Srivastava, 1983 (Indian)56 items in six dimensions: positive self-evaluation, perception of reality, integration of personality, autonomy, group-oriented attitudes, environmental masteryHigher score = better mental health; use the manual's norms
    Viva points

    Meaning of mental health (WHO; Jahoda's criteria); difference between mental health and absence of illness; GHQ as a screening tool.

    Medico-psychological questionnaire

    A symptom checklist where the person answers yes or no to questions on physical complaints and emotional symptoms (e.g. the Cornell Medical Index-type questionnaires; use the version in your lab manual).

    • Purpose: screen for psychosomatic and emotional disturbance; link of body and mind
    • Scoring: count of "yes" answers, by section and overall; a high total suggests the need for further assessment
    • Use: medical and counselling settings; screening, not diagnosis
    • Viva: what are psychosomatic disorders; why physical and psychological symptoms are measured together; limits of yes/no format

    Stress

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation
    Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10), Cohen, 198310 items on how unpredictable, uncontrollable and overloaded life felt in the last month; 0–4Reverse items 4, 5, 7, 8; total 0–40: 0–13 low, 14–26 moderate, 27–40 high stress
    DASS-21, Lovibond21 items: 7 each for depression, anxiety, stress; 0–3Sum each subscale and multiply by 2; compare with severity bands in the manual
    Social Readjustment Rating Scale, Holmes and Rahe, 196743 life events with life-change units; tick events in the past yearAdd the units; about 150–299 moderate, 300 or more high risk (original study)
    Student or academic stress scalesStressors from exams, workload, relationshipsPer the manual
    Viva points

    Selye's GAS; transactional model (appraisal); difference between stressor and stress; PSS measures perceived stress, not events.

    Coping

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation
    Brief COPE, Carver, 199728 items in 14 subscales (2 items each), e.g. active coping, planning, positive reframing, acceptance, humour, religion, emotional and instrumental support, self-distraction, denial, venting, substance use, behavioural disengagement, self-blame; 4-point (1–4)Sum the two items for each subscale (2–8); higher = more use. Often grouped as problem-focused, emotion-focused, dysfunctional
    Ways of Coping Questionnaire, Folkman and Lazarus66 items; coping with one specific recent stressful eventEight scales including confrontive coping, distancing, planful problem solving
    Viva points

    Social support

    Social Support Questionnaire (SSQ), SarasonLists people you can count on and satisfaction with supportNumber of supporters and satisfaction scores
    Viva points

    Emotional regulation

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation

    Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), Gratz and Roemer, 200436 items, six subscales: nonacceptance, goals, impulse control, awareness, strategies, clarityHigher = more difficulty; some items reverse-scored
    Viva points

    Part B quick viva

    What baseline and recovery mean in biofeedback?

    Baseline is the resting value; recovery is the return to baseline after stress.

    BAI and BDI-II: items and maximum score?

    21 items each; 0–63.

    BHS: items and format?

    20 true/false items; score 0–20.

    PHQ-9 cut-off for depression?

    10 or more (0–27 scale).

    PSS-10 reverse items?

    4, 5, 7, 8.

    MSPSS subscales?

    Family, friends, significant other.

    ERQ subscales?

    Cognitive reappraisal (6 items) and expressive suppression (4 items).

    What do you do if a person scores very high on hopelessness?

    Stop, support, do not leave alone, inform the supervisor immediately and arrange follow-up.

    Practical (Semester 3) · Part C

    Wellbeing, Personality, Work and Neuropsychological Tests

    Quality of life

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation
    WHOQOL-BREF, WHO26 items, 5-point: 2 general items (overall quality of life, general health) + 24 items in four domains: physical health (7), psychological (6), social relationships (3), environment (8)Domain scores = average × 4, so the range is 4–20 (or transformed 0–100). Higher = better. Some items (e.g. pain, negative feelings) reverse-scored
    SF-36, Ware36 items; eight health dimensions0–100 per dimension
    Viva points

    WHO definition of quality of life; difference between objective and subjective QoL; four domains; use in health research and rehabilitation.

    Optimism

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation
    Life Orientation Test-Revised (LOT-R), Scheier, Carver and Bridges, 199410 items, 0–4: 3 optimism (1, 4, 10), 3 pessimism (3, 7, 9), 4 fillers (2, 5, 6, 8)Reverse-score items 3, 7, 9; ignore fillers; total 0–24 (higher = more optimistic)
    Viva points

    Dispositional optimism vs explanatory style (Seligman); optimism and health; why there are filler items.

    Self-efficacy

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation
    General Self-Efficacy Scale (GSES), Schwarzer and Jerusalem, 199510 items, 4-point (1–4), belief in coping with demandsTotal 10–40; higher = stronger self-efficacy; compare with norms (mean about 29 in many samples)
    Viva points

    Bandura's four sources (mastery, vicarious experience, persuasion, physiological state); general vs specific self-efficacy; link with motivation and health behaviour.

    Vedic personality

    What it measures

    The three gunas: sattva (balance, clarity), rajas (activity, passion), tamas (inertia, dullness), as in the Bhagavad Gita and Samkhya (see Indian Psychology, Unit III).

    Tools

    Vedic Personality Inventory (VPI), Wolf, 1998; triguna scales by Indian psychologists. Items describe thoughts, preferences and behaviour; response format and norms are in the manual.

    • Scoring: separate total for each guna; the highest shows the dominant guna; compare the pattern, not just one score
    • Interpretation: high sattva suggests calm, clear, balanced; high rajas suggests ambition and restlessness; high tamas suggests lethargy and dullness. Everyone has all three; the aim is a movement toward sattva
    • Limits: still a developing field; scales vary; do not label the person
    Viva points

    Meaning of the three gunas; svabhava; difference from Western trait theories; Ayurvedic prakriti and manasa prakriti.

    Job anxiety

    Measures anxiety related to the job: worry about work, performance and job security. A well-known Indian tool is the Job Anxiety Scale (A. K. Srivastava). Higher score = more job anxiety; use the manual's norms. Relevant to organisational psychology (Psychology at Workplace, Semester 4).

    Viva points

    Sources of job anxiety (overload, insecurity, role conflict); effects on performance, health and absenteeism; difference from general anxiety.

    Job satisfaction

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation
    Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire (MSQ), Weiss, Dawis, England and Lofquist, 1967Short form 20 items; 5-point; intrinsic, extrinsic and general satisfactionSum; higher = more satisfied
    Job Descriptive Index (JDI), Smith, Kendall and Hulin, 1969Five facets: work itself, pay, promotion, supervision, co-workersFacet scores
    Indian job satisfaction scalesAdapted to Indian workplacesPer the manual
    Viva points

    Herzberg's two-factor theory (motivators and hygiene factors); job satisfaction and commitment; global vs facet satisfaction.

    Occupational stress

    ToolDetailsScoring and interpretation
    Occupational Stress Index (OSI), Srivastava and Singh, 1981 (Indian)46 items, 5-point, in 12 dimensions: role overload, role ambiguity, role conflict, group and political pressure, responsibility for persons, under-participation, powerlessness, poor peer relations, intrinsic impoverishment, low status, strenuous working conditions, unprofitabilitySum the items (some are reverse-scored); higher = more stress; compare with norms for low, moderate, high
    Job Content Questionnaire, KarasekJob demands and decision controlHigh demand + low control = "job strain"
    Viva points

    Stressors at work and their effects (burnout, absenteeism, ill health); Karasek's demand–control model; role conflict vs role ambiguity.

    Leadership

    ToolDetailsInterpretation
    Least Preferred Co-worker (LPC) scale, FiedlerDescribe the co-worker you least like on bipolar adjectivesHigh LPC = relationship-oriented leader; low LPC = task-oriented (Fiedler's contingency model)
    Leader Behaviour Description Questionnaire (LBDQ), Ohio StateTwo dimensions: consideration and initiating structureFour combinations (high or low on each)
    Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire (MLQ), Bass and AvolioTransformational, transactional, laissez-faire stylesHigher transformational scores link to better outcomes
    Lewin's stylesAutocratic, democratic, laissez-faireDemocratic leaders often get highest satisfaction
    Viva points

    Trait, behavioural and contingency theories; Fiedler's model; path-goal; transformational leadership.

    Neuropsychological tests

    Tests of brain-related functions: attention, memory, language, visuospatial ability, executive function. They help detect brain damage and plan rehabilitation. Take care: administer only under supervision; results need expert interpretation.

    TestWhat it measuresHow it worksInterpretation
    PGI Battery of Brain Dysfunction (Pershad and Verma; Indian)Screening for organic brain dysfunction: memory, perception, motor and verbal functionsBattery of subtests; scores for eachTotal below cut-off suggests dysfunction; per manual
    Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test, Bender, 1938Visuo-motor coordination, perceptionCopy 9 geometric designs on blank paperErrors: distortion, rotation, perseveration, integration. Scored (e.g. Koppitz method); many errors suggest brain damage or developmental problems
    Trail Making Test (A and B), ReitanAttention, speed, mental flexibility (set shifting)A: join numbers 1–25 in order; B: alternate numbers and letters (1–A–2–B…)Time to complete; slow Part B means executive weakness
    Stroop Colour–Word TestSelective attention, interference controlName the ink colour of colour words (e.g. "RED" in blue ink)Slower on the incongruent card = interference
    Digit span (Wechsler)Short-term and working memoryRepeat digit strings forward and backwardNormal about 7 forward, 5 backward
    Wisconsin Card Sorting TestExecutive function, cognitive flexibilitySort cards by an unstated rule that changesPerseverative errors suggest frontal lobe problems
    MMSE and MoCAGlobal cognition screening for dementiaMMSE 30 points; MoCA 30 pointsMMSE of 23 or below suggests impairment; MoCA below 26
    Precautions
    • Check vision, hearing, fatigue, medicines and education level
    • Quiet room; follow timing exactly; note effort and behaviour
    • Do not tell the person they have "brain damage"; refer if concerned
    Viva points

    Brain areas (frontal lobe: executive; temporal: memory; parietal: spatial); difference between neuropsychological and psychological testing; why one test cannot diagnose; effect of education and age.

    Part C quick viva

    WHOQOL-BREF: items and domains?

    26 items; four domains: physical, psychological, social relationships, environment.

    LOT-R: which items are fillers and which reversed?

    Fillers 2, 5, 6, 8. Reverse-score the pessimism items 3, 7, 9.

    GSES range?

    10 items, 10–40.

    What do the gunas measure?

    Sattva, rajas and tamas: balance, activity and inertia in personality.

    Occupational Stress Index: items and dimensions?

    46 items, 12 dimensions (Srivastava and Singh, 1981).

    High LPC in Fiedler's model means?

    A relationship-oriented leader.

    Two LBDQ dimensions?

    Consideration and initiating structure.

    What does Trail Making Part B test?

    Executive function: attention and set shifting.

    Advanced Social Psychology · Unit I

    Introduction and Prosocial Behaviour

    What is social psychology?

    Social psychology studies how other people, whether real, imagined or implied, affect the way we think, feel and behave. It looks at the individual in a social situation, while sociology looks at groups and society as a whole.

    Gordon Allport (1954/1985)

    "An attempt to understand and explain how the thoughts, feelings and behaviour of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others."

    The classic definition. Learn it word for word.

    Baron & Branscombe

    "The scientific field that seeks to understand the nature and causes of individual behaviour, feelings and thought in social situations."

    Four key features (from the definition)

    Scientific

    Uses the scientific method: experiments, surveys, observation. It values accuracy, objectivity, scepticism and open-mindedness.

    Focus on the individual

    Studies how one person is affected, not whole societies.

    Nature and causes

    Not just describing behaviour but explaining why it happens.

    Social situations

    Other people, even imagined ones, change our behaviour.

    Where social psychology sits

    Scope: what it studies

    Social thinking

    Social cognition, perception, attribution, the self, attitudes

    Social influence

    Conformity, compliance, obedience, persuasion

    Social relations

    Prejudice, aggression, helping, attraction, love

    Groups

    Group processes, leadership, decision-making, conflict

    Applied areas

    Health, law, workplace, environment, education, politics

    RememberScope = Thinking, Influence, Relations (+ groups and applications): "how we think about, are influenced by, and relate to one another" (David Myers).

    Importance

    • Understanding everyday life: why we help, conform, fall in love or hate.
    • Solving social problems: reducing prejudice, violence, communal conflict and bullying.
    • Health: changing health habits (e.g. hand-washing, vaccination campaigns).
    • Law: eyewitness accuracy, jury decisions.
    • Workplace: teamwork, leadership, motivation.
    • Self-understanding: knowing our own biases helps us think more fairly.

    Short history

    1898Triplett

    First social psychology experiment: cyclists and children winding fishing reels went faster with others present (social facilitation).

    1908First textbooks

    William McDougall (psychologist) and E. A. Ross (sociologist) both published books titled Social Psychology.

    1924F. H. Allport

    Made it an experimental science.

    1930s–40sKurt Lewin

    "Father of modern social psychology". Behaviour = f(Person × Environment).

    1950s–70sClassic studies

    Asch (conformity), Festinger (dissonance), Milgram (obedience), Latané & Darley (bystanders).

    TodayNew directions

    Social neuroscience, implicit processes, culture and diversity.

    Prosocial behaviour

    Prosocial behaviour is any act that benefits others, such as helping, sharing, donating, cooperating or volunteering. It may or may not cost the helper something, and it may or may not have selfish motives.

    Prosocial behaviour

    The widest term: any helpful act, whatever the motive.

    Helping

    An act that intentionally benefits another person.

    Altruism

    Helping purely for the other's benefit, often at a cost to oneself, with no expectation of reward.

    The bystander effect

    Real event · 1964

    Kitty Genovese, New York

    Newspapers reported that 38 neighbours witnessed her murder and none helped. Later research found the number and details were exaggerated, but the case inspired the research below.

    L&D
    Bibb Latané & John Darley (1968)Students heard another "participant" have a seizure over an intercom. Alone: about 85% helped quickly. With 4 others believed present: about 31% helped.

    Bystander effect: the more bystanders present, the less likely any one person is to help. The main reason is diffusion of responsibility: "someone else will do it."

    Five steps to helping (Latané & Darley)

    RememberN-I-A-K-D: "Never Ignore Anyone; Kindly Do help."

    Empathy

    Empathy is the ability to feel and understand another person's emotional state, to "put yourself in their shoes".

    Affective (emotional) empathy

    Feeling what the other person feels: their sadness makes you sad.

    Cognitive empathy (perspective-taking)

    Understanding what they think and feel, even without feeling it.

    Empathic concern

    Feeling sympathy and wanting to help. This is the part that most strongly predicts helping.

    Empathy shows early (babies cry when other babies cry), increases with age, and is partly inherited (twin studies) and partly learned from parents.

    Why do we help? Four explanations

    CB
    C. Daniel BatsonEmpathy-altruism hypothesis (1981 onwards): true altruism exists.
    1 · Empathy-altruism hypothesis (Batson)

    When we feel empathic concern, we help purely to relieve the other person's distress, even when we could easily escape.

    2 · Negative-state relief model (Cialdini)

    We help to relieve our own bad mood: seeing suffering makes us feel bad, and helping makes us feel better. Selfish motive.

    3 · Empathic joy hypothesis

    We help because we enjoy seeing the positive effect of our help on the other person.

    4 · Genetic determinism (kin selection)

    Evolution favours helping genetic relatives, since it helps our genes survive. We help family more than strangers.

    Determinants of prosocial behaviour

    What makes helping more or less likely? Group the factors into situational, personal and emotional.

    A. Situational factors

    Number of bystanders

    More bystanders → less helping (diffusion of responsibility).

    Ambiguity

    If it's unclear whether it's an emergency, people hold back.

    Time pressure

    Good Samaritan study (Darley & Batson, 1973): seminary students in a hurry rarely stopped to help a groaning man, even on the way to give a talk on the Good Samaritan.

    Similarity and liking

    We help people who are like us, attractive, or part of our in-group.

    Deservingness

    We help more if the victim is not responsible for their own problem.

    Role models

    Seeing others help increases helping.

    Place

    People in villages and small towns help strangers more than people in big crowded cities.

    B. Personal factors

    Altruistic personality

    High empathy, belief in a just world, social responsibility, internal locus of control, low egocentrism.

    Skills and competence

    People with relevant training (e.g. first aid) help more.

    Religion and values

    Values such as seva and dana encourage helping, especially when they are internalised.

    Gender

    Men help more in risky, heroic situations; women give more long-term, nurturing help.

    Culture

    Collectivist cultures help in-group members more strongly.

    C. Emotional factors

    Good mood

    Usually increases helping (feel good, do good), unless helping would spoil the mood.

    Bad mood

    Guilt often increases helping. Sadness can increase helping if helping lifts the mood (negative-state relief).

    RememberDeterminants = S-P-E: Situation, Person, Emotion.

    How to increase helping

    • Reduce ambiguity: say clearly "This is an emergency!"
    • Assign responsibility: point to one person ("You in the blue shirt, call 108").
    • Teach skills (first aid) and model helping.
    • Build empathy and a shared identity ("we are all one community").

    Unit I self-test

    Allport's definition of social psychology?

    An attempt to understand and explain how the thoughts, feelings and behaviour of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others.

    Who did the first social psychology experiment?

    Norman Triplett (1898): people performed faster in the presence of others.

    Prosocial vs altruism?

    Prosocial = any act that benefits others. Altruism = helping purely for the other's sake, often at a cost, with no expected reward.

    What is diffusion of responsibility?

    With more bystanders, each person feels less personally responsible to help.

    Latané & Darley's five steps?

    Notice, interpret as emergency, assume responsibility, know how to help, decide to help.

    Who proposed the empathy-altruism hypothesis?

    C. Daniel Batson.

    Negative-state relief model?

    Cialdini: we help to relieve our own bad mood.

    What did the Good Samaritan study show?

    Time pressure strongly reduces helping (Darley & Batson, 1973).

    Long-answer outlines

    Explain the meaning, scope and importance of social psychology. 10 marks
    1. Definitions (Allport; Baron & Branscombe) and four features.
    2. Relation to psychology and sociology (draw the overlap).
    3. Scope: thinking, influence, relations, groups, applied.
    4. Brief history.
    5. Importance with examples; conclusion.
    Discuss empathy and altruism. 10 marks
    1. Prosocial behaviour vs altruism.
    2. Empathy: affective, cognitive, empathic concern.
    3. Four explanations: empathy-altruism (draw Batson's model), negative-state relief, empathic joy, kin selection.
    4. Evaluation; conclusion.
    Explain the determinants of prosocial behaviour. 10 marks
    1. Meaning of prosocial behaviour.
    2. Bystander effect and five steps (draw).
    3. Situational, personal and emotional determinants with studies.
    4. Ways to increase helping.
    Advanced Social Psychology · Unit II

    Social Cognition and Social Perception

    What is social cognition?

    Social cognition is how we interpret, analyse, remember and use information about the social world: about ourselves, other people and situations.

    We have limited mental capacity, so we are "cognitive misers": we save effort whenever we can. So there are two modes of thinking.

    Low-effort (automatic) thinking

    Schemas

    A schema is a mental framework that organises our knowledge about a topic and guides how we process new information.

    Person schemas

    About types of people: "a typical professor".

    Role schemas

    About social roles: "doctor", "mother".

    Event schemas (scripts)

    About what happens in events: a restaurant visit, a wedding.

    Self-schemas

    About ourselves: "I am good at maths".

    Schemas affect three stages of processing

    Attention

    We notice what fits (or sharply violates) the schema.

    Encoding

    What we notice gets stored in memory.

    Retrieval

    We remember schema-consistent information better.

    Priming

    Recent experiences make a schema easier to activate. Seeing words about rudeness makes people interrupt more (Bargh et al., 1996).

    Perseverance effect

    Schemas resist change, even when the evidence for them is shown to be false.

    Key study · 1968

    Self-fulfilling prophecy: "Pygmalion in the classroom"

    Rosenthal & Jacobson told teachers that some randomly chosen pupils were "late bloomers". By the end of the year those pupils showed bigger IQ gains: the teachers' expectations (schemas) changed how they treated them.

    Heuristics: mental shortcuts

    Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman (1974)Showed that people rely on simple rules of thumb that are quick but cause predictable errors. Kahneman won the 2002 Nobel Prize in Economics.Photo: nrkbeta, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons
    Representativeness

    Judging by how similar someone is to a typical member of a category, while ignoring base rates.

    "He is quiet and wears glasses, so he must be a librarian, not a farmer."

    Availability

    Judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.

    After news of a plane crash, flying feels more dangerous than driving.

    Anchoring and adjustment

    Starting from a reference point (anchor) and adjusting too little.

    A shop's "original price ₹2,000" makes ₹1,200 seem cheap.

    Status quo heuristic

    Assuming the existing option is better than a new one.

    RememberR-A-A: "Really Available Anchors." (Representativeness, Availability, Anchoring)

    Types of automatic thinking
